PUNCH TO THE PREMIER. Dlr. Gladstone completed his seventy-second year on the 29th December.] BeVenty-two years old, friend Willy, seventy-t,wo years old! But never a sign that 5 our heart's getting chilly, a hint that t= your fancy grows cold. 'You can smite in the fight like a yowaker—can talk, as of old, for three hours by the clock, 'Though your voice may not be quite so silvery, Willy, your hair such a raven-hued shock. They whom the Gods love die young, friend Willy; so said your favourite Greeks: They whom the Gods love never grow old, is the moral your history speaks. Kappier. later Titbonus, friend Willy—a wiser Aurora's your friend, Your youth's warm and bright in her light, friend Willy—and so may it be to the end !

THE TWO GATES. A pilgrim once (so runs an ancient tale), Old, worn, and spent, crept down a shadowed vale; On either hand rose mountains bleak and high; Chill was the gnsty air, and dark the sky; The path was rugged, and his feet were bare; His faded cheek was seamed by pain and care; His heavy eyes upon the ground were cast, And every step seemed feebler than the last. The valley ended where a naked rock Rose sheer from earth to heaven, as if to mock The pilgrim who had crept that toilsome way; But while his dim and weary eyes essay To find an outlet, in the mountain side A ponderous sculptured brazen door he spied, And tottering toward it with fast-failing breath, Above the portal read, "The Gate of Death." He could not stay his feet, that led thereto; It yielded to his touch, and passing through, He came into a world all bright and fair; Blue were the heavens, and balmy was the air ; And, lo! the blood of youth was in his veins, And he was clad in robes that held no stains Of his long pilgrimage. Amazed, he turned; Behold! a golden door behind him burned In that fair sunlight, and his wondering eyes. Now lustreful and clear as those new skies, Free from the mists of age. of care, and strife, Above the portal read, "The Gate of Life." .Harper's Magazine for December.

If a man's biography is called history, why should not a wornan's be called her•story ? Ambitious Man: "Is there any fixed rule for writing poetry ?" There is. Don't? . The dishonest man gives no more light in the world than a candle, and when he dias he leaves as bad an odour be- hind him. Christians, like Eastern mountaineers, if they would safely climb the rugged way, must be bound together, not literally, but with cords of love. "I should have no objection to my wife's reigning," said an affectionate husband, "if it were not for the fact that when she reigns she is so apt to storm also." "There, I have it !" exclaimed Jones, who had been look- ing at Slapdash's painting. "The trouble is this; he uses too much ochre." " Yes,"said Fogg; "mediocre." " Yes, sir," said the old coloured man, "de firs' yeah, when I gave 50 dollars to de church, dey call me Mistah Richard Johnson, Esquah ; de secon' yeah times were bad, an' I couldn't giv more dan 25 dollars, an' dey call me Braider Johnson ; de next yeah I couldn't give noffin', dey call me Ole Niggah Johnson." A young lady being addressed by a gentleman much older than herself, observed that the only objection she had to a union with him was the probability of his dying before her, and leaving her to the sorrows of widowhood. To which he made the apt and complimentary reply, "Blessed is the man who has a virtuous wife, for the number of his days shall be doubled." ON ICERPrNo Tomos CLEAN.—It is better to keep clean than to make clean; and without order, there is no corn- tort; without comfort, no health; without health, no per- fect happiness. Yes, from garret to basement there:must be order and regularity in every department of domestic labour, and sound practical knowledge and powers of con- trivance brought to bear on the work of each day. And, on' mothers, I know there are times when you long for the wheels of the household machinery to be silent, if only for a moment—you get so weary of "the trivial round, the common task," and the labour seems so much in vain. Ah, well! you know after all that it will not do to slacken your hold upon the domestic reins, or all will soon go wrong; and if you have the satisfaction of conviction that you are doing all in your power to instil into your children habits of tidiness, order, and punctuality, and the necessity of, having "a place tor everything, and everything in its Voce ;" if you are daily impressing upon them the fact that all waste, whether of food, time, money, or talents, is sin, you are casting bread upon the waters that must bear rod fruit in the days to come, and providing them with weapons that shall stand them in good stead in the life- battle that is before them. Habits formed in childhood are seldom, if ever, totally eradicated. Home must be the real training school; see that it is the charmed magic circle it ought to be; let books and music find a place—and a pro- minent one—in your house, for by their influence they do much towards knitting together all members of a family in bonds of love, kindness, and harmony. THE FEAR OF COMING TROUBLES.—I believe that many people plod heavily through their daily work and worry; else in the morning, go out to out-door occupation, sit down at their writing-table at home, look at the faces of their children, and even at the steadily-wearing belongings among which they live, fearing the changes which must come. And assuredly when you have topped the summit and have begun to go downhill, this is many times so. Strength and spirit for work cannot last; the step can- not always be light and active as it would need to be if the %day's task is to be done in the day; and the right hand which has served you so faithfully through all these years must stiffen, to say the least. I often remember how the wife of one who did with his might what his hand found to do if ever mortal did so, told me of the awful day on which he pointed to that hard-wrought right hand ad said, " powerless." He was but sixty. He said few words more, and before sunset of that bright autumn day he was gone. I could easily frighten you, reader with gray hair and with mach depending on you, for I know the things of which I am often afraid. myself. But I am sure we are wrong in being so much afraid as we are, and what I desire in these pages is that we inky cheer and help one another. And this is not to be done by bidding a man who dreads that a ghost is following him to whistle and look another way. Just the opposite of that. We shall not be cowed by un- defined fears. We are not going to walk onward, hearing heavy footsteps behind us, and afraid to look round and see what is there. We do not pretend to be very brave. For that matter, all I know are arrant moral cowards. But we shall pluck up courage enough to look in the face the things we fear, to scan them from head to foot, we must know the truth. The truth, at the very worst, is never so bad as the vague terror of what is coming, which embitters the entire life of many anxious men and women. I have a strong conviction that if we go right up to some very threatening Shapes they may even melt into mist, and prove to have nothing at all. Likewive, that certain troubles which seem sure to come, and which have weight and dimension, may be abated by taking their measure, and composedly reckon- ing them up. This is a world in which to actually count what appears a large number always greatly diminishes it, and in which to get a heavy mass into the scales and, reso- lutely weigh it, does, if 'the weight be what is called Moral, almost invariably bring down tons to pounds.—Good Words. litoN 'TURTLE SOUP.—An attenuated individual with a great affluence of hair, and a soft, seductive smile, gently swaggered into a restaurant down town not more than a week ago, hung his hat on a nail, took a seat, and commenced to drum for the waiter. The latter appeared in due time, and began to brush around the tumblers with a great deal of energy. The diner ordered some turtle' soup, and while he was sipping it, chipped in, "Pretty good soup this; what's the vintage ?" "Ten am.!' replied the waiter, as he pre- pared to hurl the check down like a boomerang. "Made of land turtles ?" inquired the festive guy. "Land turtles?" repeated the waiter, in astonishment. "Yes, land turtles," continued the diner; "those big, corpulent, speckled, punch- nosed reptiles that walk around rye-fields with initials and dates cut on their backs." The waiter assured him that he was positive that was not the brand of turtle employed in the construction of their best soup in the city for ten cents a plate, including a roll. "No, I suppose it is not," con- tinued the guest. "I suppose it is not; I presume you use these littleblack, red-spotted specimens that infest woodland brooks and bird-stores at three for a quarter. These little polka dot rascals that float on corks, chock full of medita- tion. I suppose you get them in quantities, and open them like Little Neck clams, and spring the result on innocent people for terrapin. Does any intellect light on the scheme?" The waiter didn't reply, and the guest went on, "Perhaps you use snapping turtles—those fellows that grab at any- thing so hard that it makes them tired. These ignoble beasts that draw the skin over their eyes when you look at them, and who have skin enough for each eye to make a Masonic apron, strings and all, and—" "We use an iron turtle," broke in the waiter, who was tired of being guyed. "An iron turtle?" "Certainly, an iron turtle." "To make turtle soup ?" "Why, of course, to make turtle soup, not to make lamb stew, or a fricandeau of nightingale, or an epigram of tapir's kidney." "But," said the diner, "how do von make soup out of an iron turtle ?" "Why, we wiha bins up." "Wind him up ?" "Precisely- he has a key-hole in his back; you wind to the right until you can't , wind any longer. Then you throw him into the soup, and the m,chieeey starts, and he kicks and splashes around for hours. We have a few eight-day turtles that- "But; where does the nutriment come from?" inquired the , astonished guest in tones of excitement. "Why, from the isogredients—the calf's head, and the beef, and the carrots, and the lemon." "Then, what is the use of putting in the turtle ?" "Why, he furnishes the motion." " What, motion in soup ?" "Of course; we throw him into the soup, and he splashes around with his great paddle feet—o "To tone the system with iron ?” "Oh, no; just to keep the soup from burning. It's a great deal cheaper to work the turtle than to hire a boy to do the stirring." Then tha out-guyed diner left with a sadful look, as though he had just come downstairs with some manuscript and half a dozen series of editorial footprints all over him.—Puek. SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

A CAVE OF Gars.—Among recent American discoveries,, the most remarkable is that of a cave of gems in South Carolina. No further detail of the locality is given besides that of the State. But we are told that a Mr. udder, whose name seems suggestive, has found a perfect treasure-house in a cave there. The walls of the cavity were frosted with crystals, some of them of very large size. Among them were what are described as the finest emeralds ever dis- covered in the United States. They were nine in number, in colour a clear grass green. The largest was eight and a half inches long, and-had an average diameter of one inch; others were six inches, three inches, and two inches long. The largest emerald found in the mine previous to this last discovery was less than two inches in length, and was not quite three-quarters of an inch in diameter. If anyone wishes to find emeralds as big as potatoes, and other precious crystals in proportion, all he has apparently to do is to search South Carolina until this cave is unfolded. The area he will have to traverse is only some 34,000 square miles, and the reward is great. SLOW COMBUSTION OF FIRE-DAMP.—A VALUABLE Dn. COVERY.—A new method of dealing with fire-damp in mines has been devised by Herr Guido Kornet, of Saxony. An oil lamp has its wick, or wicks, covered with caps made of asbes- tos, the fibres of which are plated with a coating of platinum and palladium. These are raised to a red heat, while they prevent the flame from effective comaiunication with any combustible gas that may surround them. In this condition they are placed in the mine containing gas in a state of ex- plosive mixture. According to the published accounts, these glowing caps effect a slow combustion of the gas as it comes In contact with them, and this goes on quietly without risk of explosion. The quantity thus slowly burned is consider- able, and experiments are in progre Ploy which the prac- tical efficacy of this method of getting rid of one of the miner's enemies will be tested. The action of these platinised fibres is analogous to what occurs in the old experiment of "the lamp without flame." Such lamps are still to be bought of chemical-instrument makers. A piece of spony or finely divided platinum stands over the wick of a spirit- lamp. The lamp is lighted and the platinum made red-hot, then the flame is extinguished, and the platinum continues glowing, its heat being supplied by the slow combustion of the vapour given off by the wick. If a coil of platinum wire is made red-hot, and suspended above some ether con- tained in the hollow of a tall ale glass, or other similar nar- row vessel, it continues red-hot till all the ether has eva- porated.—Gentleman's _Magazine. ELECTRIC TlDES.—According to Mr. Adams, of the Postal Telegraph Department, the telegraph circuits indicate the existence of tidal fluctuations of the currents of electricity which our telegraph system has shown to be continually flowing in the earth. Mr. Adams has observed variations , in the strength of these which follow the variations in the moon's position in relation to the earth, as the fluctuations of the waters do. The subject is worthy of further investi- gation in connection with the fluctuations of the force and direction of the earth's magnetism, which have been for some time past among the objects of careful study in the magnetic observatories established in different parts of the civilised world. "True as the needle to the pole" is rather an equivocal description of the constancy of a sailor's love, seeing that the needle varies considerably, and that even its variation is inconstant. If it were true to the north or any other pole, the old theory which ascribes its direction to the distribution of iron in the earth's interior might stand, but when we find it at one time pointing considerably east of north, then gradually approaching and finally reaching due north, then going beyond and getting far to the west, and now turning back towards the north again, we must look for some other exciting cause. As a freely suspended magnetised needle arranges itself at right angles to an electric current, I the North and South direction of the compass needle may be explained by East and West currents of electricity circu- lating in the earth, and these by solar radiation; but here again the inconstancy of the sailor's love-emblem baffles the theorist, and he asks for more facts concerning these earth currents.—Gentleman's Magazine. SOME PHENOMENA OF THE RECENT ERUPTION OF Marreia-Loa.—The flow of lava from this noted Hawaiian volcano, lately in eruption, is the greatest observed there within the last 50 years. It began on November 5, 1880, and continued without interruption till the middle of August this year. Probably no lava flow has been so largely photo- graphed, and an artist, M. Furneaux, has represented various phases of it in 38 oil paintings. A published 'letter from Mr. Green, of Honolulu, states that when the lava accumu- lates on a large surface a permanent cloud of condensed vapour, with smoke, forms above. When the cloud becomes too dense the cooled vapour descends through the hot and light air below, and when the waterspout reaches the incan- descent lava it is anew converted into vapour. In such cases there is usually a surface of several square miles of lava at a red heat and more or less infusion. Photographs of the Java near Hilo show that after flowing 30 or 40 miles it was still in a very liquid state. Further up it has formed the usual scoriaceons embankments, and a tunnel of its cooled crust. Wherever it could be seen through apertures in this crust it seemed as liquid as water, and at a red-white heat. It was apparently a case of pure igneous fusion; no vapour lor gas was observable when the stream did not enter water or come on vegetation. Eight photographs were taken of a lake with vertical sides, two miles from Hilo, which was , filled with lava in one hour and 40 minutes. The pretty little town of Hilo was like to be engulfed, the lava forming a semi-circle of fire about it, and the possibility of damming and diverting the current was being considered, but happily the flow ceased in time, and parts of the arched crust falling in afterwards blocked the passages, so that Hilo, at the end of August seemed comparatively safe, at least for some months.

MILD CHEISTIKASEIII.—The laudator temporis acti always will have it that Christmases have recently become wretchedly and unnaturally mild, and leads us to under- stand that "when he was a boy" Christmas Day was Christmas Day indeed. The record of the 45 years from 1827 till 1872 scarcely supports this view. In 1827 Christ- mas Day was mild, although a frost set in a day or two later ; in 1828 the day was mild and wet; 1829 finished up with a very cold winter; 1830 was a bitter Christmas, but the frost broke up with the old year ; 1831-2-3 had very mild Yttletides ; the Christmas of 1834 was mild, although a frost set in afterwards ; 1855-6 furnished severe winters; but 1837-3-9 were mild. Christmas Day 1840 was severe, but the following one was mild and wet. The winters of 1842-3 were mild, 1844 cold, and 1845 mild; 1846 was severe, 1847-8 mild, 1849 cold, 1850-1-2 mild, 1853 severe, 1854-5-6 mild 1857 was, on the whole, mild, and the same may be said of the two following years; 1860 had a cold Christmas, while the three following years were mild at the time. The weather at Christmas, 1864, was very cold, the following year mild, and the next year very severe; 1867- 8-9 were mild, 1870 severe; while the two following years were mild.

No one could fail to understand an argument like the fol- lowing, taken from the fiost letter:—" Now you must know that halfpence and farthings in England pass for very little more than they are worth, and if you should beat them to pieces and sell- them to a brazier you would not lose much above a penny in the shilling. But Mr. Wood made his halfpence of such base metal, and so much smaller than the English ones, that a ftrazier would hardly give you above a 1 penny of good money for a shilling of his; so that this sum ' of £lOB,OOO in good gold and silver must be given for trash that will not be worth above eight or nine thousand pounds real value. But this is not the worst, for Mr. Wood when he pleases may by stealth send over another £lOB,OOO, and buy all our goods for eleven parts in twelve under the value. For example, if a hatter sells a dozen of hats for five shillings a piece, which amounts to three pounds, and receives pay- ment in Wood's coin, he really receives only the value of five shillings." So he went on, appealing alternately to every section of the community' pointing out how their special interests would be affected by its introduction, con- cluding with the beggars, who were assured that the coin selected for adulteration was the halfpenny in order that they, too, might be ruined. These are his words :—" I will tell you one thing further, that if Mr. Wood's project should take it would ruin even our beggars; for when I give a beggar a halfpenny it will quench his thirst or go a good way to fill his belly; but the twelfth part of a halfpenny will do him no more service than if I should give him three pins out of my sleeve." These letters intensified the public excitement,and created the most terrific panic. Both Houses of Parliament joined in addressing the Crown against Wood's scheme. Parties of all denominations for once united in expressing their abhorrence of the detested halfpenny. The traders to whom the coin was assigned refused to receive them, and endea- voured by public advertisement to remove the scandal of being concerned in the accursed traffic. Associations were formed for refusing their currency, and these extended from the wealthy Corporation of Dublin down to the hawkers and errand boys, who announced to their employers that they would not receive nor offer in change Wood's drossy half- penny, since they could "neither get news, ale, tobacco, or brandy for such cursed stuff." So unanimous were the people in their refusal to accept the coin, that in Letter Four the" Drapier" is compelled to exclaim," Money, the great divider of the world,hath by a strange revolution been the great ztniter of a most divided people." The Ministry endeavoured to allay the excitement, but to no purpose. It was in vain that the coin was formally ex- amined by Sir Isaac Newton, Master of the Mint, and pro- flounced not to be as stated. It was in vain that the sum to be coined was reduced from £lOB,OOO to £40,000. The dis- trust of he people was far too•deep to be thus assuaged. Having lashed the nation into fury, the "Drapier" pro- ceeded at once to a higher and more important theme. In his famous Fourth Letter he re-asserted with commanding power the principle of Molyneux—claimed for the Legisla- tion the right of self•government, and drew with a firm and unfaltering hand the line between the prerogatives of the law and the liberty of the people; laid bare the scandals and abuses of the Irish Government, and, urging "that go- vernment without the consent of the governed is the very essence of slavery," struck a chord which for the first time vibrated through every class in Ireland. The Government at last took alarm. The Duke of Graf- ton, whom Walpole described as "a fair weather pilot, that did not know how to act when the first storm arose," was recalled. But Lord Cateret, who succeeded him, was equally unable to quell the agitation. A reward of £3OO was offered in vain for the discovery of the author of the fourth letter. Hardy, the printer, was thrown into prison. When the bill against the printer was about to be,presented to the grand jury, the "Drapier" addressed to that body a paper entitled "Seasonable Advice to the Grand Jury, ' ex- horting them to remember the story of the league made by the wolves with the sheep on condition of their parting with their shepherds and mastiffs, after which they ravaged the flock at pleasure. Alluding to the charge that he had gone too far in leaving the discussion of Wood's project to treat of the alleged dependence of Ireland, he exhorted them in these lines : If, then, oppression has not quite subdued At once your prudence and your gratitude, If you yourselves conspire not your undoing And don't deserve and won't draw your ruin; ' If yet to virtue you have some pretence, * If yet you are not lost to common sense, Assist your patriot in your own defence That stupid cant " he won't too far" despise, And know that to be brave is to be wise. Think how he struggled for our liberty' And give him freedom whilst yourselves are free. At the same time was circulated the memorable and apt quo- tation from Scripture by a Quaker :—" And the people said unto Saul, shall Jonathan die who bath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: As the Lord liveth there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground: for he wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan that he died not." 1 Sam. xiv., 45. Thus admonished by verse, law, and Scripture, the Grand Jury assembled. It,was in vain that the Lord Chief Justice Whitshed, who had caused the Dean's former tract to be de- nounced as seditious, and procured a verdict against the printer, exerted himself strenuously upon this similar occa- sion. The hour of intimidation was past, and the Grand Jury, conscious of what the country expected from them, brought in a verdict of " ignoramus " upon the bill. The first Grand Jury was discharged, and another was sum- moned. Fourteen of the new jurymen were notorious Jacobites. Their humour was so confessed that the Chief Justice dared not press them to a decision. But, being as- sembled, they refused to be passive. Instead of presenting the winter of the Drapier Letters, "the Grand Jury of the County of Dublin presented all persons who had attempted or should endeavour to impose Wood's halfpenny upon Ire- land as enemies to his Majesty's Government and the wel- fare of the kingdom." The feeling of the people grew stronger daily. La Fouche, the banker, who had voted with

A poor excuse is better than none, and the same may be said of a dinner. KISIINDERSTOOD.—Miss Argent (anxious to discover the opinion of the new curate on her favourite costume) : "I hope you don't disapprove of jerseys, Mr. Bullock?" Rev. Mr. Bullock (on his hobby) : "Welt, no, not exactly, although my experience leads me to prefer shorthorns." Economy does not mean simply carefulness in dress, and making things last as long as they will, but it has a broader meaning than this. Time, accomplishments, and opportu- nities are talents for which you will be held responsible to Him who has given them. For this reason try to econo- mize them well. A fox, going for some food, saw a crab, and said, "I will give you a race." The crab thereupon got hold of the fox's tail, unknown to the fox. The crab shouted, "Off !" and the fox set off at full speed. When they got to the win- ning post the fox gave a sharp turn round, tossed the crab off Its tail past the post, and shouted, "Where are you ? " The crab shouted, "Here," and won the race. It is one of the severest tests of friendship to tell your friend of his faults. If you are angry with a man or hate him, it is not hard to go to him and stab him with words; but so to love a man that you cannot bear to see the stain of sin upon him, and to speak painful truth through loving words, that is friendship. )3ut few have snch friends. Our enemies usually teach us what we are, at the point of the sword.

- - -- THE STRENGTH OF TOLDSTOOLS.—Mushrooms, toad- stools, and the like are known to scientific men as "fungi.' They possess a remarkable power of raising enormous weights, a fact of which Dr. M. L. Cooke has given several curious examples. A few years ago a town in Hampshire was paved, and shortly afterwards certain streets showed signs of unevenness that could not well be explained, until some of the heaviest stones were at length seen to be com- pletely raised by the growth of toadstools under them. In another case a kitchen hearthstone was lifted out of its setting three times, and was only righted by digging up the old bed and laying down a new foundation. Sir Joseph Banks records one of the most extraordinary instances of this power. The wine in a cask kept in a cellar for three years was, at the end of that period, found to have leaked away, and to have produced gigantic fungi, which filled the cellar, and lifted the cask to the roof.—Little Folks Maga- zine.

TRAITS OF CHARLES •DICKENS.—No writer ever lived whose method was more exact, whose industry was more constant, and whose punctuality was more marked, than those of Charles Dickens. He never shirked labour, mental or bodily. He rarely declined, it the object were a good one, taking the chair at a public meeting, or accepting a charitable trust. Many widows and orphans of deceased literary men have been benefited by his wise trusteeship or counsel, and he spent a great portion of his time personally looking after the property of the poor whose interests were under his control. He was, as has been intimated, one of the most industrious of men, and marvellous stories are told (not by himself) of what he has accomplished in a given time in literary and social matters. His studies were all from nature and life, and his habits of observation were un- tiring. If he contemplated writing " Hard Times," he arranged with the master of Astley's Circus to spend many hours behind the scenes with the riders and among the horses; and if the composition of the "Tale of Two Cities" were occupying his thoughts, he could banish himself to France for two years to prepare for that great work.—James T. Field.

DOLLY.—Rag, wood, and india-rubber, china, composi- tion, and wax—we can imagine the immense doll population gathering about us, impatient for attention, and all leaning up against each other, for it is a peculiarity of doll physique that, as regards standing up independently in the world, a doll is unmatched for helplessness by anything under the sun—.except a soda-water bottle. The weak point of the primitive rag baby was the human face divine in coloured chintz, until at last it has been painted on white calico. The wooden genera of the family had an objectionable stare, and were too liable to be scalped. The china cousins suffered from fragile noses (and heads), and an unnatural shining skin. India-rubber got over the danger of breakage, but the immortals have, like old Tithonus, the gift of life with the gift of youth forgotten, and the period of doll existence being over, their washed-out Care complexion is frightful to see. Composition, with a thin skin of wax is the most popular in nursery society; but the dlite of dolls will ever be the waxen fair ones endowed with human hair. All dolls' hair has at least one human property—that of falling off. But, fortunately, human baldness is a gradual sorrow; not like poor dolly's, one shock of consternation. This is a most trying misfortune to a doßloving child. A creature with only one eye, one leg, and one arm may still be cherished; but a scalped doll is a monstrosity. Yet even greater de- fects than this can be cured; indeed medical science pales beside the wonders done in a London "Dolls' Hospital." "What a beautiful doll !" we once remarked to a communi- cative•looking little stranger. "Yes," said the communica- tive little one proudly; "and this is her second head !" Journal.

man had offered to pay him in Wood's money, and the officer was hustled and beaten. The Dublin Corporation presented Swift with the freedom of the city in a gold box, while the story of the deliverance of Jonathan was made into a recitation and channted about the streets. So strong waxed the feeling of the people that at length Walpole was compelled to yield and withdraw the patent—allowing no less than £3,000 a year for eight years as compensation to Wood for the profits he had to forego. Such are the main facts of the episode which occupies so conspicuous a place in Irish history, and which certainly marks an epoch in that history. It was the first time the voice of the people had spoken, and spoken with success. It marks the transition from an age of semi-barbarism to an age of civilisation—from the government of force to the government of public opinion. "The age of Desmond and of O'Niel had passed away—the age of Grattan and of

O'Connel had begun." The " Drapier's" influence with the people after the pub- lication of these letters was unbounded. Many illustrations of this could be given. Walpole once declared that he would have him arrested, and was asked in reply whether he had ten thousand men to spare, for they would all be needed for the enterprise. When Serjeant Bettesworth, an eminent lawyer, whom Swift had fiercely satirised, threatened him with personal violence, the people voluntarily formed a guard for his protection. When Primate Boulten accused him of exciting the people he retorted with mach truth— "If I were to lift up my finger you would be torn to pieces." It is said that on one occasion he gave a guinea to a maid servant to buy a new gown with the characteristic in- junction that it should be of "Irish stuff." When he after- wards reproached her with not having complied with his in- junction she brought him his own volumes which she had purchased, saying they were the best "Irish stuff" she knew. _

Swift did not work much after the publication o " Drapier Letters." He published several minor pieces on Irish affairs—the principal of which was—" A Short View of the State of Ireland," in which he enumerated fourteen causes of a nation's prosperity, and showed in how many of these Ireland was deficient. This was in 1727. In 1743, a calamity, which he had long feared, came upon him. He had said on more than one occasion that "no head that is good for anything is long without some disorder," and now he found the muscles of his mind breaking. His brain had been through life overworked, and it now began to succumb rapidly to the same influence which bathed in darkness the once bright intellect of Lanigan, Scott, Southey, Moore, Magee, and Plunkett. During a walk with some literary friends, Swift was suddenly missed, and when Dr. Young re- turned in quest of him he found the Dean absorbed in silent meditation before a stalwart elm, the summit of which was in a state of decay. "I shall be like that tree," said Swift, "I shall die at the top first." At length the evil day ar- rived, A tumour, accompanied by most excruciating pain, arose over one of is eyes. For a month he never gained a moment of repose. The agony subsided at last, but the mind had wholly ebbed away. It was not madness. It was absolute idiocy that ensued. He remained passive in the hands of the attendant without speaking or moving or be- traying the slightest emotion. In this state for two years he lingered on, and then exchanged the sleep of idiocy for the sleep of death. He died in 1747, and was buried in his own cathedral. While we cannot but extol the Dean for the grand work he accomplished for Ireland, we must at the same time ad- mit that he was far from being perfect. For the Catholics as such he did nothing. Neither in England when he was guiding the Ministry, nor in Ireland when he was leading the nation, did he make any effort to prevent the infraction of the Treaty of Limerick. He strenuously advocated the Test Act, whieh excluded the Dissenters from office, and one of his arguments in its favour was that if it were repealed even Catholics by parity of reasoning might claim to be en- franchised. The very existence of Catholic worship in Ireland he hoped some day would be destroyed by law. But the very people he hated admired him. They knew that this was the single crack in the clear granite of his iintel- lect, and they forgot or forgave this on account of his vigorous assertion of the independence of their country. They felt intuitively that if their country was once inde- pendent their state of bondage would soon come to an end. Clearly Ireland owes much to Swift. He succeeded in uniting its people for practical ends. He breathed into them something of his lofty and defiant spirit. He made them sensible of the wrongs they endured, of the rights they might claim, and of the forces they possessed. He proved to them for the first time that it was possible to struggle with success within the lines of the constitution. The cause of Free Trade and the cause of Legislative Inde- pendence never again passed out of the minds of the people. The non-importation agreement of 1789, and the legislative emancipation of 1782 were the developments of his policy. Hiuinfluence, like his writings, has survived a century, and the foundations of whatever prosperity Ireland has since erected are laid in the disinterested and magnanimous patriotism of Jonathan Swift, Dean of St. Patrick's. North Shields.

Mr. Ricb.trdi3. Hungerford, a landlord and justice of the peace, residing at Lakelands, Skibbereen, has received a' letter threatening him with death unless he reduces his tenants' rents. On cut at the Reform and other centres of Liberalism (states a society journal), that Mr. Forster visited the Queen at her Majesty's express wish, to receive personally the Royal thanks for his effective measures for the restoration of order in Ireland. •

At an early hour on Monday morning the military made a sudden visit to Millstreet, near Cork, and, after surround- ing the place, made several arrests. It is stated that the man Connel, the " moonlight " leader who was arrested last week, has given important information to the authorities, and that it was upon this that the Government acted with such promptitude. Miss Reynolds, the lady Laud Leaguer now undergoing a month's imprisonment in Cork gaol, has written a letter pro- testing against the movement to present her with an address and testimonial from the men of Dublin, and expressing a wish that the subscriptions should be devoted instead to the Sustenance Fund on behalf of the political prisoners, whom she describes as the victims of an "intensely utter Liberal , Government."

It is stated that the arrest of Connell, the "Moonlight " leader, has proved of great importance, and "has led to the apprehension of the entire band of midnight raiders who were carrying terror into every household in the Millstreet district." Connell has, it is believed, turned informer, and given to the Government important information. At Cork, on Tuesday, the police made a search, resulting in the dis- covery of a case containing a large number of Snider rifles, a quantity of dynamite, and gun cotton and ammunition. A box of arms and ammunition has also been seized at Clon- mel, and the man who delivered the box for conveyance to Dublin has been arrested.

AN EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGR.—A Coleraine correspon- dent telegraphs particulars have just been received of an extraordinary outrage committed on a young lady, named Maggie Galt, at a rural soirée in a country district, some three miles from Limavady. The friends of the parties, as well as the police, are very reticent respecting the affair, but the facts appear to be these. A young man named Patton, a national school teacher's assistant, living in the district, had been paying attention to Miss Galt, who resented his advances. Learning that she had gone to the soiree, he attended to escort her home, but found her in the care of another person. This exasperated him very much. To evade him Miss Galt went into an ante-room, but Patton fol- lowed her, and asked her to shake hands. This she refused to do, when he drew a clasp knife and inflicted three stabs in the neck and one in the left breast. The young lady was taken home, where it is said she died on Sunday evening. Patton at once absconded, leaving part of the clothes he wore on the banks of a river so as to mislead the police, who are searching the district for him. At an early hour on Tuesday morning a number of police officers, searching manifestly on the information of some one in the secret, discovered in a vault beneath a lane in the northern district of Cork 30 Snider rifles and a large quan- tity of ball and dynamite cartridges. At a private meeting of the Dublin City Council on Tuesday a long discussion took place with regard to the Lord Lieutenant's refusal to allow Messrs. Parnell and Dillon leave of absence from Kil- mainham Goal to receive the freedom of the city. A reso- lution was passed that his Excellency should be requested to allow the ceremonial to take place within the walls of the prison. Two farmers, named Houlihan and Breen, were on Tuesday sentenced at the Munster Assizes to ten years' penal servitude for breaking into the house of John Morris, farmer, county Kerry, with firearms and blackened faces, and carrying away £lO in money, which they stated was for the purpose of " buying powder for Parnell." Some curious disclosures with regard to the writing of threatping letters were made at the Killimore Police Court on Monday. A man named Thomas Donohoe was charged with perjury, and also with writing and posting threatening letters to Mr. Lyons; and it appeared on his own confession that there were ample grounds for the charge.. Threatening letters have been very plentiful in Killimore and the neigh- bourhood, and early in December an army pensioner named Brennan was charged with writing them. Donohoe Was a witness for the prosecution, but the case failed, and the police were led to suspect that he had written the letters in question. They found that his handwriting exactly corres- ponded with the letters, and on searching his house they discoverea a copybook containing a fac-simile of a "death notice" which had been posted up in the district. A re- volver and a quantity of ammunition were also found. When called upon for his defence Donohoe admitted having written and posted the threatening letters and notices, but pleaded that he had in doing so only obeyed the orders of his master, Mr. Lyons, who wished to obtain a police guard. He added that Mr. Lyons also asked him to dig a grave in front of the hall door, and when he refused procured some one else to do the work. There was no corroboration of the prisoner's statements, and as there could' be no question as to perjury having been committed in the evidence he gave against Brennan he was sent to the assizes for trial.

The Countess of Itosebery gave birth to a son on Satur- day. The Plymouth Town Council on Saturday refused the use of the Guildhall for a meeting in sioport of Mr. Bradlaugh's claims.

The remains of Mr. William Harrison Ainsworth were in- terred on Monday, in the family grave, Kensal Green. Two salmon poachers to escape the police, rushed into the river Ettrick, near Selkirk, on Monday night, and one was drowned.
Mr. Wm. Rutherford, a Durham farmer, was on Monday attacked in one of his fields by a bull, and sustained injuries of a fatal nature.

It is said that the mortgages on the Hughenden property of Lord Beaconsfield, amounting to £53,000, have been paid off by the executors. On Saturday morning, the biscuit factory of Messrs. W. P. Barr and Co., Liverpool, was destroyed by fire. The loss is covered by insurance. By instructions from the Home Secretary, the police authorities of Leek are inquiring into the circumstances of the recent extraordinary deathbed confession. The Daily Telegraph says: Directions, it is stated, have been given for the removal of the name of Lieutenant H. Ponsonby from the retired list of lieutenants of the Royal
Navy. The Home Secretary has authorised the offer of a reward of £lOO for the apprehension of John Ross, who, on Christ- mas.night at Leeds, murdered a man named John Manley by _ .

stabbing him in the neck. On Monday, the Town Council of Heywood determined to petitioft for a separate commission of the peace for the, borough, which now contains a population of more than 23,000, and has a ratable value of more than £lOO,OOO. Colonel Yolland has reported to the Board of Trade that the Cationbury collisions were the direct result of the un- authorised mode of working the four passenger trains intro- duced by Signalman Hovey, who made "a great mistake." The Prince of Wales has written promising £25 to the fund being raised at Plymouth to celebrate the tercentary of Sir Francis Drake; and states that in the event of its becoming a national movement he will increaso the dona- tion.

On Monday, at Wrexham, Edwin Humphreys Williams, respectably connected, and lately assistant overseer, was charged with embezzling £260 of the poor rates collected in 1880; and also with falsifying his books. A Temand was granted till January 20. George Henri Cook, described as a dancing master, was tried at the Central Criminal Court, London, on Tuesday, and sentenced to five years' penal servitude for obtaining money by false pretences from young women whom he per.
suadid that be was about to marry. A serious accident has occurred at the Resolven colliry

Pontypridd. Whilst two colliers were employed in blasting operations, a spark from a lamp fell into a "tin jack" con- taining a quantity of powder, causing a terrific explosion. The men were severely burnt about the face and arms, but fatal consequences are not anticipated. We (Daily News) are informed that, in view of the pro- posal to grant a marriage allowance to Prince Leopold, a motion will be made asking Parliament to agree to the appointment of a Royal Commission to consider the whole question of future annuities and allowances to members of the Royal Family. The English Church Union now boasts of having on its books 19,930 members, but it has, all the same, to lament a debt of £22,000, in addition to which it.isin need of funds to further defend "the civil rights of our persecuted clergy," and to support them and their families while they suffer the results of defying the law. The return of the expenses incurred by the successful candidate for Nortn Durham, Sir George Elliott, has just been published. The total of the abstract is £7,161. fhe total expenses of the Liberal candidate, Mr. James • Laing, whose return was published some time ago, were £6,570. Both returns show a considerable reduction on previous elections. As the contract for public lamps in Hastings with the gas company will shortly expire, a committee has been .appointed by the Town Council to take such steps as shall lead to the utilising of the electric light in the future, one member of the Corporation going so far as to express his conviction that the abandonment of the contract would be to save the ratepayers £2,000 per annum. It was stated, at the annual meeting of the Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, that several of the local manufac- turers had very large orders on hand for countries where heavy protective duties prevailed. In one case there would be a large delivery of cotton goods at a place where 70 per cent duty would be payable. THE NEXT BUDGET.—A striking and popular Budget, remarks the • World, will be probably one of the events of the session. Mr. Gladstone will have a good surplus at his command, and he will by skilful financial manceuvering make it larger. It is likely that another blow will be struck at the landed interest by raising the succession duties to the 'same level as the legacy duties, and taking a good round I sum off the income tax. On Sunday evening, the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, accompanied by his son, Mr. W. H. Gladstone, M.P., at- tended divine service at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, New- ington, having ascertained in the afternoon that Mr. Spur- geon would preach. The congregation was large. At the conclusion of the service, the officers of the church were in- troduced to the Prime Minister, who expressed his surprise and gratification that Mr. Spurgeon had so many earnest , colleagues. Bishop Ryle, speaking on Monday at a meeting of the Liverpool Scripture Readers' Society, alluded to the failure in the supply of active and energetic young clergymen, and said that, failing clergymen, their place must be supplied by the laity, and to this end the enrolment of a body of earnest lay helpers was a pressing necessity if the Church of England were to hold her own in these perilous times. The Rev. Geo. Sanger, vicar of Carleton-in-Cleveland, was again before the magistrates at Stokesley on Monday, charged with setting fire to his church. A number of witnesses were called, and the case for the prosecution was concluded. Without calling upon the defence, the Bench unanimously expressed the opinion that the prosecution had failed to make out a case against the accused, and Mr. Sanger was accordingly discharged. The rev, gentleman was warmly cheered by the people on leaving the court. At the Birmingham Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, Albert Evans was sentenced to five years' penal servitude for steal- ing 400 gold chains, value about £l,BOO, whilst in transit for Liverpool from Birmingham. Thomas Dutton was sentenced to eight years' penal servitude for stealing several hundred pounds worth of jewellery and other goods whilst in transit upon the London and North-Western Railway, Frederick Parker, who was implicated in one of these robberies, was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment. THE DISESTABLISHMENT MOVEMENT IN SCOTLAND.—At a meeting of the North Presbytery of the Glasgow United Presbyterian Church on Tuesday, the Rev. M. Oliver sub- mitted a report on disestablishment. It recommended that the Presbytery condemn the levying of rates on heritors and feuars for the repair of the Established manses and churches, as being unjust and injurious to the interests of religion, and that a petition be sent to Parliament praying for a com- prehensive measure of disestablishment by which this and all other such grievances may be removed, In the Salford County Court, on Monday, the Judge (Mr. J. A Russell, IQ.C.)::awarded £lO to the parents of a boy named Maxwell as compensation for injuries which he had sustained through the bite of a dog. The owner of the dog, Samuel Hurst, attempted to show that the boy had been teasing it, but the learned Judge, observing that the defend- ant must have been aware of its savage disposition, said that in all such cases it was advisable to give liberal damages, because if people would keep savage animals they must effectually secure them, so as to prevent possiple mischief, or take the consequences. " GUITEAUISM" AT A GUARDIANS MEETING.—An extra- ordinary scene has been enacted at a nieeting of the lieigh- ley Board of Guardians, who were once made famous by I being imprisoned in York Castle for refusing to carry out the Vaccination Act. A member whose conduct has earned for him the sobriquet of " Guiteau" was so noisy that one of the guardians volunteered, if the Board would empower him, to put the obnoxious member out. The Board forbade this, but after the reporters had left the room the noisy guardian was forcibly ejected. Subsequently he offered to stake a sovereign on the issue of a stand-up fight with the chairman in the workhouse yard. • TIIE COUNTY GOVERNMENT BILL—The County Govern- ment Bill, on which the Cabinet is now engaged, will, it is understood, be of the most thorough character. It will establish in counties representative bodies elected by the whole body of the ratepayers, and will besides propose the appointment of a stipendiary magistrates, who will super- sede the existing Justices' place in their judicial functions. These are far more sweeping proposals than the Tories ever contemplated. The bills of the late Government never went further than the constitution of a County Board, half of which was to be elected and the other half of which was to consist of magistrates. They never proposed to interfere at all with the judicial and magisterial functions of the Jus- tices of the Peace. The bill of the Government will, how- ever, practically abolish the administrative and judical functions of the magistrates, and both quarter sessions and petty sessions will become things of the past. I need not say that a comprehensive scheme of this kind will be keenly opposed, and that the county gentlemen will resent and re- sist the abolition of the magisterial functions. Mr. Glad- stone and his colleagues have, however, made up their minds that the day for timid compromise is past, and thorough- ness is to be the badge and character of all their measures.— Loadon Corres7wndent. ,RELIIIOUS CENSUS OF EDINGDURGIT.—The Edingburgh paily Review has published a census of church attendance in the city taken on Sunday. fhe population is 228,000 and there are 155 churches. The attendance at the morn- ling or afternoon and evening servie es was 101,713, or an average for each service of 50,957. The attendance at both services at the Free Church (which leads the way with 41 churches or chapels), was 28,558- at the Established Pres- byterian Church (with 24 Churches), 27,096; at the United Presbyterian Church (with 26 churches), 20,34; at the Scottish Episcopalian (with 15 churches), 9,421. The Roman Catholics attending worship numbered 5,698 • the Congregationalists, 2,615 ; Baptists, 2,021; Evangelical' Unionists, 1,570; English Episcopalians, 847' Wesleyan Methodists, 671; Plymouth Brethren, 563 ; Catholic Apostolic, 336; United Original Seceders, 276' Primitive Methodists, 219; "Christian Church," 163 • Christadephians, 153; Glassites, 152; German, 112; Swe'clenborgians, 96 ; Unitarian, 87; Jews, .53; Welsh, 42 ; Society of Friends, I 29; Deaf and Dumb, 25. Of the 'total attendance of 101,713 the Established Church hadr, thus v 27,096, and the Dissenting places of worship 74,617.
