div.p: LITERATURE-

THE POETICAL WORKS OF JOHN MILTON (London: Bickers and Son, 1, Leicester-square).—This is an excellent edition of the works of England's greatest poet, carefully printed fr,)ln the author's copies. and in which the ortho- graphy so peculiar in the writings of Milton has been scrupulously preserved. There is no doubt that lovers of old books will agree with the opinion expressed by the Rev. John Keble on this point when he said, "Ancient books lose very much of their value by the neglect of ancient ortho- graOy ;" and, therefore, this is a particular in which the present edition is to be commended. The volume contains in addition to "Paradise Lost," "Paradise Regained," and the other works of the great poet, a well written biography of Milton by A. Chalmers, M.A., F.S.A. These beautiful poems are so well known and appreciated to need no words of commendation from us. It may, however, interest our readers to learn that Milton was a poet at 10 years of age, whilst his translation of the 136th Psalm shows his progress in poetic expression at the early age of 15. It was, however, in 1662 when he was over 50 years of age and had lost his eyesight that he was found engaged on that grand and sub- lime production—Paradise Lost—which has been so univer- sally admired, and which was a design so comprehensive, that Dr. Johnson says it could only be-justified by success. This magnificent and immortal poem was first published in 1667, and much surprise and concern have been evinced at the small pecuniary benefit which the author derived from this proud display of his great genius.. It must, considering only the merit and popularity of the poem, seem deplorable that the copyright of such a composition should be sold for the small sum of £5, and a contingent payment on the sale 2,600 copies of two other equal sums, making altogether £l5 as the whole pecuniary reward of "a poem which has never been equalled." Facing the title page of the book is a por- trait of Milton, engraved by William Humphreys, which is said to be a faithful copy of that by Faithhome ; whilst underneath it are fac-shniles of Milton's handwriting from a copy Aratus Phceomena, now in the British Museum. The work is also embellished with 24 excellent illustrations by John Martin in permanent Woodbury type. The volume is beautifully printed on toned paper, artistically bound in an elegant cloth cover, and we congratulate the publishers on having produced the works of the great poet in so charming a volume.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

A deputation of Yorkshire colliers met a committee of coal owners at Sheffield, to discuss the wages question. Messrs. Pickard and Frith, representing the Yorkshire Association, abruptly left the room. The remaining delegates agreed to recommend the lodges to accept the terms offered by the coal owners last year, which comprise a rise of 15 per cent. in wages for every one-eighth advance in the net selling price of coal, and the principle of the sliding scale was 4depted.

THE LANCASHIRE COTTON TRADE. ' *As a consequence of the improvement in the Lancashire cotton trade, it has been decided to apply for a general advance of wages. This decision was come to at a numerously attended meeting of weavers, delegates of Lancashire and adjoining counties, at Manchester, on Sunday, only one dis- trict voting against the proposal. The application will be sent to Mr. Rawlinson, secretary to the Masters' Association, and will be discussed by the joint committees. The object is to restore the wages to the rate paid before the general re- duction in 1878, the rate now being from 7.1-, to 15 per cent lower. The 013 ham cotton operatives, in support of their claim for 5 per cent advance in wages, state that in 1880 the average price of raw cotton was 6id per lb.; and last year only 61d. The average price of yarn exported from Eng- land was 121 d per lb. in 1880, and 12id. last year, showing together a gain of one farthing per lb. for the employers. They also state that exports are increasing. Although no intimation has been given to that effect, it is understood that there will be meetings between employers and employed re- specting the advance in wages. As to the Bolton and Old- ham operatives working together, these two towns are in quite different positions. In Oldham coarse and medium counts are spun, in Bolton fine counts. The Oldham opera- tives are taking independent action, because they believe that trade is good, allowing a margin of at least one half- penny per pound. The result of the Oldham operatives' ap- plication for an advance of wages is anxiously looked for in the Ashton-under-Lyne district, where the wages are regulated by those•of the Oldham spinners. The spinners are receiving 10 per cent less than in 1877, when the first re- ductions were made. They believe the state of trade justifies an advance of five per cent. In regard to the wages agitation in the cotton trade, it is stated that there is great unwillingness on the part of the limited companies and private firms in Oldham to entertain the application for an advance, and it is claimed on the em- ployers' behalf that they were never so much masters of the situation as at present.'" The weavers at Ashton who came out on strike last Monday haVe resumed work on the promise that the grievances they complain of shall receive attention. In North and North-east Lancashire the employers are also, it is said, decidedly adverse to the application of the weavers, whilst some of the leading men among the latter are stated to be of opinion that the movement is a little premature. •

div.head: PIIESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PIIESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board, was held at the workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday, Mr. S. Marsh presided. There were also present the Rev. T. Chambers, Messrs. Hall, Fidler, Leatherbarrow, Tyrer, Meadows, Gilbody, Kenwright, Jackson, Rowe, Sadler, Birchall, Paris, Gerrard, Syder, Leigh, Ranson, Swift, Tuson, Birch, and Eatock, with Mr. S. H. Hartley I,clerk). THE WIDNES FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY: A S. RATE TO BE

LAID. As the Clerk was reading the minutes of the meeting, the CHAIRMAN, interrupting, asked if the Widnes overseers had paid anything.—The CLERK replied that they had paid over £5OO, which was Almost as much as the arrears of the rate would realise. He had, however, a report to lay before the ordinary meeting.—At the conclusion of the reading of the minutes, the CHAIRMAN asked the Clerk what he had done in the matter of the W idnes money.—Mr. FIDLER deprecated the matter being gone into then, on the ground that when the other guardians came in they would wish to know what had been done and would it be wise to go into it twice. He understood that the preliminary business was to read the minutes.—Mr. SADLER was of a similar opinion. Rev. T. Chambers said if they remembered, Mr. Meadows asked at the last meeting what had been done, and he was told that the matter had been gone into. There were several members strolling about the workhouse grounds and they would, no doubt, like to hear the discussion.—Th'e CHAIRMAN called attention to the time and said that it was quarter of an hour after the hour of proceeding to business, and he would like to know whether the members did not know that 10.30 was the time for starting business.—Further discussion on the question was postponed till the applications for relief had been disposed of.—Subsequently the CLERK said he had met the overseers of Widnes. and they had gone carefully through the 2.0 counts, and the, overseers had now determined to lay a rate of 35. in the pound, made payable in two instalments, which would raise £15,627. The total liabilities of the overseers up to March, 1883, would he about £lB,OOO. The overseers thought, and he quite agreed with them, that if they Bould get tbis £15,627 collected by the end of September, it would give them time to prepare a new valuation list and renew the rate to meet their liabilities next year. The only difficulty now was to get out the new rate.— Mr. SADLER said, as had been stated, they went carefully through the accounts, and there was something like £lOO to come in at that time. They had about £4OO in the bank, but they could not meet the demand of the Guar- dians. Since the clerk and the overseers met, the latter had seen the assistant overseer, and had promised to push the matter forward and get the rate laid as soon as possible.—ln reply to Mr. Paris, Mr. HALL said the overseers bad paid £sso.—Mr. SADLER remarked that nearly all the rate was collected. There was not more than £5O or /GO to come in. —lt was ordered that the resolution to proceed against the Widnes overseers, as passed at a previous meeting, stand over. THE MAINTENANCE OF LUNATICS AT WHITTINGHAM ASYLUM. The CLERK read a communication from the Whittingbam Asylum, stating that froin the Ist instant the charge for maintenance would be reduced from Bs. 9d. weekly to Bs. 2d. THE .LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD AND THE APPOINTMENT OF

• THE ASSISTANT OVERSEER fOR BOLD. The CLERK read the following communication :—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 19th ult., retuning the form of queries containing the particulars of the pro- posed appointment of Mr. James Houghton as assistant overseer for the Bold district of the Prescot Union. Adverting to the fact that Mr. HOUGHTON is a licensed vic tualler, and to the observations contained in your letter of the 16th ult. with respect to the arrangements made for the management of the business, the Board direct me to inquire whether the Guardians before p, ()needing to elect him had fully considered the objections generally to the appointment to the office of assistant overseer of a person who is the holder of licensed premises. The Board also direct me to inquirewhether Mr. HOUGHTON has any office other than the public-house at which rates can be paid. EDWARD SUTTON. —THE CLERK said he had received the following letter from Mr. Houghton: Crouton, January 11th, 1882.—" In answer to yours I beg to say that my office is in every res- pect detached from my dwelling and public house, it being ' 4931 yards from the latter and situate at 37, Chapel-lane, Crouton. The dwelling and licensed house is situate in , Liverpool-road in the aforesaid township. My office consists of a general or outer office on the first floor and two offices on the second floor approached by a staircase.t I may also say that my wife has managed the licensed premises for over seven years and continues to do so."—lt was resolved that a copy of Mr. Houghton's letter be forwarded to the Local Govern.nent Board. WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. The MASTER reported that there were 503 inmates in the workhouse this week, as compared with 503 in the previous week, and 480 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 147 boys and girls at lidrkdale schools. THE APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER FOR LOWER WIDNES. The CLERK said he had received a letter from the Local Government Board, confirming the appointment of Dr. Cooper as medical officer of health for lower Widnes district, at a salary of £3O per annum. THE REVALUATION OF THE RAILWAYS IN THE UNION. In pursuance of notice given at the last meeting, Mr. Meadows moved that Messrs. Marshall and M'Connell, of London, be appointed to assist the Assessment Committee
X

until the completion of the valuation of the railway rateable hereditaments in the Union, at the remuneration of one per cent upon the rateable value confirmed by the committee; and after hearing objections—if any—that five guineas per day and expenses out of pocket in the event of objection or appeal, be paid them, and that such remuneration be paid out of the common fund of the Union. Mr. Meadows observed that the committee considered the railways were very much under-assessed at the present time. They had not been valued for over 14 years, and during that time the committee considered the traffic had largely iracaeased. When the railways were re-valued there was no doubt it would make a wonderful difference in the rates of the Union, and every ratepayer would feel the bene- fit. He might say the Assessment Committee were unani- mous in recommending that the gentlemen he had proposed should be appointed, as from their experience and the information the committee had gathered, they seemed the most likely qualified to do the work.—Mr. LEATHEREARROW, in seconding the motion, quoted figures showing the necessity for the re-valuation of the railways in the Union. The London and North-Western Railway Company's balance-sheet for December half-year, 1880, showed that the average receipts per train per mile amounted to ss. 61-d. for the whole system, but for the lines through the Prescot Union lOs would be nearer the correct figure. The balance-sheet showed a profit of £2,530,320. The train miles were 17,916,819, being 2s. 9.89 d. per mile, whereas the Board's assessor showed a profit of £1,630 per mile, with a total assessment of £5,295 in Whiston. The 121,516 train miles running through Whiston only showed an assessment of 11.18 d. per mile, showing a short assessment of is. 10.71 d., or 66 per cent. less than the railway company's own showing as per their balance sheet.—After further discussion, the motion was carried, there being no dissentient. PUTTING THE CLERK IN THE COUNTY COURT. The CLERK said that since the last meeting he had been served with a County Court summons by a man named Tebbutt, of Widnes, for non-payment of 30s. for goods sup- plied to a woman at Widnes, in 1879. Mr. Hartley added that the man ought to have sent in the bill at the proper time. It was out of date, and he should plead the Statute of Limitation.—Several members obsemeri that this course would let others know the consequences which would result if they did not send in their accounts at the proper time.

div.head: ST. HELENS WESLEYAN SUNDAY
div.p: ST. HELENS WESLEYAN SUNDAY
SCHOOL.

The annual tea meeting in connection with this Sunday school was held on Thursday evening, in Waterloo-street School-room. About 250 sat down to tea. The after pro- ceedings were presided over by the Rev. J. M. Wamsley. Mr. Bardsley, one of the secretaries, read the report, from Which it appeared some important changes had taken place in the management of the school during the past year, and so far the working had pioved satisfactory, moreover, they had opened a way for making use of the services of the teachers, as assistants in conducting- the devotional services. The school is worked by a staff of 52 teachers and officers of whom 47 are members of the Wesleyan Methodist Society, The number of scholars who are member is 87, against 36 reported last year, being an increase of 51. The library contains about 500 volumes, about 100 less than last year, which is owing to many of the books being so far worn as to be withdrawn from circulation. The number of readers is given as 94, above 100 .less than last year, the decrease being no doubt due to the same cause. The usual quantity, 2,184, numbers of the Band of Hope Review and British Workman publications has been given to the scholars; about 120 of the new Sunday school hymn books have been sold; four Bibles have been given to scholars leavinc, the town ; and upwards of 700 of the Wesleyan book' and other magazines have been sold.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

ENTERTAINMENT.-A popular concert was given in the Viaduct Institute, on Saturday evening, by Mr. W. Attfield and party, which was but slenderly attended, so that prohably, the proceeds would not meet the expenses. It is evident the time was unfavourable; for the popular tea party and entertainment of Mr. Thomas Molyneux, now become an annual institution—held in the same place on Monday evening, was a great success. Mr. Molyneux, under the name of Household Stores, carries on an extensive co-operative grocery business, in competition with the Leigh Co-opera- tive Stores. The room had been nicely decorated, and after an entertainment entitled " Happy hours," was given, when the upper room was crowded, and in which Messrs. R. Evans, J. H. Greenwood, and G. Barton acquitted themselves very I creditably. The stage was decorated with elegant crimson fittings which might have done credit to a ladies' boudoir in 'Happy hours ;" as it was, Mr. R. Evans was no mean re- presentative of this imaginary personage, a vocalist, instru- mentalist, ventriloquist, mimic, and female character impersonator, representing, in appropriate costumes, characters we meet in every day life, including old and young of both sexes. Mr. Evans was a host in himself, and with Mr. Greenwood, an invariable favourite, and excellent pianist and buffo vocalist, the time passed pleasantly. Mr. Barton sang "The death of 'Nelson," and The white squall," with his usual good taste and recognised ability, and was vociferously recalled. SUNDAY SCHOOL FERIVAL.—The annual Sunday school festival was held in the Congregational School, on Tuesday, when a bountiful tea was provided for 300 scholars, and the Rev. J. Allatt distributed some 70 prizes for regular atten- dance and good conduct, to boys and girls, and some 90 volumes of magazines taken by the scholars during the year were bound for them and given gratis. Mr. Battersby gave a report on the attendance and state of the penny bank, a flourishing part of the organisation, and Mr. Allatt expressed his gratification at seeing so many friends present thus showing an interest in the children, the audience by this time numbering about 500. An interisting programme was then gone through which included the following :—Piano- forte solo,'" The musquateers," by Miss C. Tait; recitation, "A corn on my toe," by Master A. Jones; song, " Apperley mill," by Miss Cameron; and Miss Jones was a very accept- able substitute for Mr. Ashton, pianoforte duet, "A wedding march," by Miss Wood and Mr. A. Caldwell; duet, "The pilot brave," Messrs. Owen and Sefton; seng, " Ehren on the Rhine," by Miss Adams, who accompanied the pre- liminary hymn with which the proceedings opened; Miss Ashcroft recited a long piece without hesitancy, and Miss M. J. Stirling clearly articulated the verses, "Speak gently." Miss Jones and Mr. Caldwell sang the duet, "When the wind," and were recalled; and Miss A. K. Wood sang sweetly and was recalled; Mr. Sefton sang "The monarch of the wood ;" Miss E. Jones recited " Saturday night," audibly and well. Pianoforte solo, "Chime again beautiful hells," Miss Holmes, who also accompanied most of the songs. Mr. Caldwell gave "The gipsy's jovial life ;" and Miss Rothwell sang and was tumultously encored. Mr. J. Sud- worth sang" Down in the deep," well and firmly, and Miss Wood, and Miss Adeleide K. Wood sang" Whispering hope," with clearness and good taste, and Miss Jones sang "Olivia," admirably and was recalled he song, " Twickemam ferry," concluding the concert, which was every way satisfactory. An apple and a card with a scriptural motto, the gift of Miss Evans' of Huyton, was given to each person-on leaving. Thanks were given to Mr. Holmes, for:slecorating the room, to the vocalists to Mr. Glover, for the pianoforte, and to Mrs. Jackson, of Bridge-street, who provided for the tea so successfully.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.
1 to
LECTURE BY MR. HOLBROOK GASKELL, SEN., OF

WIDNES. On Tuesday night, a lecture was delivered by Mr. Hol- brook Gaskell, at the*Mechanics' Institute, Woolton, on the subject of "Free Trade and Fair Trade," the lecture being under the auspices of the Liberal Association of the district, of which Mr. Gaskell is president. In his opening remarks, Mr. Gaskell said the subject was one that had been largely discussed within the last twelve months. When the rumours of Protection, Reciprocity, Retaliation, and at last "Fair Trade," were first heard, they were treated with indifference and contempt, the feeling being that these doctrines were either advanced by eccentric individuals or for party pur- poses. But whatever might be the general feeling, it was thought that there were many of the younger men who felt considerable interest in the question, and to whom the Liberal Association felt.that his remarks would be acceptable. He personally had taken a great interest in this question during the greater part of his life, and his experience traversed not only the whole epoch of Free Trade, but also the darker and sadder period of Protection. Protection he conceived to have been cut down and done with for ever. (Applause.) Free Trade had now oast its roots so deeply into the soil and thrown out its branches so widely as to be quite safe against any storm that might assault it. (Applause.) Bnt three "Fair Trade" friends professessed not to be hostile to Feir Trade, but rather a desire to see it rounded and completed. Free Trade was the result of a successful revolt against Pro- tection which prevailed in this country for a very long period, and Protection was the system of imposing duties on the im- ports of foreign produce and foreign commodities, with the object of protecting special interests in this country. The leading advocates of Protection and Reciprocity declared that we had continued a policy of what they called "one- sided Free Trade," and that foreigners were making for themselves all they wanted, while we who depended chiefly on foreign trade were going to the bad. The remedy sug- gested was that we should trade freely only with those who would trade freely with us. Sir Stafford Northcote at Shef- field said he wished to see Free Trade universal and fair, and his followers of the National Fair Trade League looked with alarm at the constantly increasing value of our imports over our exports, believing this to be a sign that we were getting poorer as a nation, and that if the proportion of 411 millions of imports to 286 millions of exports of last year were not speedily reversed, we should end in bankruptcy and ruin. The Fair Trader was confident that retaliation in the matter of taxing imported commodities would secure Reciprocity. But the Free Traders admitted goods into this country free, not to benefit other countries but to benefit ouraelyes. Lest year a French Free Trader bad brought the matter into a nutshell when he asked—" Which is best for man and society—abundance or scarcity ? " We in this country preferred abundance, and we left the scarcity to those nations who wished toprotect themselves. (Applause.) That class of "Fair Traders" represented by Mr. James Lowther, who said he would raise £20,000,000 on our im- ports for the purpose of relieving laud to that extent, he (Mr. Gaskell) passed by without notice, and he only dealt with that class who professed to be Free Traders themselves. He demurred to several of the statements put forth by the Fair Trade League. One of their assumptions was that foreign nations did not act fairly by us when they taxed the commodities they bought from us • but this was falla- cious, for the tax fell on themselves, and not on us. (Hear, hear.) And so long as Free Trade was beneficial to Eng- land we should pursue it, no matter what might be its effect on other countries. (Applause.) He gave instances, such as the case of the importation of rags for the paper-making trade, to show that England was benefited by Free Trade, without reference to the likes or dislikes of foreign exporters or consumers, and went on to dual with another of the Fair. Traders' statements to the effect that the excess of imports over exports had to be paid in bullion, or by the transfer of securities to foreign nations. This fallacy had been repeatedly exposed. Our stock of bullion always tended to increase, and our foreign investments were enormous and as large as ever. He quoted the figures given by Mr. Glad- stone at Leeds, showing that from 1876 to 1880, when im- ports amounted to £622,000,000 in excess of our exports, our imports of bullion were £3,000,000 in excess of our exports. A still more comprehensive statement was that during the years from 1866 to 1879 our imports exceeded our exports by by the enormous amount of £1,225,000,000, and in those years we imported upwards of £66,000,000 more of bullion than we exported. (Applause.) There was an end of the argument of the Fair Traders that we were paying in bullion for the excess of our imports; and as to their statement that we were realising our foreign invest- ments to pay for the excess, all competent authorities, with- out exception, were agreed that year by year British investments abroad were steadily on the increase. The Bankers' illagazine put it on record that our foreign invest- ments were £1,290,000,000, and our dividends on that and the interest accruing from loans amounted to £55,400,000 per annum. Another source of income which the foreigner paid to us was the earnings of our merchant vessels, which were computed at £60,000,000 a year. These facts at once explained the apparent anomaly of our importing a larger amount than we exported. The foreigner owed us large sums, which he paid in goods. He had to remit to this country £60,000,000 for freight on the goods which our ships carried for him, and he had likewise to pay us £55,400,000 for interest on our loans and dividends derived from investments in foreign railways, mines, &c. Thus the £286,000,000 worth of goods which the foreigner bought from us last year about balanced the amount of our impbrts, when these additional sources of' income are taken into con- sideration. The foreigner paid us in goods and not in pro- duce, and this illustrated the well-known fact that all trade resolved itself at last into barter. (Applause.) Mr. Gaskell gave a very simple and apt illustration of this by taking the case of an "export "from Woolton of a load of stone worth 405., which upon its arrival in Liverpool, with the cartage came to 505., and the owner bringing back a load of coal, arid charging the return cartage, the " import " into Woolton would appear in their records—if they bad any— as one of 60s. against the 40s. exported, and yet the owner would be richer, and not poorer by the transaction. (Ap- plause.) It was also said by the Protectionists that the policy of retaliation would be successful because, our im- ports being greatly in excess of our exports, we had more to tax than the foreigner had; but he again demurred to their argument, and asked his hearers to go a little below the sur- face and enquire into what these imports consisted of. Let them observe that in taxing these imports we would be taxing ourselves in all the prime necessaries of life in order to "spite the foreigner," for it must always be remembered that all taxes fell eventually on the consumer. (Applause.) Of the £411,000,000 of imports, £156,000,060 were for food and £170,000,000 for raw material; £33,000,000 consisted of certain foreign and colonial commodities on which taxes were already levied, such as tea, coffee, and wines and spirits, making a total of £359,000,000 and leaving only £52,000,000 to deal with, and which might consist of manu- factures which we could tax without ruinous consequences to ourselves—that was only 14 per cent. of the total amount of our inports. It had been conclusively shown in tbe action taken on various occasions by the working classes, and particularly at the Trades Union Congress, when "fair trade" delegates were elected, that the people of this coun- try would never consent to a revival of the import duties on food and on raw materials, which, after infinite struggle and agitation, they succeeded in throwing off in 1846. (Ap- plause.) The Farmers' Alliance had taken a similar step to that of the working men's delegates, and declarea that fair trade was a delusion and a snare, so that our productive classes were opposed to all taxation on food or on raw materials, which formed three-fourths of our total imports, and of the £52.000,000 of imports that remained, it included many items that ought to be removed to the other class of raw materials. And in taxing these commodities, they must remember that they would not only be raising the price of foreign goods to the British consumer, but they would he enabling the British manufacturer to raise his price to the same level. Neither must they forget that two could play at this game of "beggar my neighbour." The foreigner would probably retaliate upon us, end as he had most cards he would probably win. (Hear, hear.) Our exports of manufactured goods last year amounted to £180,000,000, and our imports to £52,000,000. Taking the tan of the United States, while our imports of articles of food and raw material from there amounted to upwards of £104,000,000 sterling, the amount of manufactures exported from America to England was only £3,000,000, of which nearly one-half was for hides, which probably the shoe- makers would consider were "raw material " in their trade. (Hear, hear.) Well, wkile our imports of say " manufac- tures" were under £3,000,000, our exports were £25,000,000, so that the proportion was ten to one. If he had ten win- dows in his house and his neighbour had only one, and te quarrelled with ram, would it be prudent for him to throw stones at fiis neighbour's window? (Laughter and applause.) The result would probably be that he would have the whole of his ten windows broken, while his neighbour could only have one broken. (Applause.) There was an old adage that "those who lived in glass houses should not throw stones," and we eertainly lived in a glass house in respect to this matter of retaliation, while the Fair Trader was the man who recommended us to "throw stones," not at one neigh- bour, but at all our neighbours, and make friends of them by that means. (Laughter.) He thought they would not by any means take that advice; they had better by far put the poor Fair Trader out of the way into a lunatic asylum. (Laughter and applause.) The Fair Trader attributed the depression of trade and the falling off of experts, which had undoubtedly existed for some years past, to the system of "one-sided Free Trade;" but there were far more obvious factors in the problem than this. Without dwelling on the wars which we had experienced during the late Administra- tion, which disturbed trade and crushed the people with heavy taxation, he pointed out that the main reason for bad trade was one over which we had no control. It had pleased Providence to withhold its sunshine from the tilled lands of Europe, and the British farmer had Buffeted from deficient harvests as well as other causes. Mr. Caird, a great authority, on all agricultural questions, had estimated the agricultural loss in the last three years at £150,900,000 sterling. But some improvement in trade was already apparent, and when it pleased Providence to restore the productiveness of the earth, the full volume of the trade would roll on again. In the meantime we should be thankful th theat prescience of our predecessors had secured fur us through Free Trade a large share of the bountiful harvests that had blessed other and distant lands. Our foreign trade was enormous, and most striking when compared with that of other ceuntries where Protection existed. (Applause.) The Fair Traders in their discussion failed to tell the younger generation that similar evils as regards bad trade and distress existed during the period of Protection, only with a hundred-fold greater intensity than anything that was known now. Mr..Gaskell then proceeded

TEA MEETING AT WilisFonn.—The annual tea meeting ,connected wiith Weaver church took place in the Weaver schoolroom, on Monday last. A large number attended, many coming from a distance. The tables were all given by the ladies of the congregation and a few well-wishers, such as Lady Delamere, Sir P. Egerton, Miss Verdin, Mrs. Perrin, Miss Knowles, Mrs. W. Verdin, Mrs. Leigh, Mrs. Turner (Over Mrs. Lea Mr. J. D. Kay, &c., &c. After tea a public meeting was held, and addresses were given by the Rev. Canon Blackburne, the Rev. W. Hopkins (Moul- ton), and the Rev. C. Kay (vicar of Wharton). The chief topic was the difficulty under which the congregation laboured owing to subsidence, the church becoming so dan- gerous that it had to.be taken down, and a lighter structure is going to be erected in its place, the services for the present being conducted in the schoolroom. The Misses Turner and Woodyatt greatly contributed to the enjoyment of the even- ing by their songs, as also did Mr. T. T. Thompson and Mr. James Turner. The Misses Wilson played a pianoforte duet very ably, and the usual votes of thanks brought the meet- ing t 6 a close. The schoolroom was nicely decorated, and an artistic effect was produced by the flowers supplied by Mr. J. Beeton. • _

DETECrIVES Ow:WITTED.-- For a considerable period the Liverpool police authorities have been keeping a sharp look out for a notorious female swindler, whose moclus operandi consisted in taking lodgings in respectable quarters, and disappearing after a few days, not only without paying her bill, but with, as a rule, some of the householder's property. This, of course, is not a very unusual circumstance, but the extent to which it was carried in the present instance by this lady, who is described as about 35 years of age and of respectable appearance, brings the case out of the ordinary groove, and gives to it a degreee of importance which is usually wanting in this class of crime. Last week, however, the woman's career was cut short for a time as she was caught redhanded by one of our detectives, and placed in durance vile. On being taken into custody she informed the authorities that the most of the goods she had purloined had been pawned in various places in Manchester, and Superin- tendent Williams at once ordered the officer to proceed to the last-named place, along with the prisoner, to try and recover the stolen property. On the superintendent asking him whether he thought he could manage the case by him- self, the detective replied, of course, to the effect that he , would have no trouble as far as that was concerned. But to make assurance doubly stare a police-constable in plain clothes was ordered by the superintendent to accompany him, the trio reaching Manchester on Wednesday all right ; but at night time, when passing one of the theatres while the audience was coming out, the lady gave them the slip, and, mingling with the crowd, was rapidly lost to sight. Although they searched high and low in the neighbourhood, their efforts were unavailing, and they had the mortification of having to telegraph to the Liverpool police that the bird had flown. Continuing their inquiry, however, on Saturday last the detective recovered the object of his search, and placed her where she will have but little chance of escaping for some time. As the result of the affair we understand both the detective and the police-constable were suspended for a time, and on Monday the head-constable reduced the former, who has been several years in the detective force, and was regarded as one of the smartest men in it, to a first- class constable, while his companion has been relegated to the second-class.

SA_TURI)AY JANUARY 14, 1882. • ,r FREE TRADE AND FAIR TRADE. Lo relate in eaphie terms his own experiences of the dread- ful sufferings of the people during the famine periods prior to the abolition of the corn laws, ard he quoted at length some exceedingly interesting and startling passages from Mr. Henry Dunckley's book, " The Charter of the'tiations ; or, Free Trade and its Results," showing the literal and wholesale starvation and extraordinary distress which pre- vailed in those times in the manufacturing towns of Lanca- shire, which condition of things was of repeated occurrence within his (Mr. Gaskell's) own experience and knowledge. He concluded by quoting the eloquent and pathetic perora- tion of Sir Robert Peel's speech upon his resignation of office after abolishing the obnoxious corn laws. This inter- esting and comprehensive address was listened to through- out with the deepest attention and appreciation, and Mr. Gaskell at the close was cordially applauded. A vote of thanks to the lecturer was passed, on the motion of the Rev. George Beaumont, and the proceedings then terminated.
THE E
AMIN
TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES.

Daring this week the members of the 1.0.G.T. and the Sons of Temperance have held a temperance mission in Lacey-street school-room, Widnes. The mission was com- menced on Saturday, when Mr. Thomas Horrocks, "the converted clown and temperance lecturer," of Darwen, preached two sermons, afternoon and evening. There was a good attendance.
On Monday evening a meeting was held, at which the Rev. T. Hughes (Welsh Wesleyan) presided, for the purpose of hearing a lecture by Mr. Horrocks.

The CHAIRMAN said he feared that the efforts of the friends of temperance were sorely needed in Widnes; but he was glad to find that their organisation was in full and active operation. Speaking on the temperance question generally, it was a pleasing sign that there was now on all hands a quickened interest in the matter. All religious denominations were taking a more active part in the move- ment. Our legislators, too, were rousing to action. They might have some of them read the speeches of Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain to their constituents at Birmingham last week, and they would notice that they treated the liquor traffic as one of the burning questions of the day. Of course, there were many who would not go so far as the Permissive Bill went; but he hoped they, as temperance advocates, would be temperate in this matter also. If a bill were brought forward next Session he hoped they would accept it; though this accept- ance would not prevent them from "asking for more." Mr. T. HORROCKS then proceeded to deliver his lecture, which he varied by the introduction of several temperance songs, in the choruses of which the audience joined. He said he had lectured and sung at one period every night for eleven months. During that time he travelled 6,000 miles, and during the whole time drank nothing stronger than water. He next alluded to the presence of the Rev. T. Hughes in the chair. He thought that a minister of the Gospel was never in a place more befitting his office than when he pre- sided at a temperance meeting; and this reminded him of the conduct of another clergyman who lately was chairman at the licensed victuallers' meeting in London. He was not there that night to advocate the temperance cause. He lived in the street called Teetotal-street—not in that nick-named temperance—for those who dwelt there lived in a dangerous land. There one might have one's half-pint of porter, and still be "temperate." This was temperance; but teetotalism meant that man should enjoy his food, as God meant him to, without the aid of intoxicating liquors. He traced back the origin of teetotalism to the days when it first began to make its way at Preston as a principle. There had been a day when he had not been a temperate man—when he had stood at the corners of public-houses with no occupation but that of polishing the stones beneath his feet. He had seen a good many men " polishing stones" at Widnes. (Laughter.) Men with nothing but holes in their pockets—(laughter)— and two pockets to let. (Renewed laughter.) At first those who espoused his cause of teetotalism were denounced as lunatics. But let them go to the governor of any asylum and ask him how many men and women were there through drinking God's pure water; and the answer would be—none. But ask him how many drink had brought there, and he would tell them that 75 out of every 100 who passed beneath those portals were driven there by the curse of drink. Since the day that the movement had begun at Preston it had waxed powerful, and its adherents had increased, and now they had six millions of teetotallers in the land, and one million Band of Hope children. But the drink traffic was still an enormous evil. During one year they had spent 150 millions in drink, and consumed 85 million bushels of barley in the manufacture of alcoholic drinks. He next alluded to the changes wrought in favour of the temperance cause at the last general election. (Applause.) They had got rid of a Greenall—(loud cheers)—and they had displaced a Wheelhouse at Leeds—(applause)—and pat in his place a Gladstone. (Great cheering.) What was it that could ruin England? Drink. And what alone could render ruin impossible? Teetotalism. To no one was this ques- tion of more vital importance than to the working men of England. Teetotalism would ennoble them, but they could never soar aloft amidst spitoons and sawdust. (Laughter and cheers.) The lecturer next went on to describe the de- gradation which attended drunkenness, and pictured the con- temptible state of the drunkard as he reeled homewards, singing Bacchanalian songs. Reeled homewards? But did he reach home? Did he not oftener fall into the clutches of the policeman' and awoke next morning in a prison cell, next to be taken before a magistrate, and to undergo the nameless degradation of the police court? He had ex- periepced these things, and had realised their horror. They might be called fanatics—they who were advocates of total abstention—bat whether it was fanaticism or not, after what he had seen, he would live and die a hare-brained fanatic. He contrasted the manner in which rich and poor were treated when under the influence of drink. The working man was apprehended and locked up, brought before the magistrates, fined, and his name published; but if the rich man got "a little over the line," a policeman kindly saw him home, and no more was beard of the matter. He thought rich and poor ought to be put on a more equal footing in the matter. If the name of one was published the other ought not to escape public disgrace. What was this beer? In a quart of the liquor they would find 35 parts were water, two ounces alcohol. But besides that it contained two ounces of sediment of salt and gum and other substances. He held liquor to be in every way injurious. It shortened a man's life, it sapped his strength, it destroyed his vigour. The teetotaller, they would find, was generally the better and more enduring workman than the habitual drinker. The latter might possess a passing vigour, bat it could not last. Its effect waned, and left its victim weak, nerveless, and unstrung. He next alluded to the great error he considered Mr. Gladstone had made in giving wine and beer licenses to grocers. Thereby many an English home had been ruined. The usual votes of thanks and the singing of a hymn brought the proceedings to a close.
ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wed- nesday, Dr. Twyford presiding. There were also present Aldermen Mcßryde and Gamble; Councillors Belsher, Jamison, Wilcock, McKechnie, Brook, Johnson, with Dr. McNicoll (medical officer), Mr. Hart (surveyor), and Mr. Craik (deputy town clerk).
THE PROPOSED ALKALI WORKS INSPECTOR FOR ST. HELENS.

Mr. CRAIII said that in accordance with the instructions given at the last meeting of the committee, the Town Clerk had written to the Local Government Board respecting the appointment of an inspector of alkali works solely for St. Helens. During the last month a communication had been received asking whether the Corporation wished the appoint- ment of an inspector under the 19th section of the Act which provided for such appointment by the Corporation paying a moiety of the salary. The Town Clerk replied saying that the Council considered St. Helens was of sufficient import- ance to have an inspector uholly for St. Helens at the Government's cost. Nothing had further been heard of the matter.

EMPLOYING AN UNQUALIFIED
PRACTITIONER AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday afternoon, an inquest was held by Mr. J. E. VVorsley, deputy coroner, at the Runcorn Town Hall, on the body of a child named Stanton, aged one month, whose father is named John Stanton, of Allcock-street. The mother stated that on the previous Tuesday afternoon, the deceased was ill, and she took it to Dr. Robinson's surgery, where she saw Mr. Salkeld, one of his assistants. He told her to take the child home, keep it very warm, and also handed her a bottle of medicine labelled "A teaspoonful every hour." Mr. Salkeld likewise advised her to let the Rev.. Father Fennelly see the little one, so that he might baptize it, as he believed it was in a dying state. The child grew worse, and on Thursday night she again went to the surgery. Mr. Salkeld said he would go to see it, but after- wards it. was agreed that Mr. Bankes, another assistant to Dr. Robinson, should do so. Mr. Bankes said she had better go down to the surgery for more medicine, but she did not do so, and the deceased died on the following morning. Daring the whole illness deceased was in convulsions.—la reply to Dr. Robinson. who was in court during the enquiry the witness said she thought her child was dying when she took it to the surgery, and Mr. Salkeld told her she had better take it to Dr. Bagnall, who lived on the opposite side or the street. ,Dr. Bagnall was not in, and afterwards Mr. Salkeld gave her the medicine, but did not ask for any pay-. ment.—Mr. F. C. Salkeld deposed that he was a student at the Liverpool School of Medicine, and resident assistant with Dr. Robinson. He (witness) was 17 years of age. and received a salary and was provided with board in his situa, tion. He prescribed for patients after communicating with his employer, when they desired it.—ln reply to Dr. Robin- son, witness described the medicine he gave to the infant.— The Coroner: I think there is no class of people who give more gratuitous services than doctors.—Dr. Robinson: And no class who seem to get into more trouble through doing so. —Mr. W. H. Bankes, another assistant to Dr. Robinson, said he had been with that gentleman about three months. He never prescribed for patients.—Dr. Robinson observed that he had never seen the deceased, and at the time when his assistants spoke to him, he thought it was another child belonging to the parents, which he had often seen.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from convulsions—The Coroner said be really thought that although Mr. Salkeld might. in the future be a good medical man, and succeed well in the most honourable pro- fession he had chosen, yet he was not of opinion that the young gentleman was at the present time qualified to pre- scribe for and attend to patients without supervision. That case might have assumed a rather serious nature, had they not come to the conclusion that the death was from con- vulsions; and they might have had a very unpleasant duty to perform. Though he was inclined to think that such a thing would not be permitted to occur again, yet he could not help saying he felt that the attendance upon and pre- scribing for patients by a gentleman of Mr. Salkeld's present position in the medical world, was not right. It was no doubt right that a pupil should act under his principal's instruc- tions, but that he should take upon himself to cope with disease and death in an unqualified position, was, at his very early age (to say the least of the matter) very undesirable. It was not fair to the young gentleman that he should be placed in such circumstances, for if any serious consequences followed his prescription, both he and Dr. Robinson would be in a very serious position.—Dr. Robinson said he should like to observe that he altogether disclaimed any responsi- bility for this particular Case.-The Coroner said the jury had placed no responsibility upon him in relation to this specific case.—Dr. Robinson: You cannot do it sir. The doctor also asked the Coroner whether he was to understand from the remarks he had made, whether, if a case of emergency were brought to the surgery, and he (the speaker) was not in, his assistants could not deal with it, and give the parties the benefit of the knowledge they possessed. His assistants certainly had some knowledge, and it would be against the law not to give persons so applying the benefit , of it.—The Coroner said they were not dealing with cases, of emergency, but with actual facts ; and it would by all means be better for persons to wait until a properly qualified medical man had seen the case.—The inquest then terminated.

div.head: GLOBE ALKALI COMPANY.
div.p: THE GLOBE ALKALI COMPANY.

Mr. CRMIC said that communications had been seat to the London North-Western Railway Company, calling their at- tention to acid in tb e canal, and to the Globe Alkali Company calling their attention to acid in the brook. The railway company replied that their district engineer would be com- municated with upon the subject. The Globe Alkali Com- pany wrote denying having run acid into the brook as the liquors passed. through a neutralizing well at a cost of £2OO per annum, so that all liquors were neutralized. The com- munication said that the Company had caused to be tested, almost daily, the water in their exit drain and found it neutral. A later communication from the Company stated that on Thursday afternoon the Corporation's Inspector left at their laboratory two samples of water taken near their works and those samples contained respectively '325 per cent and .14 of acid.
Dr. JAMISON said that it appearel that the company ad- mitted that the samples contained that amount of acid, and he should move that Dr. Angus Smith's attention be called to the fact. _ _ _ _ _
Mr. BELSIIER seconded the motion, which was carried. FEVER IN ST. HELENS.

Mr. CRAM read a letter from the Local Government noard saying that Mr. Spear would shortly come to St. Helens to inquire into the prevalence of fever as reported in the Registrar General's quarterly returns, and hoping that the committee would instruct its officers to afford every facility to Mr. Spear in the prosecution of his inquiry. In a future communication the exact date of the visit woull be stated.
Dr. JAMISON : IS that communication addressed to many towns, I wonder? Mr. CRAIK: It is not a printed letter; it is written. Dr. JemisoN asked what wag meant by fever in that case. _ _

Dr. I.llcNicou, said what was referred to meant typhoid and other fevers which were not scarlet. The last year or two the number of deaths from fever were 38 or 40—some- thing getting on to one death a week all the year round. Dr. JAMISON: But that does not give an idea of all the fever in the town, as there was mild fever, which was al- most constant. In the last quarterly returns St. Helens waci specially mentioned as having a good deal of fever. Dr. Jamison went on to say that the stink in Phythian and Kirkland-street and that locality was sometimes dreadful. Mr. BROOK said that he suggested a short time since that a shaft should be put in Glover-street, but he thought that the matter was placed on one side on account of the cost. _ .

The SURVEYOR said that Mr. Glover would not consent to it, and the cost to place one down was considered exces- sive. Dr. JAI§IISON did not think the cost ought to be compared with the lives of people who ought to have the best chance of living in this world. With regard to the Kirkland-street neighbourhood, it was said that fever could not be avoided there. The SURVEYOR said it could not unless there was an alteration in the brook. Until the brook was lowered ex- tending at least from Spray's Bridge down to the Naviga- tion Bridge, there was certain to be a large accumulation of mud and sediment which could not possibly be liberated, because after a flood it would be higher than the sewer. Dr. JAMISON did not think they should have a permanent cause of fever in the town. Alderman dAMBLE said the chart system of detecting zvmotic diseases was an excellent one. By their officers making a chart they could see at once in what locality dis- ease was found to be running. It was understood that the system would be adopted; and instructions were ordered to be given to the officers of the department to aid Mr. Spear in his enquiries.

div.head: MONTH'S MORTALITY.
div.p: THE MONTH'S MORTALITY.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that during the feur weeks ending January 7th there had been 172 births. The deaths were as follows :—Measles, 7; scarlet fever, 2; diphtheria, 0; whooping cough, 0; fever, 4; diarrhcea, 3; other zymotics, 1; total zymotics, 17; all other causes, 109; from all causes, 126. Of these 63 were males and 63 females, 47 being children under 5 years of age. The rate of mor- tality per 1,000 during the mouth was 28.62, as compared with 20 45 in the corresponding month of last year.

div.head: STATE OF BROOK.
div.p: STATE OF BROOK.

The MEDICAL OFFiCilt--reiCoried: inspector Williams has taken samples of Eccleston branch of the brook at the usual places, from Spray's Bridge to Messrs. Lyons Bottle Works. All these are free of acid. The samples taken by Inspectos, Houghton from different points in Hardshaw brook are also free of acid. The flow of acid from the St. Helens Chemical Works continues, but in diminished strength, and less in quantity. Acid is found in one of the samples taken from a drain belonging to the Globe Alkali Company. The over- flow from the canal into the brook near Messrs. Lyons' Bottle Works is slightly acid.

LODGING HOUSES. The MEDICAL OFFICER reported: At our last meeting, Inspector Williams reported the application of a lodging- house-keeper in Mount-street, to add an adjoining cottage to his already licensed lodging-house. The inspector objected on the grounds of a want of accommodation in the back yard of ashpit, ezc. It was referred to the Medical Officer to re- port. As the yard accommodation to the said cottage has been increased to the satisfaction of the Medical Officer and the Nuisance Inspector, the license may be granted. Alderman GAMBLE said he should like to know something about the lodging-houses in the town. He had a particular reason for it. Several people had been before the magistrates in cases in which the conducting of lodging-houses was brought into question. A man in charge of such a house was supposed to keep a lot of rough fellows in order. He would propose that the surveyor be instructed to make a return of all houses licensed as lodging-houses, and of all reports made on such lodging-houses during the past year.—This was carried.

div.head: HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT WARRINGTON.

The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) and the Ex-Mayor (Councillor Farelough) were occupied for a considerable time on Monday last, at the Warrington Borough Court, in hearing a case of highway robbery which occurred at Bewsey, on New Year's Eve. The prisoners, Wm. Moran (17), factory hand, John Kearns (16), bottle hand, Michael Flanagan (17), factory hand, and. Charles Pollard (20), forge labourer, were charged with violently assaulting and stealing from the person of John Lee, flatman, when near Bewsey Lodge, at 1-30 p.m., on Sunday, the Ist instant, about 7s. in silver, a pocket knife, and a silk handaerchief, his property. The Clerk said the case had been twice before the court, but the principal offender was still at large.—The Chief- Constable said they had done their best to apprehend Darby Bohan, who used the most violence, but had not as yet suc- ceeded.—John Lee, fiatman, Sankey Bridges, said on Sun- day morning, the Ist instant, about one o'clock, he was on his way from Bewsey Locks to Sankey Bridges. When he got to the end of Bewsey-lane, where it joins Lovely-lane, four or five youths came up to him and one of them asked him for a new year's gift. He replied, "I don't know you, I have not got any new year's gift for .you." As soon as he had spoken one of them "took a running top" at him, struck him on the chest, and "sent him reeling." He recovered himself, and they dragged him down the lane. They took 7s. from his left hand trousers pocket, a handker- chief out of his coat pocket, knife out of his right hand trousers pocket, and a handkerchief from his neck. They then left him. It was very dark where it happened. He had had some drink, but knew perfectly well what be was doing. He could not identify any of the prisoners owing to the glare from a watchman's fire. The silk handkerchief produced was his property, and was taken from his neck. His left hand trousers pocket was torn with the force in taking the money.—David Skidmore, a youth, neighbour to last witness, said on Sunday morning, the Ist instant, about one o'ciock, in company with George Ward, he was retura- ing from his aunt's who lived in Pierpoint-street, where be bad been to let in the new year. When they got to the top , of Bewsey-road they found three watch fires where a railway bridge is being built, and they saw Kearns, Pollard, and. Flanagan tossing money by the light of the fire. They followed witness and his companion to the fires, and while they were there Moran and a bigger man came up. Moran asked them if they had a piece of string to mend his clog. Presently they heard someone coming along singing from the direction of Bewsey Locks. He passed the fire where witness was and had reached the fire where the prisoners were standing. Moran caught hold of him and said" How do you do, Captain. Have you got me a new year's gift 9" Mr. Lee said " No; I don't know you. Is George Clare here 9" Kearns replied " Yes, he issbere," and went to the big man who had meanwhile entered the cabin and fetched him out. Lee asked him, "Is your name George Clare," and he said "Yes." Lee said "You are not George Clare," and the big man replied "Yes, I was bred and born George Clare. I am Irish, but I cannot help it." The big man then ran at Lee with his head and struck him on the breast. He and the four prisoners then backed Lee dawn Lodge-lane, towards Bewsey Lodge. Two of them held up Lee's arms, while two others rifled his pockets. Pollard tried to pull prosecutor's coat off, when the latter's hat fell off. Pollard put it back and joined witness and his friend, Ward, who remonstrated with him for taking part in such a bother, and Pollard made a threatening reply. Twice while the scuffle with Lee was going on, Ward and he attempted to interfere, but the big man ran them away.—George Ward confirmed the evidence of the last witneas.—lnspector Proffitt deposed to apPrehending Moran at his own house in Black- hurst-street, on Sunday evening, the let inst. The same evening he apprehended Kearns, and Flanagan. Pollard was afterwards apprehended by P.S. Spinks. He charged the four prisoners the following morning. Moran said "I have now't to say against it, only I was there. "Kearns said he had nothing to say against it; Flanagan made a similar reply ; and Pollard said "I was there at the same time, and Kearns showed me the silk handkerchief,' and said this will fetch 2d.'" Tne same day the prisoner Moran asked to see wit- ness and made the following statement: "Between one and two this morning I was in company with Rohan, Kearns, and Flanagan, in Bewsey-road. I saw Bohan with silver in his band, and he said 'I have got it.' I said got what," and he said 'the money.";—P.S. Spinks, stated that he appre- hended Pollard on Sunday morning the 2nd lost, at his father's house. He said "I will tell you all about it." He cautioned prisoner, and told him he bad better consider and keep what be had to say until he got to the police station. When they got to the police station he made a statement, in which he admitted being with the Other prisoners, and said Kearrs showed him the silk handkerchief which he said would fetch 21. and he put it round his neck. Inspector Singleton said he heard the atatement made by Pollard, and afterwards searched Kearns, and found the silk handkerchief produced, tied rourad his thigh. Kearns said he found it in ' the gutter when the row was on.—The prisoners were , committed for trial to the assiv.is, Pollard being admitted to bail.

NEW LIEUTENANT FOR Da NCOR N VOLUNTEERS.-Mr Jolliffe, solicitor, has the lieutenancy of the F and G corn- panics of the 2nd C.R.V.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Thursday evening, an old man named William Owen, of Cholvnondeley-street, was crossing the line of rails in Messrs. Gaskell and Dea- con's works, when two wagons were set in motion, and his arm was caught between the buffers and terribly mutilated. He was taken to the hospital, and attended by Drs. McDon- ne] and McLennan, but the injuries were of so serious a nature that the limb had to be amputated. RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND IMR. T. BEA,SLEY.—A special •meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners was held on Tuesday morning, to consider what action sheuld be taken in respect to the writ issued by Mr. Thomas Beasley, late of Waterloo House, Runcorn. Our representa- tive attended the meeting, but Dr. Steele said no reporter could be admitted as the meeting was private. TRE CURACY OF HOLY TRINITY, RUNCORN. This curacy, rendered vacant by the resignation of the Rev. T. Robinson, has been accepted by the Rev. D. Llewellyn, who has for some time acted as chaplain at the church built and carried on at the sole expense of Mr. E. 0. V. Lloyd, of Berth Hall, in the vale of Clwyd. On leaving that district, a geld watch aid ring, and a handsome Bible were presented to Mr. Lloyd as tokens of the esteem in which he was held.

TREAT TO THE BAND AND NON- COMMISSIONED OFFICERS OF THE RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS.—The members of the band and non-commissioned officers of the F and G Companies of the 2nd Cheshire Volunteers were entertained to supper on the night of the 6th inst., by Quartermaster- Sergeant Hankinson, at his residence, Camden House, High- street, Runcorn. During the evening the Quartermaster- Sergeant, in responding to the toast of his health, remarked that the corps being now uuder the command of a captain in whom they placed every confidence, and whose energy and determination had placed them in so sound a condition, he had every hope for the future. "The Health of Captain Hazlehurst" was drunk with enthusiasm.

CHARGE OF STEALING AN UMBRELLA AT FRODSHAM.— On Tuesday, at the police station, Louisa Palmer, a married woman, residing at Frodsham, was charged before Mr. E. A- Wright, with having, on the 2nd November last, stolen an umbrella of the value of 145., the property of Miss Simpson, of Dunsdall, Frodsham. It appeared that on the day in question, a sewing meeting was held at the girls' school- room, Church-street. Miss Simpson attended it, and inad- vertently left her umbrella. Prisoner, on i hat day, was engaged to clean the school, and the next day Miss Simp- son saw the prisoner in the school, and asked her respecting the umbrella, when she denied all knowledge of it. It was found in a pawnshop at Runcorh, where the prisoner had pledged it. The prisoner, in defence, said that she bought the umbrella. She was committed to take her trial at the next intermediate sessions to be held at Knutsford, bail being accepted, her husband in £2O, and two sureties of £lO each.

KINGSLEY.—The annual tea party and concert took place in the National Schools on the evening of the sth inst. A large number sat down to an excellently-prepared tea The concert was one of the most successful ever given at Kingsley. The room was crowded, many from a distance being unable to obtain admission. The following ladies and gentlemen appeared before an appreciative and delighted audience, viz. :—Miss Wyatt, of Acton; Miss James, of Frodsham ; Miss Braun, and Miss Wilding; also Messrs. G. Bebbingtpn, Booth, Farrington, Hitchen, Hilbert, Lord, Nickson, and Parr. The parts they took were all well rendered, and elicited rapturous applause. The result of the entertainmentis the best criterion of its success. After paying all expenses, the handsome sum of £26 6s. 4d. remains to hand over to the churchwardens' fund. HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting of this society was held ou Tuesday evening, when Mr. William Collier read a paper on the " Ashantee Expedition," which was doubly interesting as he (the essayist) is a veteran of that war. Mr. Collier had also with him a copy of Sir Garnet Wolseley's instructions to the officers and men, which they had given to them pre- vious to their crossing the river Prab, which was the centre of ,operations ; this he read to the assembly, and concluded his essay with an illustration of a voyage homewards, after having defeated King Koffee's black army, giving glowing accounts of the receptions they received at the various depots they called at before arriving in England, and also from the crowds assembled at Portsmouth, where they dis- embarked, and Shorncliffe, their station. The following members commented on the paper :—The Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Baguley, R. Tandy, I. Wright, C. W. Brown, T. Miller, and J. Hancock.

INQUEST AT RUNCORN.—On Thursday afternoon, at the Grapes Inn, Halton-road, Runcorn, before Mr. Ridgway, county coroner, an inquest was held on the body of Alice Atkinson, of Porter-street. On Tuesday deceased was con- fined, and about ten minutes to four in the afternoon she re- quested Mrs. Olmen, who was attending upon her, to go to the house of Mrs. Riley, Union-street, Runcorn, who acted as a midwife. She went, and returned with Mrs. Riley. At about 10 minutes to 6 the child was born, and about an hour and a half after deceased went very faint. Mrs. Riley requested John Sheen, with whom deceased had been living, to go for Dr. Bagnall, but deceased would not permit of this, and said she was all right. At about eight o'clock, however, Mrs. Riley insisted on Sheen going for a doctor, which he did, but whilst he was away she expired. Dr. Bagnall afterwards examined deceased, and expressed an opinion that no one was to blame.—The jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes." [ADVERTISEMENT.] THE DEPUTY-CORONER ON UNQUALIFIED MEDICAL ASSISTANTS AT RUNCORN. Runcorn, January 11th, 1882. We, the undersigned, being gentlemen of the jury sitting on the inquiry respecting the circumstances of the death of the child of Mrs. Mary Stanton, in which case a verdict of "Death from convulsions" was returned, attach no blame in any form whatever against Mr. Frederick Charles Salkeld and Dr. Robinson. On the contrary, we think under the circumstances Mr. Salkeld did that which was just and right in the steps he took. (Signed) SAMUEL WORRALL, Foremaa of the Jury. ROBERT GORST Juryman. A PROTRACTED RUNCORN "PLEASURE" L n ARTY.—In the Liverpool Court of Passage on Monday, the case of he Tranmere Ferry Company (Limited) v. Stephens was heard. Mr. Sparrow, with Mr. Tobin (instructed by Messrs. Gill and Archer), appeared for the plaintiffs in the case, and the de- fendent was unrepresented. The action was brought to re- cover £2l for hire of the steamer Kingstown, and £8 damages for breach of contract. In April last the defendant arranged with the plaintiffs to hire the Kingstown for a pleasure trip at a charge of £l5 for twelve hours. A stipu- lation was made that there should be an extra charge of 30s. for every hour beyond the time fixed. On the 22nd May the £l5 was paid, and the steamer proceeded with the party to Runcorn. In returning late at night, the vessel stranded in the river, and the passengers remained all that night and next morning on her amid a scene of indescribable con- fusion. When the steamer got afloat again and arrived at her destination it was found that she was 14 hours overdue, for which the Sum of £l4 was claimed. On the 26th May the defendant entered into another engagement with the plaintiffs for the hire of the Kingstown for five hours, at a charge of £B. In consequence of that arrangement another offer for the hire of the boat was refused, although when the 26th came around the defendant did not call' for it.— Judgment was given for the plaintiffs for £29. SINGULAR CASE OF FRAUD.—A novel kind of matri- monial hoax—which will probably be attended with serious consequences to the hoaxer if he gets into the clutches of the police—was perpetrated the other day on an overlooker living at School-lane, near Preston. On Thursday evening a man, also representing himself as an overlooker, paid him a visit, and stated that he had just arrived from Blackburn, where, he understood, there resided a widowed sister of the School-lane orerlooker, with an encumbrance of four children. He admitted that he was paying court to the sister, and was now prepared to marry her forthwith. He had £3OO in the bank, and several houses, and he thought with that recommendation, coupled with his high personal qualities, the School-lane overlooker ought to receive him with open arms as a prospective brother-in-law. So, too, thought the worthy host, and forthwith proceeded to invite his visitor to make himself at home. The invitation was accepted with great alacrity, a good supper was prepared and discussed, and the party retired for the night. The wedding was stated to have been fixed for the following Thursday, and it was understood that when the marriage had been con- summated the pair should come down to School-lane and have a grand dinner. The so-called Blackburn overlooker departed next morning, after despatching a hearty breakfast, but before leaving the district ordered a wedding dinner at the Withy Tree Inn for a certain day, at an estimated cost of £5, and managed somehow or other to obtain half-a- sovereign on the strength of the order. So far all seemed smooth and straightforward. The stranger apparently knew all about the School-lane overlooker's affairs, and was equally well acquainted with Blackburn and the neighbourhood in which his sister .lived. He also volunteered the information that he was a singer at one of the Blackburn churches. No suspicion was aroused until several days had elapsed, when the School-lane overlooker, hearing no furOer of the affair, made enquiries at Blackburn, and was astonished when in- formed by his sister that she did not know the man, had received no such luck as an offer of marriage, and moreover was fully convincod that the wh9le affair was a rank im- posture, as her brother, if be had had his wits about him, ' could easily have perceived. From that time to this nothing has been heard of the quondam wife-hunter, but the matter, we understand, has been placed in the hands of the police,

WESTON WESLEYAN IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—At the sixth annual meeting, held this week, Mr. James Ball, sen., presided, and Mr. Thsmas Ford was elected president for , the year, and Mr. John Ball secretary. HIGHER GRADE CLASS AT HOLY TRINITY SCHOOLS, RIINCORN.—The managers of Holy Trinity School, Run- corn, have opened a select class, where students may obtain all the advantages of a good English education, under Government inspection, at the rate of 9s. per quarter. MR. BANTOCIE PIERPOINT'S CONCERT AT RUNCORN.— This concert, which will take place at the Public Hall, on Wednesday, promises to be a very successfut one. We have previously spoken of the array of talent which is forth- coming, and we hear that the tickets are going off remarkably well.

COCKHEDGE MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —The tenth weekly meeting of the session, was held on Monday night, in the Mission Room, when impromptu speeches by the members were given upon various subjects. The president of the society, Mr. B. Farrar, occupied the chair. _
SUBSIDENCE OF LAND IN CHESHIRE.—The subsidence in

- - the neighbourhood of Dunkirk, Northwich, and following the comse of the Peover Brook, continues to extend very rapidly. A day or two ago a bank fell in at the foot of the hill near Platt's rock salt mine, which was flooded in 1880. The large volume of water running into the main has raised the brine in the shafts on the Dunkirk fully 30 yards, and it stands now higher than at any time since the great subsidence in 1880. The sinking continues near Ashton's works and holes have recently gone in there to a consider- able depth. The whole district seems sinking fast, and a very extensive lake is forming. A JUDGESHIP FOR Sin Joux HOLEER.—The Tall 211a11 Gazette announces that the Queen has been pleased to appoint Sir John biker, M.P., to succeed the late Lord Justice Lush as a member of the Court of Appeal. Sir John biker was born in 1828, was called to the bar at Gray's Inn in 1854, and was appointed a Q.C. in 1808. He was elected member for Preston, in the Conservative interest, in Sep- tember, 1872, and was, on Mr. Disraeli's accession to power in 1874, appointed Solicitor-General, and in the following year succeeded to the post Attorney-General, which he held until the fall of the Beaconsfield Administration in 1880.

FIRE AT Noßrawic.a.—Between eleven and twelve o'clock on Monday night a fire was observed in one of the storerooms of the Cheshire Amalgamated Salt Company, situated on the banks of the Weaver, at Northwich. An alarm was speedily given, but before the arrival of the engine and brigade the extensive buildings were enveloped in flames. The flames were fed by a large quantity of in- flammable material, and before the fire could be got under two extensive warehouses, a double-roofed stove and store- house, and an engine and boiler-house were burned to the ground. Several hundred tons of salt ready for shipment were considerably damaged, and some valuable machinery and tools altogether destroyed. The loss is estimated at about £2,000.

THE CHESHIRE LINES. —On Saturday evening, a supplementary dinner was held at the house of Mrs. Butter- worth, Ram's Head, Horsemarket-street, to commemorate the opening of the Cheshire Lines Committee's-new works, Battersby-lane. The company comprised the inspectors and foremen engaged at the works. A substantial dinner with seasonable delicacies was served up with the hostess's usual ability. After the tables were cleared, Mr. D. S. Duncan presided, and was supported by. Mr. S. Dale. Various toasts were given and responded to, including that of "The Engineer's Department," "Our Healths," "The Absent In- spectors," "Our Wives and Sweethearts," &c. Songs and recitations were given at intervals by Messrs. Brehan, Dixon, Evans, Everett, Walker, Hemingway, Dale, Devin, and Ward, and a very enjoyable meeting was spent. WALTER BONEHILL LODGE OF 1.0.G.T.—A fruit banquet and entertainment was held at Golborne-street Baptist Schoolroom, on Tuesday evening, in connection with the Walter Bonehill Lodge of Good Templars. There were about 100 members and friends present. The chair was taken by Mr. G. H. Millington, who said he had been a total abstainer for 30 years, and during that time he had worked as hard as any man. Yet he could always work better, sleep better, and eat better by being an abstainer. The following programme was gone through :—Selection, the Band ; duet, Mr. and Mrs. Groves; recitation, Bro. Houghton ; concertina solo, Mr. W. hittaker ; recitation, Bro. W. Gallop ; selection, the Band ; recitation, Mr. Brierley. ANOTHER NIGHT POACHING AFFRAY IN CHESHIRE. —At Crewe police court, on Monday, before Mr. H. J. Tol— lemache, M.P., and other magistrates, Richard Clarke, an elderly man, was brought up under a warrant charged with night poaching on Lord Combermere's estate near Audlem. —Colonel Cotton, who is staying at Combermere Abbey, said that himself and his lordship's gamekeeper went out about midnight for the purpose of trying to ca.tch poachers. They disturbed the prisoner and two others who had nets, on a piece of land near Audlem. He knocked the prisoner down with a stick, and the keeper at once identified him. The two others made off, but returned shortly afterwards with seven more, who hurled a large quantity of stones at him. One of them struck him, and another bit the game- keeper. He saw it was useless to try to overcome them, there being ten against two, and he and the gamekeeper went away.—The prisoner, who had been previously convicted of a similar offence, was sentenced to three calendar months' hard labour.

THE DISESTABLISHMENT OF BELLS.—The law has, in the matter of bells, less disregard for the nerves than regard for the privileges of religion. Secular bells of all kinds have one by one been disestablished in the metropolis. The muffin bell, together with all other noisy modes of adver- tising wares, has been, in theory at least, silenced. The call-bell for ringing workmen up to time is prohibited, like steam whistles and horns, used for the same purpose, with- out the sanction of the sanitary authority. Musical hand- bells are liable to the same suppression as the street organ, the common enemy of all mankind who live above the basement floor. Church bells alone, except at one time the unorthodox bells of Roman Catholics, have been subjected to no statutory repression. Bells in their purely musical function may, if they pass the bounds of the definition of nuisance, be restrained by injunction, as happened in the well-known case of the Roman Catholic chapel at Clapham; but the passing bell, the funeral bell, and the bell for service are not only allowed but enjoined by the canons. Some re- pression on these most disturbing forms of ringing may fairly be asked. Passing bells may well be dispensed with altogether in towns, and funeral bells in the near neighbour- hood of houses might, without impropriety, be required to be closely muffled. Better reminders of mortality are found nowadays in the first columns of the daily newspaper than in the church steeple.—Law Journal. DEATH OF A CENTENAEIAN.—A. remarkable case of longevity is recorded in the death of Mr. R. Chesterton, who had, within 12 days reached the patriarchal age of 100 years. The event took place recently at the residence of his son, Mr. Robert Chesterton, jeweller, Bowling-green- street, Leicester. He leaves a family of four daughters and one son, whose united ages amount to 331 years. There are also in the family 34 grandchildren, 65 great grandchildren, and four great great grandchildren, making the total number of descendants 108, all living. Some years ago one of his sons, Mr. Joseph Chesterton, who died last summer, kept a jewellers' shop in Granby-street, opposite the Old Post- office. He was the first inventor of wrought iron fortifica- tions and floating batteries, dating as far back as 1848. The plans and specifications were presented to the British Govern- ment at that period. Mr. A. Chesterton, of 35, Golborne- street, Warrington, is one of the deceased's grandchildren. Up to within a short period of Mr. Chesterton's death his memory was remarkably retentive. His cheerful and happy disposition rendered him a favourite with all with whom he came in contact. The deceased a few months back was knocked down by a cab, which undoubtedly hastened his end, other- wise there was every prospect of adding some years to his already long and eventful life.
