RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. PROPOSAL TO CLOSE. The annual meeting of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian's Association was held on Wednesday at the rooms in High-street. Mr. Robert Shaw, the President, occupied the chair, and though notice had been sent out to each of the members that a proposal to close the building would be considered, there was only a moderate attendance of members. Mr. B. SMITH read the sixth annual report, from which it appeared the committee were sorry to state that the hopes they indulged in 12 months ago had not been realised. The total membership at the close of last year-106—was then regarded as favourable, but the number, unfortunately, de- creased. This, it was feared, was owing chiefly to the fact of raising the subscriptions from five to eight shillings per year, which amount many el the young men have felt was more than they could afford to pay. The roll of member- ship had also suffered, as heretofore, in consequence of some of the young men having had to leave the town. The num- ber of books in the library catalogue was 507, and perhaps it might have been better had the balance of £2 3s. in, in the hands of the treasurer been spent in the purchase of new books, as it was feared the falling off in subscribers which the committee had to report might be due to the feet that most of the volumes had been in circulation for some time. arid read by most of the members. The fruit banquet left a balance, after payment of all expenses, of £3 15s. 10d. Mr. Nickson kindly prOmised to undertake the instruction of members in shorthand, and a class had been formed con- sisting of four members, and fees amounting to £1 Os. had been handed to him by the treasurer. The number of hon- orary subscribers was 10, with 54 active or associate mem- bers, which gave a total for the year of 64, or a decrease of 42. The financial year had closed with a deficiency of £49 6s. 7d., which was a far larger sum than the balance carried forward last twelve months. Under these circumstances, the committee much regretted to state that they saw no possible way of carrying on the work of the association. After much thoughtful deliberation, they had agreed to suggest the desirability of closing the rooms at as early a date as possible. In conclusion, the committee were sorry that it was not in their power to present a more favourable report, and though their efforts had not been crowned with that success which they anticipated, they felt that notwithstand- ing all the difficulties which had passed upon them, the association must that year, as heretofore, have proved a blessing to many of its members. Mr. J. D. JONES read the treasurer's statement for the year ending 31st December, which showed that the income for the 12 months had been £43 Sc 6Ld, including subscription from Mr. Robert Shaw £lO, members' subscriptions £l9 9s, honorary members £2 2s, donations £2 is, proceeds of picnic £3 13s 4d. tea parties £4 us 10d, subscriptions towards the expense of painting reading room £2 9s, making a total of £4B 8s 6!A. The expenditure included the following:— Balance brought forward 116 198 id, paid on account of rent, rates, and water account £lB 3s 11d, coal account £2 16s, insurance premium 3s 9d, Mr. Yarwood's account for painting reading morn £2 15s, housekeepers' salary £5, printing, stationery, and postage 18s, sundries 8s 111 d, balance in hand £1 3s 10d. The unpaid accounts amounted to £53 14s 7d, and other sums had been received towards this which would leave a balance of 149 Gs 7d. The CHAIRMAN observed that though the reports were considerably better than last year's, they were not anything I like so good as to warrant a continuance of the association. There had been a reduction in the number of members, but they had actually received more money from members' sub- scriptions this twelvemonths than last. He supposed they must reluctantly come to the conclusion that unless such a 1 society was very nearly self-supporting, in a place like , Runcorn, at all events' there did not appear to be any possi- bility of its continued existence. It was not possible for them tp go on in debt year after year. He felt sure that : ever since the association was formed—some six years ago—the committee had done all they possibly could to , make it a success, but as the young people of the town did ' not appear to appreciate its advantages in such numbers as to make it a paying concern, there did not appear to be any prospect' of keeping open. (Hear, hear.) Most of the gentlemen connected with the committee had had very large claims upon them in connection with the various churches I which they were associated with, yet for a long time they had made a sacrifice of time which none of those present could appreciate, in order to carry on that body. No doubt the society had been a means of great good to the young men of Runcorn, and to that extent, it would be much missed. He had fora long time considered that, even with the increased price of the subscription, the committee were not asking the members to pay more than twopence per Week for the many conveniences and privileges connected , with the rooms, yet they could not secure a sufficient num- ber to make them anything like sell-supporting. He was not of opinion that the Mechanics' and Literary Institution had injured the society, because the two bodies were upon 1 such a different foundation. If they could raise between 400 and 500 members, they would not need to be dependant upon anyone. The committee could only express regret that 1 their efforts on behalf of tee young men of the town had not been better appreciated. (Applause). Mr. C. Niciesoen in moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet, said that a few years ago the committee were in receipt of £45 in honorary members' subscriptions, whereas this year they had only amounted to two guineas. Mr. HUMPHRIES seconded the motion, and it was passed. Mr. SMITH moved that the following recommendation of the committee be agreed to :—" That we close the rooms at , the end of March, provided Messrs. Hazlehurst will release us from our engagement." Mr. KNIVETON seconded the motion, and said it appeared to him that they required something like 200 members in order to carry on the institution, arid they had never had more than about half that number. After the statement made by Mr. Nickson, it was quite evident that they could not depend very much upon the help to be given them by the honorary subscribers. Mr. SMITH observed that two members of the committee went out one night for the purpose of visiting the honorary subscribers, and they came back with two shillings. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN had no doubt that the falling off in the annual subscriptions might be accounted for by the depres- sion of trade during the last few years. Many people had had as much as they could do without giving to outsiders. In reply to the Bev. E. WILLIAMS, who remarked that there had for some weeks been a report in the town to the effect that the committee had decided to close the rooms, and this might account for the small amount of two shil- lings being collected, Mr. HUMPHREYS said the visits were I paid about a fortnight ago by himself and Mr. Joues. He (the speaker) believed that the whole of the honorary sub- scriptions paid in 1880 might have been collected last year, if they had been looked after at the right time—(hear, hear); and he was of opinion that they were still good. Mr. RHODES (a member) spoke of the benefit which he found in the association when he came to the town as a stranger. Mr. Garnett, the treasurer, moved to Manchester at the early part of the financial year, and the consequence was that the collection of subscriptions had not been carried out thoroughly. He knew of several members of the Literary Institute who were likely to join them, if the rooms were kept open. The Rev. E. WILLIAMS said they all felt grateful to their President for the liberal support he had rendered the associa- tion since its commencement. He (the speaker) thought they were under some kind of moral obligation to carry on the work of the rooms. He believed they had every reason to expect an accession of members from gentlemen who had in the past been connected with the Literary Institute, but no one would join a moribund society. Many young men, he knew, had derived incalculable benefit from the existence of the association, and what was to becoaie of them if it were closed, as there was no place in the town to which they might go when they left their workshops and offices to read the papers. They knew where many of them would go under such circumstances ! He did not believe in the annual deficits which they had had year by year. The better course would have been for them to have cut their coats according to their cloth. He should not be ashamed of going to much smaller rooms, and they could never be in pleasant circum- stances whilst their expenditure was greater than their income. Mr. J. W. Owl:ran said the rent, rates, and taxes of such a building as that they occupied must amount to about £4O, which was a very heavy sum to meet each twelve months. He advised that they should take one room at a yearly rent of about -.E.10, and sell the larger portion of their valuable furniture and books so as to commence work, free from the curse of debt. Mr. SHAW, seamen's missionary, did not know of any Young, Men's Christian Association in, the country which was entirely self supporting. He knew that the association had,done a vast amount of good. He concluded, his remarks by suggesting several ways in which the sum necessary to meet the deficit might be obtained. Mr. COVFNTRY spoke strongly in the same strain. Mr. HUMPHREYS said that Mr. John Simpson had told him he considered it would be a great pity for the committee to close the association now that the Literary and Mechanics' Institute had become defunct. Mr. JOHNSON also delivered a brief speech in favour of closing the rooms under the circumstances. The Rev. E. WILLIAMS moved, and Mr. SMITH (secretary) seconded an amendment to the effect that the meeting should be adjourned for a fortnight, ha order that several gentlemen (including the Rev. E. Williams, Mr. Shaw, mis- sionary, and Mr. Coventry) should see. what. .c9uld be done to raise the sum required to.pay off, the The amendment was carried by a fair majority, and was ultimately passed unanimously, as a substantive motion, after which the proceedings terminated. div.head: TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES. Continued from page S. On Wednesday evening, in the absence of Bro. B. Kirkus, district secretary, of Liverpool, Mr. T. Horrocks gave another lecture. Mr. S. B. Stringer presided. ,
div.p: TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES. Continued from page S. On Wednesday evening, in the absence of Bro. B. Kirkus, district secretary, of Liverpool, Mr. T. Horrocks gave another lecture. Mr. S. B. Stringer presided. ,

On Thursday evening, about 400 people had tea together. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Misses Hudson, Gaffie, Booth. Birchall, Roughsedge,Smith, Turton, Prescot, Ramsey, sem. Ramsay, jun., Plover, and Mesdames Fair- dough, Smith, Whalley, Burton, Glover, and Reay. At the public meeting which was afterwards held, the following occupied seats on the platform, Bro. R. W. Williams, pre- siding :—Bro. Malins, Grand Worthy Chief Templar of England; Sister A. M. Green Right Worthy Grand Super- intendent of the Juvenile Temple of England; Bro. T. Horrocks, "The converted clown '-" Bro. J. W. Hall, Rev. —. Hunt, and Bro Thomas, Grand Worthy Chief Templar of Wales. The following local officers were also present : Bros. T. Reay, J. Thompson, and W. Rescall, 'Worthy-Vice Templars ; Sister Glover, Sister Regina Hudson; Bros. J. Johnson and J. Wilson, Past Worthy Chief Templars: Bros. T. Harrison, C. Webb, and S. Turton, Worthy Secretaries; Bros. W. Bradshaw, J. Makin, J. Ireland, T. Bald, J. Mcßride, W.V.T. (Runcorn), and J. Faulkner, W.M. (Run- corn.)—After a few remarks from the Chairman, Bro. , THOMAS delivered an address on the advantages of temper- ance. He stated that nine years ago, he opened 118 lodges in the Principality during one winter.—A stirring address, chiefly dealing with the evils of the drink traffic was then given by Sister GREEN.—Bro. Mums was received with muck enthusiasm. He said the Good Templar order was established in the United States more than 30 years ago. In 1847, in the United States, there existed an order of Good Samaritans, formed for the purpose of reclaiming the intem- perate. There existed about the same time another order called the Knight Templars of Jericho, which was formed for the advocacy of the pl ohibition of the traffic in strong drink. Persons acquainted with both orders determined to unite the main features of each, and in doing so combined a part of the names of each, and thus they tormed the Independent Order of Good Tern- piers, whose object was total abstinence for the individual and prohibition by the State. (Cheers.) Every member was made a legislator and a voter in the order with perfectly equal rights. The total abstainer of 40 years' standing was admitted on the same principles as the man who had just been reclaimed from intemperance, and subscribed the same amount. Passing from the United States the order became established in Canada, and in fact existed throughout Noitti America when he (Mr. Malins) united with it at Philadelphia some 14 or 15 years ago. He joined the order in 1867, and on his return to England in 1868 determined to endeavour to extend the order there. On the Bth September, 1868, the Columnia Ledge No. 1 of England was constituted at Birmingham. Since that time their organisation bad had many ups and downs, but it stood to-day :the most aggressive, the most wealthy, the most permanent, and numerically the strongest of all the temper- ance organisations England has ever seen. (Cheers.) At that very moment there were 500 lodges holding their weekly session. In fact, whatever week-night they liked to name, there were 500 lodges in the United Kingdom holding their meetings. Thus they would see they hael 3,000 lodges besides 1,000 juvenile temples. These 4,000 temperance organisations held an aggregate of 200,000 sessions a year, in addition to which, in England alone, they held 1,000 public meetings per month. Their order was meant to bene- fit all ranks. At the last general election their three Good Templar members of Parliament were returned unopposed. He referred to Mr. Benjamin Whitworth, Mr. David Davies, and Mr. Thomas Burt. (Cheers.) Their order was formed on. an equal rights basis and open to both sexes. They could have no better proof of the purity of their proceedings than the presence of the gentler sex. They circulated more temperance literature than any other temperance order in the world, and were thus the means of accomplishing a vast amount of real good. Besides so many adult Templars, they had also 50,000 juvenile Templars, whose motto was " truth, love, and purity." He then went on to speak of the Orphan- age established by the Good Templars' order and the vast contributions that yearly were raised to support it. Of course their great aim as to reclaim those who were drunkards, but they had enrolled many who had never known the bitter- ness of drunkenness, and they would not if they remained with them. The speaker gave statistics showing to what extent a teetotaler's life was held of greater value than a moderate drinker in insurance societies. View it in what- light they would, temperance would stand the most search- ing criticism. Let them come and help them to free the country from its drinking customs. Any kind of a man could drink, but it took a man of will and power to give it up. He asked them to demonstrate that they had the power. People said they could either take it or leave it. They had proved that they could do the one, let them now prove that they could leave it. (Cheers.) After a further selection of music by the band, Mr. T. HORROCKS addressed the meeting. He said that he had that day heard of the establishment of the League of the Cross in Widnes. He wished the movement Godspeed. In the street where the League had been established, he was told that a publican had found it necessary to shut up his house and go to the chemical works. (Cheers.) He urged upon all orders of temperance advocates to join their forces and then every grog- mill bearing the name of Walker in Widnes would soon be closed. (Applause.) Mr. Horrocks then gave several temperance songs, the choruses being joined in with great enthusiasm by the audience. Before the meeting broke up, as on previous evenings, a large number of people signed the temperance pledge. .

PRESENTATION' AT LYMM.—OR Saturday evening the employes of Messrs. M. and F. 0. Moston, of Lymm, held their annual tea meeting in the Mission Hall, Newfield. About 150 partook of tea, the tables being presided over by Mesdames Moston, F. 0. Moston, Ast.ley, Bond, &c., and Misses Moston, Picton, Goldsmith, &c. Subsequently an entertainment was held, in which several ladies and gentle- men took part. Mr. J. Mercer, of Warrington, who sang several songs in character, was encored for his rendering of " The schoolmaster" and "The muffs are out to-day." Mr. Mercer presented to Mr. and Mrs. F. 0. Moston, on behalf of the employes, as a mark of their esteem, on the occasion of their marriage, a copper kettle and china teapot, a set of trays and flower vases, and a brass pan, which represented the Newfield, Lymm, and Rookery shops respectively. Mr. Mercer said he was not aware when he left home that a duty like that was to fall upon him, but having known Mr. Moston for a considerable time, he could not refuse to perform such a duty, when the committee waited upon him for that purpose. Having spoken in high terms of Mr. Moston, he handed the presents to him. Mr. Moston, who was received with applause, said he was at a loss how to thank them for the very handsome presents they had given him. He should look upon them with a feeling of thank- fulness that the people who worked under him had so testi- fied their kind wishes to himself and wife. And he assured i them that it would always be his aim in the future, as t had been in the past, to study their welfare as an employer should. He wished them all a very happy and prosperous New Year. The room was then cleared for the games, which were kept up with spirit for soma time.

div.head: FRODSFIAAI.
div.p: FRODSFIAAI.

THE " MESSIAH " AT FRODSHAM. A very successful rendition of Handel's masterpiece in oratorio's, " The Messiah," was given by the Frodsham Musical Society, in the Town Hall, on Wednesday evening, to a crowded and overflowing audience, the principals being Miss Kate Nono, of Liverpool, soprano; Miss Lily James, of Runcorn, con- tralto;, Mr. Eaton Batty, of Birkenhead, bass; and Mr. Palliser, of Liverpool, tenor (who appeared in the absence through illness, of Mr. Morrison, of Widnes). The orchestra was composed of upwards of 20 instruments from Liverpool, Runcorn, and Widnes. It would be unfair to view the per- formance in a strictly critical sense, as the society has only been formed about three months, aud has had only twelve rehearsals, but under the very efficient leadership of Mr. Argent, the choruses were given by about 60 voices with that precision and swing which would have reflected credit on a society of longer standing. Many difficulties had doubtless to be Overcome, and the °sees-lye heat of the hall seriously affected the string instrummts, but notwithstanding this important disadvantage, the audience strongly testified their appreciation, and individual opinion was freely ex- pressed in flattering terms. If in some parts the treble were somewhat weak it proved that the remaining parts were ex- ceedingly well balanced, and showed that the alto's were of high merit. "Unto us a Child is born "was evidently a great favourite, and the " Hallelejah Chorus" was well rendered, although some slight hesitation was observed at the commencement. The " Amen " chorus, which is generally considered to be a severe test, was given with re- markable spirit and power. Miss Kate Nono possesses a very sweet and effective voice, and "Rejoice greatly, 0 daughter of Zion," and "I know that my Redeemer liveth," were deservedly applauded. She was equally successful with Miss James in "He shall feed His flock." Mss James was in excellent voice and achieved a success beyond the highest anticipations. Mr. Eaton Batty has a clear 'and telling voice and completely carried his audience with him. The air, , "Why do the nations," was rapturously encored, and he kindly repeatedly the whole of the piece. Mr. Palliser's best effort was the recitative and air, "He that dwelleth in heaven," in which he seemed to enter into the theme and spirit of the words of warning. The orchedtra was all that could be desired, the blending of the instruments in the pastoral symphony being most effective. It may be stated that the present Musical Society at Frodshaw is but a re- vival of a successful society which existed a quarter of a century ago, and included both vocalists and instrumentalists, and many of the then members recall with pleasure the efforts that were then made, and take an interest amounting to enthusiasm in the success of the present movement.

ST. ELPHIN'S MOUNT GIRLS' MIDDLF.-CLASS SCHOOL.— I This school, which has been established for the daughters of tradesmen and others, under the direction of the Rector and other managers, is in a very flourishing condition. The following extract from the Government report for 1881 certainly reflects credit on Miss Coupe, the mistress, and her assistants :—" The general tone and discipline of this school are very gratifying, and the instruction is sound, intelligent and successful. The reading is bright and expressive, and is made a valuable in- strutnent in developing the intelligence of the girls, as is also grammar, in which subject I hardly know any school which can surpass this. The needlework also is very creditable."

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

The quarterly meeting of this Board was held in the Board Room at Daresbury, on Thursday. Mr. Edward Grecian , presided, and there were also present Sir Richird Broake, Bart., (ex-officio): Messrs. Joseph Capper, John Mayer, James Knowles, William Wilkinson, J. P. Percival, John Yarwood, William Bradford, James Parr, P. Bennett, H. Houghton, W. M. Salt, W. Beswick, James Handley, James Barber, Joseph Cliffe and H. Linaker (clerk).
PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF THE RIGHW. AT ACTS.

The CHAIRMAN said he had received the following from Col. Harcourt, M.P.:—" Suggestiona for amendments of the Highway Acts, submitted to a meeting of magistrates and others in the Crown Court, at Oxford', by E. W. Harcourt, Esq., M.P., and adopted by the meeting, Nov. 5, 1881. I. That all public roads throughout the country, with the ex- ception hereinafter mentioned, shall be divided into (a) main roads; (b) ordinary highways. 2.—That the above shall not apply to any roads (a) in Boroughs by separate courts of Quarter Sessions, (b) in towns or other p3aces, having or which shall hereafter have, Local Boards under the provisions of the Public Health Acts. 3.—That all roads in each parish, which in the opinion of the county authority are in the nature of through roads, or accommodate principally traffic whose source is not within the parish, shall be deemed to be main roads subject to the following proviso: That each county authority shall submit, for the approval of the Local Government Board, a map showing the roads which in its opinion should he main roads, subject in the same manner to subsequent revisal, if neces- sary, from time to time upon alteration of circumstances. 4.—That all public roads, other than main roads, shall be deemed to be ordinary highways. s.—That the cost of the maintenance of the main roads, and of all bridges thereon, shall be in the first instance defrayed entirely oat of the county rate, and that one-half of such cost shall be repaid to the county from money provided by Parliament (by the ap- propriation of taxes, licenses, or otherwise). 6.—That the cost of maintenance of ordinary highways in each parish shall be defrayed by means of a separate parish rate, made by the vestry and levied upon the basis of the poor rate assessment. 7.—That the entire management and repair of main roads shall be vested in the county authority for the time being, subject to the approval of the scheme of manage- ment froi time to time by the Local Government Board. B.—That the management and repair of ordinary highways shall be vested in one or more waywardens, elected annually by the vestry of the parish. 9.—That two or more parishes may unite for the purposes of road management and repairs, and may appoint a paid surveyor and other paid officers, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board. 10.—That the county authority shall have the same rights 'in Jeference to de:arming ordinary highway autho- rities as under existiog_ Acts. 11.—That the, cost of the management and repair of all roads wb:ch are,. or shall hereafter be, within the area of any tewn, or place being, or which shall hereafter be, a Local Government district, shall (save in the case of now existing main roads, created such by sections 13 and 15 of the Highways and Locomotive (Amendment) Act, 1878), in the area of such district, be defrayed as at present by the Local Board Authority. 12.-I'he above suggestions -have no reference to Scotland, Ireland, South Wales, Isle of Wight, nor to any part of the Metropolis.—Further notes: Main road and parish road accounts to be audited by poor law auditor, as at present. Forms of account in each case to be approved by the Local Government Board. Ratione tenura liabilities to be compulsory." The CHAIRMAN said the document had been before the Oxford magistrates, and they concurred in it. There was no doubt there would be an alteration in the Highway Act, but what that would be they could not tell. The question was whether they would reply to Colonel Harcourt and give him their views. Perhaps he ought to tell the Board that, as regarded the clauses 6 and 8-, what he proposed was that the management and repairs of ordinary highways should be vested in one or more waywardens, selected by the vestry of the parish. That seemed to be going back to the old system of overseers; and certainly that would not work well, because many of the gentlemen in that room had been overseers.
Mr. PARR asked why Colonel Harcourt suggested any alteration in the roads and incurring of unnecessary expense.
The CHAIRMIN suggested that if the Board thought fit to entertain the matter a small committee be appointed to deal with it.

Mr. PERCIVAL proposed that a committee be appointed, to consist of the Chairman, the Vice-Chairman, and the Clerk. Mr. BENNETT said he thought a great portion of the ex- penses should be borne by the county, and paid out of the county rate. They would, he thought, as a Board, be losers by the adoption of the suggestions contained. in the paper just read, and he proposed as an amendment that the docu- ment be laid upon the table. The CLERK said he had thought about the matter, and believed that the Board would suffer by the alteration. Mr. WILKINSON seconded the resolution, and upon the respective motions heing put the amendment was carried.

div.head: PROPOSED HIGHWAY IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: PROPOSED HIGHWAY IMPROVEMENTS.

The CLERK said he had recived the following communi- cation from Messrs. White, Mac E'er, and Co., respecting the proposed widening of the back lane at Fogs Farm : "Estate Offices, Warrington, 17th December, 1.881.. Dear Sir,—Enclosed we beg to hand you tracing showing pro- posed straightening and widening cf the back lane at Fogg's Farm. We propose to make the lane 25ft. wide from fence to fence as our client'sl(Mr. Marson) land goes on both sides, and then the new line will be 121 feet from the centre of the roadway where he owns one side only. Mr. Mayer the way- warden of the district, met us on the ground and agreed as to the width of the road. As regards the pipes required, Mr. Marson is prepared to put them in at his own cost, but we think that the Board may reasonably be asked to contribute smiething towards it. We shall be obliged if you will kindly bring the matter forward at your next meeting, and in the meantime we will arrange to meet your surveyor on the ground and see how the drainage can best be carried out."

Mr. MAYER, in reply to the chairman, said he thought the arrangement suggested would be very fair if Mr. Marson asked the Board to pipe the ditches, that he should give greater width. The CLEF K : Ti a letter says Mr. Marson is prepared to do it and pay all the costs. Mr. BENNETT.: Who will be most benefited by this altera- tion?

Mr. MAYER thought the township would be most benefited. It was decided not to object to the proposed alteration. A SURCHARGE REMITTED. The CLERE said the following bad been received with reference to the recent surcharge on tte Surveyor :—" To John Darbyshire, District Surveyor of thii Highway Board of the District of the Daresbury Division of the Hundred of Bucklow.—Whereas, the Local Government Board have re- ceiv( d from you an appeal against a disallowance of the Sum of £9l 3s. 2d., made by the auditor of the Cheshire audit district at the audit of your accounts for the year ended at Lady Day, 1881, in a book of account kept by you as District Surveyor of the Highway Board of the above named district. This is to certify, that the Lecal Government Board, having duly inquired into and considered your appeal, have found that such disallowance has been lawfully made, but tint the subject matter thereof was incurred in such circumstances as make it fair and equitable that the same should be remit- ted, and they do hereby direct such disallowance to be remitted accordingly. As witness my hand, this 30th day of November, 1881.—Jomg LAMBERT, Secretary, acting on. behalf of the said Board under the authority of the general order, dated the 26th day of May, 1877."

LIVERPOOL CORN.—There vvaa a moderate attendance at our Exchange to-day, and wheat, which was quiet, met with a fairly good inquiry at barely last Tuesday's quotations. Flour was steady, but not active. In Indian aorn there was rather more business passing at 5s 19id to 5s lid per cental for mixed American, and at 6s to 6s 21d per rental for round. Two youths who in the late esamination at the coring - ton Mechanics' Institution in connection with the Science and Art Department gained three years' scholarships in the Dublin University, where l they afterwards proceeded, have been recalled on account of an irregularity having been dis- covered in connection with the examination in question, and the secretary to the evening classes has been required. to resign. •

fIMERLTION SOCIETY. —The Manchester District Branch Committee are making arrangements for a meeting to be held in the Free Trade Hall, on Tuesday, January 31st, 1882, for the advancement of the principles o religious equality. Many well-known supporters of the movement have engaged to be present. Events have so hurried on the necessity and the desire for Disestablishrnent within and without the Established Churches on both sides of the border that this meeting will have mor4 thau %siva interest and political weight.

div.head: LATEST NEWS,
div.p: LATEST NEWS,

Last night, while two policemen were lying in atnbu-Sh near Zrimoleag-e., a man fired into be house of a farmer suspected of payilig rent. The police ebased the man some distance but failed to catch him. His Royal Highness the Prince of Wa!es; who has been

(on a visit to Lord Stamford, at Bradgate Pa, left yesterday afternoon, and passing through Leicester, where thettreets were decorated, proceeded by special train to Lo4don. A PAUPER SENTENCED TO DEATH.— At Cie Wilts- As- sizes at Devizes, yesterday, Charles Gerrish, a pauper, was sentenced to death for having thrust a red hot poker into the nesk of another pauper named Coleman, in the work- house.

The passenger train from Stoke to Leek had a nayrrow es- cape yesterday afternoon. When near Backnell station the foremost carriages collided with a brake van, whist, at- tached to an engine, was slowly entering the siding. Several door handles were tirn off and windows broken, bet- for- tunately the carriages did not leave the metals. One passenger was slightly cut, but beyond this no one-was hurt. •

Yesterday two. Land League demonstrations took plan' in the Loughrea district, one at Kill eenadeema, and the other at Killimore. Triumphai arches had been erected, and drum and fife bands attended. The proceedings ;etre orderly, and after resolutions had been passed, sympathising with the prisoners arrested under the Coercion Act,.the demonstra- tions concluded with loud and prolonged cheers' for the suspects.

At an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Oak Spinning Company, Limited, at Oldham last night, it was resolved to increase the share capital of the company from £BO,OOO to £lOO,OOO. A new mill is to be built at an expected average cost of .£2 per spindle. It was stated that the co-operative and limited liability companies in Oldham realised an annual dividend of £150,000, besides depreciation on fixed stock to a like amount, giving a total of more than a quarter of a-million annually.

A Central News telegram from Paris yesterday, says France has consented to prolong the present treaty Of com- merce for one month, from the 6th of February, to, permit further negotiations with a view to coming to some a:-range- ment as to a new treaty with England. The 111iniisterial journal, 77te Paris, states that the Government will to- day demand a vote of confidence. Among the articles for the revision of th Constitution is one to abolish public prayers at the opening of the L'essiun.

THE EXTRAORDINARY CONFESSION.—The excitzment as to the fate of Johnson and Clowes continues to increase in Leek and neighbourhood, and the decision of the Home Becretary is anxiously awaited. A man named Rogers, living in Leek, who formerly worked with Brooks, states that he heard him say long ago that he could get two men out of gaol if be opened his mouth, In azcordance with instructions from the Home Office. Johnson and Clowes were removed from the Chatham con- vict prison yesterday morning to Mil'bank Penitentiary preparatory, itis understood, to their immediate release. _

Miss Macauliffe, Miss Harrigan, and two other ladies of • Drumcollogher Land League were charged before Newcastle, County Limerick, magistrates yesterday with having held a meeting of the Ladies Land League at Drumcollogher. The constable in charge of the case said he found defendants and fifteen other ladies holding a meeting and called on them to disperse. They refused, and he then arrested them. The magistrates after hearing the case retired, and returning in an hour said the majority had decided that it was an illegal act to hold a ladies Land League meeting.—Defendants were therefore ordered to keep the peace and find sureties, or in default to be imprisoned one month.—Defendants re- fused, to find bail, and were committed to prison. The case will be brought before the Queen's Bench. MR. BRADLAUGH AND THE PREMIER.

Lt Plymouth, on Thursday, Mr. Bradlaugh explained his position in the constitutional struggle now pending. He observed that the keenest thing he felt was the attempt of the House of Commons members, who had not courage of their utterances, to stab Mr. Gladstone with the stiletto of the bravo. He could not but pay his tribute to the grand old man who, almost at the end of his public career, stood a giant be- side pigmies and wasps, and wretched things who were assailing him through the Speaker 32solutiors supporting Northampton in the constitutional struggle, were passed by immense majorities.

div.head: PRESTON ELECTION. A LIBERAL CANDIDATE.
div.p: PRESTON ELECTION. A LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

A deputation of Preston operative spinners waited upon Mr. Thomas Mottershead yesterday, to ask him to stand as a candidate for the borough. This he consented to do if asked by the united Liberal party. The following letter from Sir Stafford Northcote, the leader of the Opposition, has been received at Preston this morning :—" Burghley House, Stamford, Jan. 12, 1882.—Dear Sir,—Your letter of the 10th has been forwarded to me from Exeter, and only reached me this morning. I have telegraphed to you that I think the name excellent. Mr. Raikee was one of the best, if not the very best, chairman of the Committee of Ways and Means that I have ever known, and his presence in the House of Commons would be of the highest value to us next session, when the question of the rules of the House and methods of dealing with obstruction would come prominently forward.—Wishing you a triumphant success, I remain faith- fully yours, STAFFORD H. NORTIICOTE.

TRE PRESTON VACANCY.--Mr. Raikes has consented to stand as a Conservative candidate for the vacant seat for Preston. Sir John biker's valedictory address has been issued. He remarks that the position to which he has been appointed is one of great dignity and importance, and which any member of the profession might be proud to hold. He has endeavoured, he says, during the term, now nearly ten years, in which he has represented Preston, to serve the borough faithfully, and he assures his former constituents that it is in some respects with very great regret that he relin- quishes the position of their representative. On Thursday, Mr. H. Cecil Raikes arrived at Preston, and addressed a number of Conservatives. He referred briefly to the state pf Ireland, Parliamentary procedure, and local option. He ;eared that the proposals to be made by the Government as to the conduct of debates would make legitimate opposition almost impossible, without punishing the obstructionists. He declared himself opposed to the principle of "local option."

THE CHRISTMAS TREE AT ST. JAMES'S SCICOOL.—The sites from the Christmas tree which was held in St. James's schoolroom, Latchford, last week, realised £24, which amount will be added to the funds of the church.

DELIVERY OF PASSENGER? LFGGAGE.—Passengers by the London and North Western Railway when proceeding to London, Birmingham, Liverpool, and Manchester will, in future, have no trouble in looking after their lugguge. The company, following the American custom, have extended their arrangements so as to enable the public using their lines to have their luggage sent to any given address in the above places by parcel carts (within the usual limits) at a uniform charge of sixpence per package. The packages must be fully and legibly addressed to the place of delivery, and the passenger has only to see that the luggage is properly booked at the time of starting. He will receive a voucher in exchange for the luggage, and need have ro. further concern about it until its arrival at his residence or destination. There are fifty stations, including Warrington, Chester, Crewe, and Wigan, from which the luggage can be booked.

BANKRUPTCY OF A WARRINGTON ACCOUNTANT. —3lr. John Lea, accountant, late of Commercial Chambers, War- rington, has just filed his petition in bankruptcy, an 4 the first meeting of creditors was held yesterday, at the Office of Mr. Tunstall, accountant,4'Sankey-street. Mr. McMaster, of the firm of Clare and McMaster, solicitors, Liverpool, presided. Mr. L. Voisey (Messrs. Davies, Voisey,. an 4 Davies,) attended on hohalt of a number of creditors and persons interested in business transactions arising out of Mr. Lea's liquidation. The statement of affairs sukmitted iie die debtor showed the liabilities to be, unsecured creditors, £1,200; partly secured creditors, £C93 9s. 41.; and fully:secured creditors, £2,273- 7s. ed.; total, £4166 16s. 10d. The assets were estimated at £271 Os. lid. After some discussion. the meeting decided to liquidate by arrangement, and Mr. Voisey was appointed trustee. Mr.M'cMaster, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, solicitor, Warring- ton, and Mr. Longdin (Messrs. Nicholson and White) were appointed a committee of inspection. There is very little probability, it is stated, of ths creditors receiving* an divi- dend. The question of the debtor's discharge was deferred to a future meeting.

CONCERT AT THE WORKHOUSE.—A praiseworthy endeavour amusementhas a n.d delight been made to relieve the monotony of the existence of the inmates of the Warrington Union Workhouse during the long winter evenings. The movement was commenced a b short time ago by the Roy. B. B. Prescott, vicar of Christ's Church, Latchford, who, with the assiEtanco•of a number o! friends, givenelisger to l the institution, and also to the poor children who have been left to the care of the Guardians. Last evening another ' concert, promoted by Mrs. Wilkinson, wife of the Work- house Chaplain, was 'given, and was equally 2 successful as its predecessors. The chair was occupied by the Rev. B. B. tchoen ca2gr aged ts awnhdicinhflr have aiNie nm affordedsdeodf Prescott, and there were also present the Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, the Roy. E. St. A. Duke, Major Cartwright, Mr. Barlow, the Master (Mr. Mackey), &c. The programme songs by Miss Woods, Miss Smith, Mr. fburnam and Mr. J. Mercer; pianoforte duets by the Misses Geddes, a reading by the Bev. E. St. A. Duke, a carol by Maters Scattergood and Radford, and a recitation by Master W, Seed, all of whom acquitted themselves with great credit. The concert concluded with votes of thanks to the chair- man, Mrs. Wilkinson, and those who had taken part in the entertainment, who are deserving of pr3be for the inteieet, . they have shown in the poor folks.

div.p: MIL

WARRINGTON BLUE COAT BROTHERLY SOCIETY. The annual dinner of the members and friends of this society took place in the Assembly Room of the Lion Hotel, Warrington, on Monday, which was well attended. An ex- cellent bill of fare had been provided, but the viands would have been better enjoyed if some of them had not been allowed to grow cold and the waiters had been a little more attentive to the guests, a circumstance which was commented upon. The kind and genial countenance of the president of the society, Dr. John Bowes, was also missed, and his serious illness had a somewhat depressing effect, although the gathering was decidedly pleasant and harmonious. Col. Ireland Blackburne, M.P., presided, and Mr. E. Auckland occupied the vice-chair in the absence of Dr. Bowes. There Were also present :—The Mayor (Ald. Picktnere), Captain Reynolds, Mr. Ed. Greenall, jun., Mr. H. B. White, Mr. E. J. Nicholson, Mr. Charles White, Alderman Webster, Mr. J. White, Mr. J. H. Gornall, Rev. T. Bridge, Rev. E. St. A. Duke; Messrs. T. Morris, T. Sutton, J. Warburton, G. Shaw (Stretford), W. H. Bowes (Linslade), J. O'Neill (Liverpool Blue Coat Brotherly Society), W. S. Burgess, T. S. Burgess, J. O'Brien, S. Birtles, J. Povev, W. Chester, Newns, R. D. Toplis, W. Warbuton, T. Warburton, Chester (Withington), Forshaw, W. Porter, J. Whittle, T. Lane, T. Hill, W. Green, D. Jones, J. B. Isaac, Vernon, R. Hewitt, J. Stanistreet (Manchester), J. Lea, jun., Thos. Lea, J. Lea, J. Allen, C. Bowes, T. Clare, G. Roughlev, P. Morris, T. Whittaker, J. Ashcroft. J. A. Short, Wareham, J. Baines, T. Rowlinson, _ _

and A. Mackie. • After justice had been done to the good things provided, the Chairman called upon Mr. FORSHAW to read the annual report. Before doing this Mr. Forshaw stated that he had received letters of apology from a number of gentlemen who were unable to be present. Sir Richard Assheton Cross, M.P., wrote stating that the meeting of the Royal Commission prevented him being present, but he hoped the gathering would be a very successful one. He had received a letter from Alderman Joseph Davies, which stated that business of importance kept him away, but he wished to be remembered to the worthy Chairman, and asked him to express his hearty desire that the dinner might be a success. Mr. Marson wrote :—" As I shall notbe able to be present at the dinner of the Warring- ton Blue Coat Brotherly Society to-night, I beg to enclose a sovereign towards the expenses." (Applause.) He had also received letters of apology from :—Mr. H. Stanton, Lieutenant Colonel Greenall, Mr. Thomas E. Withington, Messrs. J. Charlton Parr, P. Stubs, Jas. Nicholson, James Marson, Joseph Davies, Jno. Tinsley, and P. Smith, Rev. Canon Greenall, Messrs. John Pearson, Thomas Litton, W. Robinson, Joseph Harrison, C. M. Merchant, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. Edwin Jones, Messrs. James Birchall, Chas. Skinner, Councillor Percival, Councillor Monks, Messrs. Thomas Hough (Barnard Castle,) W. Woodhead (Leek), Thomas Rigby (Preston Brook), C. Twice, D. W. Finney, J. Smith (Kingsbridge, Devon,) Sortwell (Oldham,) Hardy, (Chester), J. Hartley, G. Crosier, (Manchester) J. Finch, W. Sanson, W. Brobbin, Thos. Leather, Edward Gibbon, W. Taylor (St. Helens), J. W. Ptitchard, Brakell (Liverpool), Richard Davies, P. Winstanlev, J. Winstanley, H. J. Gaskell, J. Gaskell, S. E. Hughes (Latham), G. Gleave, W. Wilcock, W. Whittaker, S. Davies, Langhorne, W. H. Robinson, W. Dannett,and Thos. Ashton. The report, as adopted on the 20th ult., was as follows : "The committee, in presenting their twenty-seventh annual report, are glad to state that the work of the society during the past year has been carried on quietly, efficiently, and they believe successfully. The chief objects of the society are the visiting of children after they leave school, render- ing pecuniary assistance where necessary, and the making of grants of clothing, itz., to enable them to present a decent exterior, and thereby encourage their regular attendance at public worship. These objects are and have always been kept steadily in view by the committee, and the experience of carrying those objects into effect for over a quarter of a century proves the necessity of such a society. The com- mittee now adopt a plan practised by many other similar societies, viz., that of meeting applications in part, and they find that the adoption of this plan proves very advantageous. Among other things it encourages thrift among the boys and girls, and enables the society to extend its benefits over a larger area. The committee again repeat that great en- couragement would be afforded them by a more general co- operation of those who are indebted to the institution for their education and training, either as day scholars or Blues, and who as yet have not become members of the society. If all old scholars rallied round the society and became mem- bers, the funds would be increased, the committee stimulated in their exertions, and the sphere of the society's usefulness largely extended. That the benevolent aim the society has in view is appreciated, not only by those who have felt its value but also by others, is proved by the continual increase of subscribers. The committee take this opportunity of - reminding their friends that left-off clothing would be gratefully received. There is nothing remarkable to mention that has occurred in the history of the society during the past year. The committee are glad to announce that the society's financial position is of a satisfactory character, there being a balance to the credit of the society's account at the savings bank of £76. The committee again desire to express their sincere thanks for the enceurag,ement afforded to the society by the trustees, and at the same time earnestly hope that by continued exertions they may still continue to receive the same favour and support." (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN, who was heartily received, said: Mr. Mayor, gentlemen, and brother Blues, I think I am not doing wrong in addressing you as brother Blues, having so long had an intimate connection with all those societies hav- ing reference to the good of the Blue Coat School. (Applause.) I address you in the first place as Chairman with the utmost regret that I cannot see at the end of this table our excellent and worthy friend T r. Bowes. (Applause.) There is not a man in this room who does not join with me in the utmost regret at his absence, and who does not pray that he may recover and come among us again. (Hear, hear.) At any rate I hope he will be satisfied with the re- sult of this meeting. He has been long connected with the society, he has looked after it, and brought it to its present _ excellent position. I think we shall rejoice if he is satisfied when he hears to-morrow what has taken place this evening. (Hear, hear.) The first toast I have to propose is one that - will need no words of mine to commend it to your notice. It is "The Queen," whom God preserve. (Applause.) It is not necessary to say much on this subject to loyal Englishmen assembled at their banquets or public meetings, because they love and regard their Queen with the utmost veneration. (Applause.) The toast being drank with the _ singing of the National Anthem. The Chairman next gave 'The Prince and Princess of Wales and the rest of the Royal Family," and referred to the enthusiastic reception accorded to the Prince and Princess of Wales at Liverpool, - to the other Royal princes at Manchester, when Lancashire men vied with each other how best to show their loyalty to the Queen. This toast was received with the singing of " GERI bless the Prince of Wales." The Mayon, who was greeted with much applause, said: I have the honour to propose "The Church," coupling with it the "Bishop and Clergy of the Diocese." This is about the first time I have had the honour to propose this toast. At the same time, I think there is no man in the kingdom who can agree with it more heartily and sincerely than I can. The Church of England is doing a great work, and now that we have got a man like Dr. Ryle, of Liverpool, whose heart is in his work, I think we are very well served as far as the Bishop is concerned. (Applause.) The Church ef England has within its pale a large number of gentlemen • who devote themselves to the service, and do their best to -• meet the spiritual wants of all in the kingdom. I have not been accustomed to propose this toast, but when I look round and see that we have a "duke" to lead us on— ilauglater)--aand if we tome to the waters of strife a 1-‘ bridge " over them, I think we are very happily situated In Warrington. (Laughter and applause.) We have a I shining light in our friend the Rev. T. Bridge. I am glad he is getting on so well, and I think he is a pattern and an example to all his brother Blues. He has done that which he believed to be right, and has gone on prospering since he left the Blue Coat School of Warrington. (Applause.) I beg to propose the toast which has been entrusted to my care, but I will not except the ministers of all other denomi- nations. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Rev. T. BRIDGE in responding, said: The duty of res- ponding to a toast became a pleasure when one had to reply to such kind words as those used by the Mayor. He was always vleased to come to these meetings, because he thought they .ended to do what the Church is always striving to do, eamely, to make men of one mind, and to make them in eality brothers. There are too many influences at work now separate those who have in early times been associated ogether. There is the bitterness of party politics the ran- cour of religious strife, the differencesof class, and the vary- ing interests of self. These things tended to separate them, and it was such societies as these which promoted that kindly feeling that tended to keep men together. Was not that one of the great objects the Church set herself? The Church was now making a great effort to do her duty. She had awoke from her lethargy, and was stretching every arm, not only to give meat in due season to those who belong to her, but to bring into her fold those who from her own careless- ness had been obliged to seek that food which they ought to have got in their own spititual homes. They needed such institutions as this school to give a good religious education, and earnest men who would devote their time, energy and attention to promote the good cause, and to make the Church one grand brotherly society, where all will be love and peace. (Applause.) The Rev. E. St. A. Denen also responded and referred to the imstruction the children in the Blue Coat School received in the principles of the Church of England. Alderman WEBSTER, in proposing "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," said: I do not know on what principles of selection I have been appointed to propose this toast, cer- tainly not that rendered so celebrated by Mr. Darwin, the "selection of the fittest," because it would be impossible to find a more unfit person to propose such a toast. I am essentially a man of peace, and in the presence of our chairman and other military men I feel a diffidence in going upon untrodden groudd. I think you will agree with me that the selection is not a very happy one. (Laughter.) However, I will Yield to no one in my respect for the army, navy, and reserve forces. I esteem and honour them; and I think the British army is respected over the entire world. I fully coincide with the observations of the chair- man with regard to the absence of our dear friend Dr. Bowes. It is a matter of extreme regret to all that now, for the first time since the establishment of the society, he is stricken down by illness and unable to be present. I hope the report he will receive of the success of the meeting, and our regret at his absence, will be pleasing to him. I hope God may grant him speedy restoration to us, for his is a hand that cannot be spared in the work he has undertaken. I know that in this society his fondest hopes are centred, and

Mr. JOHN WHITE, in giving the toast of "The Mayor and Corporation of Warrington," said, I do not think we suffi- ciently appreciate the services rendered by the Mayor and Corporation. Some of us think there is a great deal of honour in being called Alderman, Councillor, or Mayor, but I do not think the highest dignity, that of Mayor, sufficiently compensates for the time and trouble given. I think the Corporation of Warrington will compare favourable with the corporations of other towns in Lancashire. (Hear, hear.) We are represented in the Council Chamber by men of great ability, intelligence, and respectibility. I don't know when we speak of the Corporation that we confine ourselves to the aldermen and councillors. I should be inclined to extend the toast to the paid officers of the Corporation. We are singular fortunate in our Town Clerk, Borough Treasurer. Borough Surveyor, Medical Officer of Health, and Chief Constable. (Hear, hear.) They are men who have the con- fidence of the members of the Corporation and the whole of the inhabitants of the town. (Hear, hear.) I suppose I have been called upon to propose this toast because I never was in the Corporation, and because I have no intention of ever going into it. (Laughter.) Therefore I can speak of the Corporation with the greatest impartiality. Ido not say that the Corporation is as laear perfection as it is possible for a Corporation to be. If the Corporation would widen Bridge-street, take up the setts, give us better gas, reduce the rates, and place some restriction on those cumbersome vehicles on four wheels which go about the town at all hours of the day, not leaving behind them the most delightful of odours, the Corporation would leave nothing to be desired. (Laughter and applause.) I couple with the toast the name of the Mayor. He has filled the office with great ability, dignity, and unbounded hospitality. (Applause.) And he has made it very difficult for any one to follow him, se difficult, that I think the suggestion which has been made will have to be carried out, that he occupy the position for the term of his natural life.' (Laughter.) Ido not know whether he. is prepared to so; but we have such a good mayor that we have no desire to change. (Applause.) I see no reason why we shoul4 change at four years. (A voice: " Seven years," and applause.) The MAYOR, responding, said: This is not the first time, as you may well suppose, that I have responded to this toast. Ido so with very great pleasure, because you have received it so graciously, and Mr. White has proposed it in such handsome terms. He has been too flattering. He tried to throw a little cold water on the Corporation at first, but ended his speech by saying that Warrington was one of the best governed towns in the kingdom. The Corporation, since I have been connected with it, has endeavoured to do the best for the town, and every subject brought under the notice of the Council is carefully considered. We do the best we can for the ratepayers. The result is that you have a town very fairly governed, and I will take credit to myself, as well as the other members of the Corporation, that the town is very well governed. (Hear, hear.) You have good streetS and sewers, and I am in hopes that in a short time, I will not say how long, the price of gas will be considerably reduced. The gas question is one about which there has been a good deal of fighting. We have excellent new works, and when they begin to pay, and we have paid off a little of the debt, you will find that we shall have our gas bills as low as in any town in England. Mr. White made a refe- rence to sanitary matters. lam afraid that although cer- tain vehicles go about the town wh:ch disturb one's olfactory nerves, you forget that the air we breathe at night is purer than it was, in consequence of the ash middens having been taken away. When a man goes to bed he is in his weakest state, and if he has not pure air the doctors will tell you that his health must suffer. And I believe that the decreased death rats of Warrington is in a great measure caused by those dirty ash middens and cesspools being taken away. Reference has been made to the rates. They are rather high just now, but the Sanitary Committee have a large piece of work before them. Other towns are in the same condition, and have had to spend a large amount of money to carry out a system of reform in sanitary matters. That causes an in- crease of rates. That will, of course disappear in time. You have an infectious diseases hospital. Politicians of all kinds in Warrington once said they would have a free hos- pital. Politics had their way. The Whigs, Tories, and Radicals vied with each other and said, "We must have a free hospital," but they never thought of the cost. The cost of that free hospital is nearly £2,000 a year. That is not a small sum for a town like Warrington to have to pay. I have always thought that some charge should be made for the admission of patients. I will not further discuss the matter, but conclude by thanking you for the kind manner in which the toast has been received. (Applause.) The VICE-Clean:max proposed the health of Dr. Bowes. He said he regretted to hear that their friend was so dangerously ill, but hoped he would be speedily restored to health and strength. The toast was drunk with musical honours, and cheers were given for Mrs. Bowes. Mr. BOWES, jun.. responded on behal f of his father, and said he should convey to Dr. Bowes the kind expressions uttered, and thanked those present for their sympathy. Mr. E. J. NICHOLSON proposed "The Warrington Blue Coat Brotherly Society," and said: The society has been instituted for the purpose of supplying the place of a father, a parent, or a guardian to a young man or woman at time most important period, perhaps, of their career, namely, when they are released from the ties of school and are thrown upon the world to fight out their own destiny, and left to their own powers and feelings as to what is right and wrong. (Hear, hear.) This society Steps in when the schoolmaster has stepped out, and assists the young people to make their way in the world so new to them, and for which they are so ill-prepared. This society was instituted Dr. Bowes more than a quarter of a century age, ana that is a long time in the life of most present. He hes fos- teredtl it, kept it up, and encouraged us; and believe this first is the time in the history of this society he has not been present at this antimal. gathering.
