WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Thompson, judge. THE GROCER AND THE BEERSELLER.—Mr. Massey ap- peared for a Mr. Williamson, grocer, who sought to recover £9 odd from Mr. Doodson.—Mr. Massey said that an order hae been made, but nothing had been done to pay off the debt. They now asked that an order of 10s. a month be made. The defendant was a beerhouse keeper in one of the most populated neighbourhoods of St. Helens, and in addition to that he collected money on commission.—Defendant (excitedly) : What Mr. Massey here speaks is an abominable story. lam not collecting ; lam only travelling now for pictures. We came to an arrangement with Mr. Williamson, at least my wife did, and that is the reason I did not appear against the default summons. He made arrangements with my wife that 63. per month be paid. He, however, came and sold me up. The house has never done as well since, and lam only keeping it on until the week end. I should have attended to the summons if arrangements had not been made, but now he has taken the business cut of my hands. —His Honour : It is very foolish of you to let him get into I debt to the amount of £9.—Mr. Williamson: He was in al position to pay then.—His Honour: Very well then why did you allow him to get into debt ?—Mr. Williamson: Well, he wanted me to allow him to have groceries on credit as he was going into this beerhouse.—An order of Gs. a month was made. ACTION AGAINST THE TREASURER OF A ST. HELENS SOCIETY.—John Lea, publican, East-street, St. Helens, was sued by Thomas Forrest, liquidator of the Lily of the Valley Lodge of Free Gardeners, for whom Mr. Massey appeared, for the sum of £l2 2s. 3P.—Mr. Massey said the plaintiff was suing the treasurer of the lodge, John Lea, for the above-named sum belonging to the lodge. On the 29th October, the lodge was called together to consider the insol- vency of the lodge, and on explanation and an account of the lodge being made to the members, it was resolved that the society be wound up and that Forrest should get in the estate of the society, and that after the payment of all accounts that the balance in his hands should be divided equally amongst the members. The defendant Lea attended that meeting, signed the deed for the dissolution, and also admitted that under the heading "Assets of the society— funeral fund" there was a sum of £l2 2s. 31d. So far there was nothing to connect the defendant with that sum, but he would point to the fact that the item was there, and if he (Mr. Massey) could show that defendant was treasurer of the funeral fund, he asked that His Honour would hold that the liquidator was entitled to a verdict. There was one of the auditors of the society present, who would say that the accounts of the society had been audited and certified to be correct. Unfortunately for the plaintiff's side, the secretary of the society, who principally had to do with the books of the society, was not able to leave his house, being in a very I bad state of health. The secretary would have been of material assistance to them in proving their case. However, they were obliged to do the best they could, but he thought after his Honour had heard the evidence and seen the deed, and heard what took place between Forrest, Anders, Lea, and others at the time of the meeting as to that particular amount; he would have no doubt about the matter. That particular amount was mentioned as being in his hands, and he never in any way repudiated his statement, which ought to leave and would leave the impression on his Honour's mind that the amount was a correct one owing from Lea to the society. In March, 1881, the balance according to the books in the defendant's hands was £4 ss. sp. • In December, March, and June three sums were taken from the sick fund and placed to the funeral fund. Some time ago the society was before his Honour as defendants in the action, and there were two funds—the funeral fund and the sick fund. The amounts transferred to the funeral fund were a sum of £3 18s. 6d., and two sums of £3 7s. Bd. Lea was treasurer of both funds, so that really no money changed hands, and he ought still to have had in his possession £27 145., the only change being that the funeral fund would be increased and the sick fund decreased. The money in his hands in respect of the sick fund would be reduced to £l7 Os. i and increase his liability n regard to the funeral fund -to £l4 19s. 3P. The claim was made up of that aniount, less what Lea had already paid at the winding up of the society, thereby leaving the. balance of £l2 23. 3p. Those accounts had been audited and found correct by the auditors of the society, Thos. Houghton and James. The defendant had £2 2s. 341. in his posses- sion so that there were exactly £lO wro lg.—Thomas Forrest said he was present at the time of the audit. Lea was shown the amount owing by him. Witness was asked if he could read, when he replied in the negative.—His Honour: Do they employ a liquidator who can't read ?—Cross-examined by Mr. Riley, witness did not know what the item was that had been scratched out of the book, as he never had anything to do with the books. He believed that Lea at the meeting said he had £lO missing, and that he had had that amount missing for two years.—Mr. Riley, for the defence, said that the defendant had only £2 2s. aid., and the money had been kept separate from his own, and used only for the purposes of the society. In common with the other officers of the society, his client was unable to either read or write, and all the entries made for him had been done by a third person. The only check w)rich his client had was the keeping of the money in separate bags. His client was prepared to swear positively that £2 2s. 30. was all the money belonging to the society that he had in his hands. Whether he had been debited with £lO he had never received, or paid that amount on the death of a member, wife, or mother, and never been credited, they did not know; but if so that would account for the mistake. It seemed to him that before the mere pro- duction of those books were to be regarded as positive proof against him, they ought to have vouchers produced for those sums. Mr. Lea had no desire to withhold anything that was due, but would only be too glad to pay. He was completely at the mercy of those who had kept his books for him. It was significant, as he pointed out at the last hearing, that in one of the books produced there had been a scratching out of a sum which appeared to him to have been exactly one of £lO, and which would have been to the credit of the defendant.—Mr. Massey pointed out that even if that were the case, the defendant never paid anything without receiv- a cheque.—His Honour: This is what I have repeatedly pointed out before. People should not scratch out any sum, but make an entry on the other side to balance.—Defendant said he was formerly treasurer of the Lily of the Valley Lodge of Free Gardeners, and the lodge held its meetings at his publichouse, at the corner of East-street. As he was unable to read or write, the entries were made by Mr. Atherton, who held the office of District Secretary. He never scratched anything out of the book, and he had always kept the monies of the society safe in a safe and in different bags. Excepting that way he had no check whatever on the entries in the books. When straightening up he had only £2 23, and some coppers. He had never, under any circumstances. used the money in his own business. He told the auditors, Forrest, Anders, and others that he was exactly £lO wrong; he had mentioned it many a time. He first found it out 18 months or two years ago. When the deed winding up the society was read to him by Mr. Massey's clerk, he objected to schedule 2 which said there was a sum of £l2 2s. 3P. in the Funeral account.—Mr. Massey; Oh, its a mistake.—Mr. Riley: Well then, why should we hear it.—Mr. Massey: Its his mistake; it is not ours at all events.—Mr. Riley said there were 20 members in the society when it was wound up.—Mr. James Houghton, one of the auditors, gave evidence in the case.—His Honour said: I think the .onus of proving the mistake lies on the defendant, and he has failed to prove it. The entries had been made either by him- self or with his concurrence, and he is perfectly able to read figures and see what the books contain. If he had pointed out, as he might well have done with his limited education, the mistake, it might have been inquired into and corrected. But it is..not until lie is called upon to cash up, that he sets up this, or makes this allegation that there are £lO charged against him that he has never received. It might be that somebody has pilfered it from him; but he is chargeable for I it. I shall give judgment for the amount.

ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. FRlDAY.—Before his Worship the Mayor, and Colonel Gamble. AN INCORRIGIBLE DRUNKARD—Bridget Kildare made her 116th appearance, and was charged with behaving in an indecent manner on Wednesday night.—Bridget complained that they said she was doing wrong when she was only walking in the streets.—Comtnitted to prison for two months with hard labour.

SENDING A POKER AT A POLICEMAN.—John Sloane, of Rainford, was charged with being drunk and assaulting P.C. Dutton, on the 17th ult.—The police officer stated that the defendant was drunk on the Saturday in question, at twenty minutes to one; ond on the 22nd, when serving the summons upon him, defendant threw the poker produced at him. The poker dropped at his feet. Defendant, when throwing the poker, said "You deceitful -- I will knock your brains out."—Defendant, who has been up 27 times for drunken- ness, assaults on the police, felony, &c., was fined ss. and costs or seven days on the first charge ; and £2 and costs , or one month on the other.

ASSAULT ON A FATHER.—John Rigby (30) was charged with assaulting and beating Charles Rigby, his father, on the Ist inst.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the complainant. On Sunday the defendant went to his father's house at St. Ann's, and created a disturbance. Complainant had been to church, and after be had reached home the defendant came, " punched " at the door, ran the two servants upstairs, and on returning seized the complainant, with whom he struggled for some time. Defendant got hold of complainant's hair, but eventually complainant threw his son to the ground, and held Mm there until assistance arrived. When someone came to his assistance complainant ran out of the house, and took refuge in Mr. Scott's house.—Mr. Swift said they did not wish to send defendant to prison, or to fine him. Defen- dant had been to his father and expressed his contrition, but the complainant felt afraid of defendant on account of his violence; and now asked that defendant might be bound over to keep the peace. Defendant was under the influence of liquor at the time of the assault.—Defendant was bound over in £2O, and ordered to find two sureties of £lO each for three months.

A PUBLICAN HEAVILY FlNED.—James Doming, beer- house keeper, Peasley Cross-lane, was summoned for unlaw- fully opening his licensed premises during prohibited hours. —P.C. Carter said that on Christmas morning he was stand- ing about 30 yards from Dorning's house when he saw seven men in the backyard. As soon as the men saw him they ran out of the yard, the yard door being open. He followed the men and captured two of them. He went back to the house, and saw a jug which contained a gallon of beer, fresh drawn standing on the could, er. He asked the landlord what the beer was doing theW, and the landlord replied " Nothing."—Cross-examined : The landlord did not say that the jug had been standing all night in the cellar, and that beer had been dripping into it. He had to complain to him time after time about the way in which he conducted his house.—Mr. Swift submitted that no case had been made out as the men were only in the back yard.—Superintendent Johnston : The back yard is a part of the licensed premises. —Colonel Gamble was surprised to hear Mr. Swift's 'state- ment that the back yard was not licensed property.—Mr. Swift : I only submitted it to you. sir ; it is for you to decide it.—The Mayor : We think there is no doubt about its being a part of the licensed premises.—Mr. Swift: Very

well ; that has practically nothing to do with it ; if I can satisfy you that there is such a reasonable doubt in the case that it was open for the purpose of selling drink, then you will be obliged to give the defendant the benefit of that doubt. I shall call him before you, and he will tell you that he did not open the yard door, and did not sell or supply any intoxicating liquor. Unfortunately since that summons has been taken' defendant's wife has been seized with fits, is confined to the house, and has been confined to bed, so that it is impossible for her to be here to-day to give evidence.— Defendant denied all knowledge of the door being open, and it was impossible for anyone in the kitchen to see in the yard, as the window sill was six feet from the kitchen floor, which had been recently sunk. The beer had only just been brought from the cellar by the servant girl when the officer appeared.—Dorning was also charged with supplying drink after licensed hours.—P.C. Carter said that at 25 minutes

after midnight, on the 27th ult., Doming and a young woman came out of the beerhouse, the latter carrying a jug of beer. Doming said they were taking the beer to a neigh- bour's house, and the beer was not to be paid for.—A man named Wright said Doming and his wife were at his house on the night in question. Some pork steaks were being cooked, and Dorning's wife asked Doming to fetch some beer. Witness's daughter and Doming were returning with the beer when accosted by the police constable.—Mr. J. 0. Swift contended that defendant did not sell the beer, but gave it. as he was entitled to do if he chose. He referred to a case, Frederick Sergant, in which defendant was charged with a similar offence, but it being. shown that the defendant had given the beer, saying, "You can leave me some greens," the case was dismissed. Mr. swift submitted that the present case was not even so bad as the one re- ferred to, as there had been no exchange.—The Bench decided to convict, and imposed a penalty of £2 and costs in each case, the license to be endorsed. REFRACTORY APPREN TICES.—John Brogan was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to attend his work at Messrs. Pilkington's works. Defendant enlisted in the army, and was apprehended at the Barracks in Warrington. An order was made.—Joseph Kellett, who had previously been ordered to attend work, was sent to prison for 14 days, for continuing to absent himself from work. The Mayor did not sit during the hearing of these cases.

THE DOCTOR'S PRESCRIPTION.—Joseph Hilton, described as a "baby linen dealer," residing at Windle city, was charged with killing a hare without a license. Defendant was seen to shoot a hare in a meadow in the occupation of Colonel Gamble.—Defendant: Tam troubled with diabetes and Dr. Jamison ordered me to get as much fresh air as I possible could; and I take my gun out for company.—Mr. J. 0. Swift: I don't know whether Dr. Jamison told you to get a

little game as well.—Defendant: No, but it is not bad advice after all.—Defendant went on to say that he bad parted with his gun.—Fined I.os. and costs.—Colonel Gamble did not sit in this case. _ _ _ _

THE YOUNG SHOPLIFTERS.—Edinund Woods, Parr; Peter Graney, James McDonald, Whiffle; John Leadbeater, Wigan ; Goorge McNelly, Windle ; William Kay, Eccleston ; and Edward Shields, lads, varying from 11 to 16 years of age, were charged with stealing a quantity of toffy from Robert Alex. Little, in the Market-place. The particulars of the case appeared in our issue of last week.—Woods was fined 20s. and costs, he having been previously convicted, and the others ss. and costs each.—Peter Graney, William Heaton, Jas. McDonald, D. Swift, and Jno. Leadbeater were charged with having sometime between eleven p.m. on the 24th, and eight p.m. on, the 26. h Dec., broken and entered the lock-up shop of John Donnelly, and stolen therefrom some bails, bracelets, wools, and a large quantity of other articles com- prising children's toys. Heaton and Swift were fined 203. or 14 days, and Burke, who has been convicted for stealing a Cardigan jacket from the eh no of Mr. Allen, draper, Market- place, on the 29th September.—Sent to prison for 10 days. Peter Graney and John Leadbeater pleaded guilty to stealing a pair of boots value 43., from a stall in the market, the pro- perty of Richard Jones. Graney had been previously con- victed.—The Mayor, speaking to Graney, said it was most disgraceful, but fortunately such cases were seldom brought before that court. • Graney was sent to prison for three months, and Leadbeater was sent to prison for ten days, and afterwards to go to a reformatory for two years. THEFT OF A SHAWL.—Margaret Harris was charged with stealing a shawl, value 3s. 6d., the property of Esther Ashton.—Prisoner lodged with the prosecutrix and her hus- band who is a collier, in Oldfield-street, and on Monday evening, the shawl was temporarily used as a window blind. Prosecutrix went out of the house about eight o'clock, and on returning the shawl was gone and a piece of cloth placed before the window in substitution. Prisoner had gone out and did not return. Meeting her in thee street two days afterwards, prosecutrix asked for her shawl, and prisoner said it was at Smithy Brow, and that she would return it directly. A pawn ticket, however, was sent instead.—Priso- ner was sent to prison for seven days. THEFT OF COLLIERS' PlcKs.—William Jones was charged with stealing two colliers' picks, belonging to Geo. Dawson and John Benson; and also with stealing a drill belonging to John Yates, collier, Bainford. The picks were placed in the sharpening cabin, and afterwards were missed by the prosecutors. On Tuesday P.C. Dutton found them together with a drill in prisoner's bedroom. Prisoner pleaded guilty when charged by the officer, and said that he did not know what made him do it.—He was sent to prison for fourteen days. MONDAY. Before Messrs. W. Pilkington and W. Blink horn.

THE CLOCK WHICH WAS AN HOUR Too FAST.—William Leigh was summoned for keeping open his llcensed premises during prohibited hours.—A police constable stated that at 25 minutes past eleven on the night of the 28th ult., he visited the Seven Stars Inn, Mill-brook, Eccleston. He saw six men in the front room, drinking. He spoke to the land- lady, who said she did not know what her husband was doing. He said to the men, "Do von know what time it is?" to which a man named Parr replied that it was five minutes to eleven, but afterwards corrected himself and said it wanted two minutes to eleven. It was really 25 minutes past eleven, because he had timed his watch at one o'clock that day.— Mrs. Leigh, being called, said that she commanded the men to go out of the house at five minutes to eleven, but Parr persuaded her there was plenty of time.—The police officer said that the clock was an hour to fast.—Wm. Leigh said he had only been in the house two months, and he had previously been in the service of the London and North-Western Railwaw Company ten years.—The Bench did not think the case was a very bad one. The clock was out of order, but they would all have their clocks out of order if they allowed the case to pass. They, however, would only inflict a pile of ss. and costs.—Samuel Webb, Thomas Parr, James Hall, Joseph Parr, and George Manchester were each fined ss. and costs for being on the licensed premises during prohibited hours, and Thomas Ward, who gave the police some trouble by giving a wrong name, was fined 103. and costs for a similar offence. A DEAU SllASH.—Patrick Kiggin was summoned for hav- ing on the 23rd December damaged a window to the extent of ..-C2 18s. 6d.—James Hardman, in the service of a publican named Anders, who keeps the Grapes Hotel at Parr, said that the defendant entered the "wholesale place," and created a great disturbance. Witness requested him to leave, but be

div.head: ENTERTAINMENT AT WIIISTON,
div.p: ENTERTAINMENT AT WIIISTON,

On Friday a miscellaneous entertainment was given in the National Schools, Whiston, for the purpose of raising., funds to defray the expense attending the annual treat to the Whiston Church Choir, who gave their services volun- tarily. There was a very large audience, nearly every seat in the spacious school-room being filled. The room was tastefully decorated for the occasion with evergreens, the sombre hues of which were pleasingly relieved by artis- tically made artificial flowers of varlet's colours. The vicar (the Bev. J. H. Scott) said that Mr. H. R. d'A. Willis, of Halsnead Hall, Whiston, who was always to the fore at their school entertainments had kindly consented to occupy the chair, and to do all he could to promote the happiness of the evening. (Applause.) Mr. Willis then took the chair, and after wishing all present a happy new year, bid them a hearty welcome to that their annual entertainment. The object of the concert was to provide funds for the annual treat to the church choir, who gave their services voluntarily, and for whom they felt it their pleasure and duty to pro- vide some suitable recompense. It was, therefore, with great delight they saw so many present that night. The entertainment was then proceeded with, the Misses Scott contributing the first item, namely, the pianoforte duet " Qui Vive " (W. Ganz), which was executed with remarkable accuracy, as was also the pianoforte duet "May pole " (Sydney Smith), by the Misses Willis. Mr. W. Tyrer, of Prescot, was loudly applauded for his excellent rendering of the songs, "The ivy green" (H. Russell) and "The mountain maid" (Sinclair.) The Rev. Thomas Chambers, rector of Halewood, read 'I ennyson's pathetic poem "Dora," with an amount of feeling fully appreciated by the audience and thoroughly characteristic of the piece. Mr. Chambers' other contribution was an extract from Ingolsbv Legends, entitled "The vulgar boy on Margate Pier," which caused much laughter. In her rendition of the song e "Won't you tell me why " (Blumenthal) and "Come back to Erin " (Claribel) Miss Moss proved herself to be a tolerably good vocalist, and at the conclusion of each song she was vociferously encored. Solos on the pianoforte were given by the Rev. W. T. Southward, of Huyton, and Mr. Stammers, organist of Prescot Church ; and Mr. Southward and a friend played a duet on the same instrument. "Robert of Sicily " (Longfellow) and " The charge of the light brigade," were ably recited by Mr. Holford Scott Miss Bretherton gave the songs "Waiting" (Millard) and "A summer sbower " (Mazzials), for the former of which she received an encore, as did also Miss Scott for her tasteful rendering of "The fairies " (Dolores.) Miss Scott's other song was "The Araby maid" (J. T. Surenne.) Two duets "What are the wild waves saying" (S. Glover) and " Se mi credi amato bene " (C. H. Florio" were given by the Rev. J. H. Scott and Miss B. Scott, the latter piece being a com- plete success. Mr. Good, formerly master of the Whiston

div.head: 4...,,, HUYTON-WITII-ROBY LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: 4...,,, HUYTON-WITII-ROBY LOCAL BOARD.
THE ESTIMATE FOR THE YEAR AND THE NEW RATE.

A special meeting of the Huyton-with-Roby Local Board was held at the Public-offices, Blacklow-brow, Huyton, on Tuesday evening, Mr. T. Dobell presiding. There were also present Messrs. J. Jowett, E. C. Leventon, C. Cooper, W. Burnyeat, R. Brown, W. Gore Ashton, T. Pinnington, A. Eccles, and T. Watkin, with Mr. Swift (clerk), and Mr. J. Worrall (surveyor). The meeting was called for the purpose of considering the estimate for the forthcoming year.—The CHAIRMAN read the estimate, of which the fol- lowing is a summary: interest on loans, &c., £BB6 us. 24.; macadam, Sze., £1252 55.; lighting, itc., £457 10s. ; salaries, £236; labourers' wages, £650; sundries, workmen's tools and repairs, keep of horse, Sic., £145 Os. Od.; sewerage (balance of estimated expenditure on farm £420, cost of Hall-lane sewer £49 10s.), £469 10s.; contingencies, £5O; total estimated expenditure, £4,146 Ns. 2d. Cash in bank, £286 3s. 24.; less (due Lord Derby for sewer), £5O ; leaving £236 3s. 2d.; due from county (arrears), 237 16s. 9d. ; ditto (this season's account), £270; total, £743 19s. 11d. De- duct this sum from the £4,146 168. 24. (estimated expen- diture), leaving the sum of £3,402 16s. 3d. to be raised. • A. 2s. 6d. rate had this year produced £3,400. Last year's estimate was £3,420, there being a decrease, therefore, this year of about £lB. The rateable value of the township was stated to be £28,662 17s. 7d.—Mr. JowETT said the estimate had been very carefully taken out by the Clerk, and was about what they usually wanted. He ask if any member had any remark or any suggestion to make in reference to the estimate.—Mr. LEVENTON observed that it was an esti- mate of expenditure only. There was nothing on the credit side. Would there be:no profit on the sewage farm?—Mr. JowETT said they had not taken any credit for the farm. If they got any profit from the farm it would be taken for contin- gencies.—The CLERK remarked that it would be two or three months before Mr. Goldsworth could complete the improve- ments on the farm. They were at present draining it.—The CHAIRMAN thought if the farm cleared itself they would do very well indeed this year.—Mr. LEVENTON : If it clears itself it will be a credit.—The CHAIRMAN: Without the out- lay.—ln answer to Mr. Leventon as to whether there was anything else to come in from any other source, it was stated that there were about £2O or £3O, arrears of rate, to come in. —The CHAIRMAN, in reply to Mr. Eccles, said Mr. Golds- worth gave them a verbal guarantee that the maximum cost of the sewage farm improvements would be £5OO. He thought £4OO would clear it, but he dare guarantee that it would not exceed £soo.—The CHAIRMAN said he was very much pleased with the manner in which the work on the sewage farm was being carried out.—After further discussion it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. ECCLES, seconded by Mr. JowETT, that the eetimate be adopted, and that notice be given that a rate of 2s 6d in the pound would be laid on Friday' the 20th inst. I •

div.head: PROPERTY IMPROVEMENTS AT PRESCOT.
div.p: PROPERTY IMPROVEMENTS AT PRESCOT.

It is pleasing to notice that within the last few weeks several improvements to private property, situate in different parts of the town, have been carried out, and from reports current in certain quarters other improvements are in con- templation. During this week a number of bricklayers and labourers have been engaged in demolishing a number of dilapidated and irreparable houses in Kemble-street, the pro- perty of Mr. Frederick Pemberton, of Dam House, Sutton. From appearances there was no doubt the houses were of great age, and the work of levelling them with the ground had to be conducted in a careful and cautious manner, so rotten were the walls. A slight push by one man on more than one occasion' overthrew large portions of the outward and partition walls, and the brickwork in several places crumbled beneath the feet of the workmen. It is surprising to find that notwithstanding the age of the cottages, the timber was, in most cases as sound ever, not the least sign of rot being perceivable. The bricks, though slightly narrower than those used now-a-days, are of good quality and excellent shape, and will do for use again. Mr. Pemberton intends to erect new and substantial cottages seven in num- ber, of modern cottage architecture, in the place of the old ones, and it would be a grand thing if other owners of old property in the town would imitate his example. Mr. Pem- berton owns other dilapidated houses in the immediate vicinity, and it is stated that when the new ones are com- pleted, they also will be pulled down and fresh ones erected in their stead. The alterations will considerably improve the appearance of that portion of Kemble-street, which is one of the principal thoroughfares of the town. The archi- tect is Mr. James Rimmer, of Widnes; and the contractor Mr. Richard Balshaw, also of Widnes. and the work is being carried out under the superintendence of that gentleman's son. Up to the time of writing no accident had occurred.,

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

RUNCORN ROVERS V. ST. MARY'S, WIDNES.—This match was played on the ground of the former, on Saturday last, and, after a very pleasant game, resulted in a victory for the home team. On time being called the score stood as follows: —Rovers: 1 try, 5 minor points. St. Mary's: 3 minor points. The teams were composed as follows :—Rovers: Goal, J. Gayter ; three-quarter backs, W. Hulfand, E. Hulf ; half backs, W. Yarwood, A. Worthington; quarter back, IV. Clare; forwards, Burgess, Worthington, Hulf, Kirkham, Turrcer, Eccleston (captain), Booth, Gaskell. St. Mary's : Goal, Howard; three-quarter backs, Clare, Briscoe•, half backs, Harper, Carrell; quarter backs, Hughes, Singleton; forwards, Doyle' Farrell (captain), Montgomery, Brady, Burns, Hewitt, Cayton, and Garnott.

refused, and witness was obliged to turn him out. Ultimately defendant returned and broke a window with his hand.— Robert Corrigan deposed to seeing the defendant break the window. Defendant, who was described as a chemical labourer, but scarcely ever works, was fined is. and costs and £2 18s. 6d. damages. A DARING YOUNG THIEF. Catherine Ford, aged 10 years, was charged with stealing three umbrellas from a shop in Liverpool-road. Alexander Murphy, son of James Murphy, said that at about half-past four, on the 16th inst., he went into the shop and saw the prisoner pulling three umbrellas out of the window. He asked her what she was doing there, and she replied "Don't speak; I am only hid- ing myself out of my mother's sight." She had left her boots outside the shop in a basket. A policeman charged the girl with the offence, and she replied "I did."—Superintendent Johnston said the girl was on the 20th June, 1879, charged with stealing an umbrella, but was discharged on account of her age. Last month she was fined for stealing ss. 9d. from a tobacco shop in Church-street, but in default went to prison for 14 days.—Prisoner was ordered to prison for 14 days, after that term to a reformatory for five years.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

DEATH OF MRS. JONES (LATE MISS TURTON.)—Just befoi e the conclusion of the service in the Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday evening last, a letter was placed in the hands of Mr. Turton, stating that his eldest daughter had died that morning. The minister was informed of it, and he commu- nicated the sad news to the congregation, which caused quite a commotion, almost the whole congregation manifesting the deepest sympathy for the bereaved husband and family. The deceased resided with her husband at Blackburn, having gone there after being married some 18 months ago. She and her husband had been engaged in the Wesleyan Sunday School as teacher and secretary. She was highly respected throughout the whole township. The funeral took place on Thursday, when the bereaved family and their relations assembled at the Wesleyan Chapel, and afterwards met the coffin containing her remains at Golborne station. She was interred at St. Thomas's Church, Golborne. A large crowd of people gathered about the station and church to witness the funeral.

ELOPEMENT AT GOLBORNE.—Considerable excitement, says a correspondent, was caused in Golborne on Monday week by the announcement that an elopement was about to be carried out. It appears that a married woman residing in property situated behind the New Inn, a factory opera- tive, employed by Messrs. Brewis and Co., left home early on the afternoon in question with a view of making arrange- ments for leaving her "lawful husband." Upon returning in the evening her husband soon discovered his wife's absence, and also the fact that she had taken a quantity of clothing away with her. His suspicions were directed to a house at Bank Heath, where resides—or rather used to reside, a Welshman. The husband, it is said, sought to have an in- terview, but was unsuccessful. Later in the evening he with a crowd of persons witnessed the departure of his wife and the Welshman in a spring cart, making their way towards Newton. They were hailed with shouts and yells from the disgusted observers, but made their way forward apparently unconcerned. Their whereabouts has not yet been ascertained.

OLD FOLKS' TREAT.—The sixth annual treat to the aged people of Golborne was held with great success in Mr. Brewis's school on Thursday. Year by year since the treats were instituted additional interest has been manifested both by the aged themselves and the parishioners generally. The age at which guests were entitled tq be present was 60 years. All persons—irrespective of station in life—of this age and upwards were waited upon and supplied with an admission ticket by the members of the committee. The infirm and

those within a reasonable distance of the school were con- veyed in cabs Sze., early in the afternoon, tea being provided for three o'clock. The room presented an attractive appear- ance, and was tastefully decorated. About 220 sat down to a splendid knife and fork tea, and to judge from the numer- ous happy faces the repast was much appreciated. The clean, tidy, and respectable appearance of the whole company as they sat at the tables was truly pleasing, and their presence afforded a sight more readily imagined than described. The oldest person present was Abel Forster, who has reached the ripe old age of 81 years. Immediately after tea, oranges, tea, and tobacco were distributed. The Rev. T. C. Quirk, M.A., presided, and he was supported by the Rev. Wm. Moore, both of whom in most fitting and appropriate language addressed their aged friends, and re- joiced in being present to meet the many faces whom they had long had the pleasure of recognising as neighbours and parishioners. Mr. Thomas Jenkinson (76), an old veteran, favoured the company with his usual song, "Home, sweet home," after which a very entertaining miscellaneous con- cert was rendered. Votes of thanks were accorded to the ladies who presided at the tables, to the vocalists for their services, to the chairman, and to Mr. Brewis for the loan of the room. The National Anthem brought the programme to a close. Cabs, (tc., were then set in action to convey the aged to their homes. The cater- ing, in the hands of Mr. Walmsley was efficiently carried out, and the name of Mrs. Mapei, as accompanist, is worthy of attention. The entire arrangements were carried out without the slightest bitch. Much credit is due to the com- mittee, who continue to spare no pains to make the annual event as agreeable and interesting as possible. GOLBORNE AND DISTRICT LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—A public meeting of the inhabitants of Golborne and district was held in the Congregational school, on Monday evening last, Mr. Hall, political secretary of the association, being advertised to reply to Mr. Touchstone's recent lecture at a Conservative meeting, on the "Home and foreign policy of Her Majesty's Government." At the Conservative meet- ing Mr. Hall challenged Mr. Touchstone, and offered to meet him on any public platform in Golborne at any time and place, and prove that the assertions which had been made by the lecturer were not altogether correct. Mr. Touchstone did not accept the challenge. Mr. J. Howard, of Golborne, presided at the meeting on Monday. Mr, Hall, who was re- ceived with loud cheers, read a copy of a letter he had sent ' to Mr. Touchstone asking him to meet him (Mr. Hall) that night, as be was going to reply to the assertions he had made at the late Conservative meeting, Mr. Touchstone had not deigned to send a reply to his letter. Mr. Hall then stated that some of his Conservative friends had circulated a re- port that he was defunct and would not turn up. However, he was happy to say that such was not the case, which was a disappointment to the Conservatives. He then dealt with the several statements made by Mr. Touchstone respecting the Crimean war, the Alabama claims, the Transvaal war, and the Land Bill, &c., and completely demolished the assertions of his opponent. He challenged Mr. Touchstone and the whole Conservative party to disprove what he had said. He then contrasted the legislation of the Conserva- tives with that of the Liberals. He urged those present to support Her Majesty's Government, and hoped they would always have the courage to fight under the great Liberal flag of peace, retrenchment and reform. (Loud cheers.) Mr. Ball then moved the fallowing resolu- tion :—" That this meeting of the inhabitants of Golborne and district desire to tender to Her. Majesty's Government, the assurance of their unabated confidence, believing that their past legislation will redound to the honour and stability of this great empire ; and especially rejoices at the recent message of good will to Ireland. and also deprecates the repeated attacks and misrepresentations of the leaders of the Opposition." Mr. Yates seconded the resolution, which was carried by an overwhelming majority. Mr. Entwistle then -sang "The pilot of the State." A vote of thanks was given to the Chairman, and the meeting concluded with the National Anthem.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the above Board was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday. Present : Rev. Canon Barclay (in the chair), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Ashton, W. Handley, T. Norman, J. Mclntyre, W Whittaker, G. S. Hazlehurst, J. Highfield, C. Rigby, H. Lowe, Wm. Lowe, J. Campkin, T. Andrews, J. Midwood, James Darbyshire, R. Ashton, J. W. Baguley, G. Whitlow, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk).

div.head: STATE OF THE HOUSE.
div.p: THE STATE OF THE HOUSE.

The MASTER (Mr. R. Jones) reported that there were 196 inmates as against 168 in the corresponding week in last year. During the week 7 men, 1 woman, and 2 children vagrants had been relieved. There were 30 boys and 29

-1s in attendance at the Workhouse school, and 12 boys and 17 girls receiving industrial training. Out-door relief had been administered to 634 persons at a cost of £62 13s. 3d (Runcorn £35 4s. 9d., Frodsham £l4 95., and Budworth £l2 19s. 6d.), as against 643 persons relieved at a cost of £67 Ss. 9d. in the corresponding week of last year.

FINANCE. The CLERK said they were applying to the Treasury for £l5O 4s. in respect to pauper lunatics, £lO3 in respect to the salaries of the medical officers and teachers, and £lB on account of the registrars. Mr. HANDLEY said the cheques that day amounted to £909 18s. The expenditure of the house was £522 Os. 7d., including £282 3s. 6d. for provisions and other necessaries. &c., £237 18s. 6d. for salaries, including all registra- tion and vaccination and other working expenses of the Union, £lB4 is. 3d. lunatics account for the quarter, £l5 12s. Bd. petty cash payments, and £lO cheque for the clerk's petty cash. Mr. LOWE said he could not understand how the inmates could be kept for V-,d. a day. Mr. HANDLEY said he made a slight mistake when he stated that amount included the cost of officers. It did not include the cost of officers, but was for the inmates alone.
Mr. LOWE : How much butcher's meat are the inmates allowed?

Mr. HANDLEY said the dietary table used to be on the table for the inspection of the Guardians. Mr. LOWE said if they took the cost of butcher's meat from the 41.-d. there would not be much left for anything else. Mr. HANDLEY said if Mr. Lowe would divide a working- man's wages he would find they were kept for less than the amount he had stated. DISTRICT NEWS.

A DRUNKARD COIIIXITTED IT PRESCOT.—On Monday morning at the Prescot Police Court, before Mr. W. L Evans, William Dwyer, an old offender, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk on the previous Saturday night. As he could not meet the fine, he was committed for seven days. A SCHOLARS' TEA. MEETING AT ST. HELENS.—On Tuesday evening, Mr. Jesse Boydell and Mr. Martin gave a tea to their Sunday school scholars in the institute of the Brook-street schoolroom. About 30 sat down to tea. Mr. James Marsh and Mr. Sharples, who were present at the gathering, addressed a few suitable remarks to the young men, and afterwards the scholars of Mr. Boydell's class pre- sented a splendid teacher's Bible to him, as a token of their regard and esteem. The presentation was none the less' pleasing on account of its being unexpected by the recipient. Several songs and readings were given, and these, with games. combined to produce.a very agreeable and enjoyable meeting. SCALDING FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.--On Saturday, at the New Vaults, Sutton, an inquest was held by Mr. T W. Barker, deputy coroner, on the body of Robert Mont- gomery, aged 66. Deceased lived at 19. Sutton-road, and for the last nine years had been employed as a labourer at Messrs. Kurtz's chemical works. On the 20th of last month' he was fixing a pipe to a boiling down tank, containing chloral, and whilst doing so stood upon a three-inch plank. The board slipped and snapped, precipitating deceased par- tially into the boiling liquid. His right foot and leg were badly scalded. A man named White, a fellow labourer, pre- vented his total immersion by seizing him. He was taken home and attended by Dr. Donnellan. He died on Thurs- day. A verdict of accidental death was returned. DINNER TO RAILWAY EMPLOYES AT ST. HELENS.—The 37th anniversary of the dinner to the employes engaged in the goeds department of the London and North Western Railway, at St. Helps, was given on Saturday evening, in the Fleece Hotel. About 70 persons sat down to an excellent dinner served up in Mrs. Taylor's best style. Mr. Faulkner, goods agent, occupied the chair, and amongst the invited guests were Mr. Poole, of the traffic department, Mr. Newton, of the locomotive department, and Mr. Moss, of the passengers' department. Ihe loyal and patriotic toasts were given, after which "The town and trade of St. Helens," and "The donors." were enthusiastically received. Mr. W. J. Ashton officiated as accompanist and sung several humourous songs. Mr. Merrill and Mr. Taylor also contributed songs. The company separated at eleven o'clock. The dinner, which is given annually, is subscribed for by the tradesmen of the town. The passenger's department's dinner will shortly be given. HOSPITAL SUNDAY AT HUYTON.—On Sunday last, ihe annual collections in aid of the Liverpool hospitals were made at several of the places of worship at Huyton. At the Parish Chnrch the senior curate, the Rev. W. T. Southward, preached in the morning, and the Rev. Canon Penrhyn in the eveieing. There was a large congregation at the even- ing service. The collections during the day amounted to £35 is. 6d. At the Mission Church, Huyton Quarry, the collections realised the sum of a 6s. 3d. The sermon in the morning was preached by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, and in the evening by the Rev. A. T. Waad. The Rev. Mr Dunlop, of Liverpool, preached to large congregations both morning and evening at the Congregational Church. The collections at the close of the services totaled over £36.

div.p: broke the peace, should have to be bound over in the case of this man Yarwood, who has been convicted in this court of breaking the peace in Runcorn. This terminated the proceedings in the case.

SEIZURE OF BAD MEAT IN CHURCH-STREET. - John McAvoy, butcher Church-street, who keeps an American meat store, was summoned by the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners, who were represented by their clerk (Mr. W. H. Linaker), for having in his shop, one fore-quarter, and eight pieces of beef, together with seven sheeps' heads and plucks, which were deceased, but intended for human food, on the 29th ult.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington, defended.—Mr. Chas. Dutton, market inspector, said he found the fore-quarter of beef, which was very bad, in the back part of defendant's shop. The eight pieces of beef, which weighed 431bs, were in the cellar. The plucks and sheeps' heads were lying on the pavement in the backyard. All the meat was condemned by Dr. Mouritz, medical officer, and destroyed by order of a justice of the peace.—Dr. Mouritz was called, and said the eight pieces of beef were partly putrid, and must have been so for five or six days. One part of the fore-quarter gave off a very offensive odour, when he probed it.—ln cross-ex- amination, the witness said he thought the meat had not been intended by defendant for food, but it had been put out of the way in the place where it was found.—Mr. Moore urged that the evidence of the medical officer, and the place where the meat had been found, clearly proved that it was not intended for human food. The meat had been left from the Christmas show night. On the following Monday, Tues- day, and part of Wednesday defendant's shop had been closed, as about dinner time the place was entered by a bailiff, upon whom the defendant committed an asault. The consequence was that McAvoy was locked up on a warrant, and kept in "the regions below" that building— (laughter)—for a number of hours, so that he had not a pro- per opportunity of looking after the meat.—Mr. Charles Houghton said he was in defendant's shop on the morning of the seizure, and McAvoy said it was a pity that the sheeps' heads had gone bad, and wished to put them in the ash place, but he warned him that this was contrary to the town's bye-laws.—Mr. Luke Holmes, auctioneer, was also called on behalf of the defendant.—The magistrates were of opinion that the fore-quarter of beef was exposed for sale, but not the other pieces. Taking into consideration the fact that the defedant had been interfered with in his business by a bailiff entering his premises, which circumstance must have been rather distressing to him, he would be let off with the easy fine of ss. and costs (18s. 6d.) FOUL-MOUTHED WOMEN. - Alice Rothwell and Kate Smith were each fined 20s. and us. 61 costs, for using obscene language in the public street, the former on the 30th ult., and the latter on the 15th October, 1880. The cases were proved by P.C.'s Kelly and Noden.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
WEDNESDAY. —Before Messrs. John Brock (chairman), and
but his evid-

George Pilkington. ENEMIES TO QUIETNESS.—John Donnelly, and Catherine Brennan were each ordered to find sureties, in £lO, and one in £5, to keep the. peace, owing to having on the 31st ult. and 3rd inst. respectively, created rows in the streets. FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTORS. Thomas Gilloley, James Douglass, and Thomas Loftus were convicted of having, on the 28th ult., obstructed the footpath opposite the Derby Arms, in Widnes-road, after having been warned by a police officer, and were each ordered to pay ss. and 7s. 6d. costs, or, in default, go to gaol seven days. KEEPING A WIFE AT THE EXPENSE OF THE RATE. PAYERS.—William Ross, a young man, was charged on a warrant, with refusing to maintain his wife, who had been for a considerable time chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union. Mr. Husband appeared on behalf of the guardians, and said that after the issuing of the warrant, the prisoner absconded to Glasgow. His wife, who was only young in years, had cost the Union £7 4s. 6d. in mainten- ance. Prisoner sold his furniture and went away, and his wife was at home with her father.—The Chairman said the case was evidently a bad one, and R 093 would be committed to gaol for one month. DESERT'ERS.—SamneI Davies, of the 14th Foot, and Martin Magee, of the 47th Foot, who had been apprehended for desertion, were ordered to be kept in custody to await an escort. ATTEMPTED SUlClDE.—Patrick Egan, who has lately had no settled residence, but formerly lived in Cholmondeley- street, was charged with attempting to take his own life' on the previous Thursday.—On the afternoon of that day prisoner was seen trespassing on the Cheshire Lines Rail- way, near the Central Station, by an official. As the poor fellow was covered with mud, and his clothes dripping with water, it was surmised that he had been attempting to drown himself in one of the pools near Ditton-road, and the official gave him into the custody of P.C. Robinson. On being ques- tioned, the prisoner, who had the appearance of a nun who had been drinking heavily, admitted that he had tried to put an end to his existence, but he had not found the water deep enough, and he afterwards tried to cut his throat with a pocket knife.—Superintendent Barker stated that the prisoner's mind appeared to have lost its balance through the death of his wife.—The Bench discharged the prisoner, on his promising to keep from drink and not make any similar attempts in future. COAL STEALING.—NEGLECTFUL PARENTS.—Peter O'Toole, aged 11 years, was charged, on remand, with having, on the previous Thursday, stolen 301bs. of coal, the property of thel trustees of the late John Hutchinson. Prisocer was seen to take the coal by a man from the works, and caught and handed over to P.C. Worthington.---The agent to the trustees, and the police officer having given euidence, the Chairman severely censured the parents for not having bad better con- trol over their son. He was sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod. AVOIDING PAYMENT OF A RAILWAY FARE. —Joseph McCormick, a young man employed as a labourer at Messrs. Gaskell and Deacon's, was charged with having, on the 10th Inst., travelled in a certain carriage on the London and North Western Railway, with intent to avoid payment of his fare. From the evidence of Mr. Sansom, station master, it ap- peared that on the arrival of the 6-15 train at the Widnes station, en the previous evening, his attention was called to the prisoner by William Dobson, a porter. He found the man attempting to escape from the station, after having come by the train, by jumping over some railings near the urinal, on the Liverpool platform. O'Toole fell upon the bank be- low, as if he had hurt his foot, and he caught him. On finding that he had no ticket, he gave him in charge of the police.—ln reply to the Bench, the prisoner said he was under the influence of drink at the time, and did not know what he was doing.—The Chairman said the evidence clearly showed that the man knew very well what he was doing, and he would be fined 10s., and 7s. 6d. costs. CRUELTY TO A HORSE. Samuel Mercer was charged with cruelty to a horse by working it in an unfit state.—Mr. James Allen, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, stated that on the afternoon of the 4th inst., he saw the animal, attached to a loaded cart, in Lacey- street, and in charge o; defendant's lad. Upon its back was a wound three inches in diameter, from which matter was discharging.—Defendant was fined 103. and costs.

THE BANKRUPTCY OF .A WIDNES MANUFACTURER. STRANGE DISCLOSURES. The works of Mr. John Knight, trading under the name of John Knight and Co. ralso as the Lancashire Manure Co., at Famworth, Widnes. are offered for sale by private treaty, the affairs of Mr. Knight being in bankruptcy. We have extracted the following particulars from a statement prepared by the accountants, Messrs. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

31017 DAY.—Before Messrs. James Reynolds (chairman) and Alfred Thomas. THE STRANGE CONDUCT OF A LIVERPOOL GENTLEMAN. THE ADVENTURE OF AN AMATEUR BARRISTER. Mr. William Talbot Code, described as holding a responsible position under the Liverpool Dock and Harboar Board, living at Fairfield, and who has also a residence known as Moretown House, county Wexford, Ireland, appeared on an adjourned summons, in which he was charged by Mr. Samuel Yarwood, livery stable proprietor, and auctioneer, with using to him certain violent and abusive language, calculated to incite a breach of the peace, on the 11th ult. Mr. Lake appeared for complainant, and defendant, at the beginning of the case, was unrepre- sented. The court was crowded. Mr. Lake briefly opened the case, and remarked that he did not know of any conduct which would be more likely to cause a breach of the peace than that of which defendant was alleged to have been guilty. Mr. Yarwood was then called, and said that at a few minutes to twelve on the night in question, defendant came to his door and rapped very loudly indeed. Mrs. Yarwood called to him at the bottom of the stairs, sayine. "Master, shall I open the door, or answer it ?" He replied, "Well, perhaps you better had, as it is just possible some one may have a horse very ill," and he occasionally acted as a farrier. She opened the house door, on which defendant rushed in- side, and said "I want a cab to Orme's, at Weston Point." His wife asked if defendant could have one, and he answered "Certainly not; we have not a horse that could stand on such a slippery night, as not one of them is sharpened." Mr. Code then said, "Come down, you old villain, or I will make it cost you £5O if you don't. I will let you know that I am a barrister-at-law, and you must come downstairs, or I will make it cost you £50." Witness replied "I shall not to-night, neither can you have a cab. We could not pos- sibly go even if we were to try to do so." Mr. Code made answer, "Then I shall stay here all night, Mrs. Yarwood. Bring me in a- glass of brandy." His wife said "We don't keep spirits in our house. You had batter go somewhere else." Defendant then said to her that he should sleep there that night. Mr. Code walked to the bottom of the stairs a second time and said "Are you coming down or not ?" He answered" Certainly I am not coming down to-night, neither can you have a cab. Will you please to leave my house that my family may go to bed ?" Defendant said "I shall not, and I shall stay here." His wife then ran upstairs, and said to him, "Oh, do come down Sam. You will have to do so, for this man is beginning to undress himself in the kitchen." There were three females in the kitchen at the time. Wit- ness put his trousers and stockings on, went downstairs, and asked defendant what he really wanted in the place, and to leave the house so that his family could go to bed. Mr. Code defied him.; and, in fact, the members of his family had been in fear of defendant ever since. His wife dared not go round the house at night. Defendant again said he was a barrister, and threatened "to learn them something." He next said he wanted to go another place than Weston Point, and witness began to think that he must be labouring under delirium tremens. In fact, he never saw any one so wild before. Defendant named Ashton Heyes ; said he re- quired a carriage and pair; stated that he had come from London, and made such a wandering statement that he really could not understand what he was talking about. He re- quested Mr. Code to leave several times, but he said he should not, and defied him to put him out. He ultimately granted his request, and put him out of the door; and now defendant had issued 'a summons against him for assaulting him, which he understood would be heard upon another occasion, so that he would reserve what he had to say upon that matter. Defendant then cross-examined the witness at some length. Mr. Yarwood said he usually closed his shop at nine o'clock. He could not say whether his wife supplied defendant with a slice of bread and butter; but he heard that he (Code) took some and poured some whiskey, or brandy, into the milk out of a flask. At this point defendant said he should be very sorry to implicate Mrs. Yarwood in the matter, but the complainant had told a notorious lie from the beginning to the end of his evidence. Further cross-examination: Did you say "Are you a keeper on the spree ?" No; I never made use of such an expression.—Did you take hold of me by the throat, kick me in the side, and throw me on the floor? No.—l have got the mark of your vile hoof on my body now. (Sensation). Did you throw my hat, my gloves, and my cane outside the door after me? No sir, I did not. Mrs. Yarwood, who is about 43 years of age, was next called, and corroborated the statement of her husband. She added that during the conversation defendant said, "What sort of a man is your husband? Is he an old-look- ing man? Has he any teeth in his head r To this she replied, "You will findthat my husband is a far better look- ing man than you are." (Loud laughter). Cross-examined by defendant.—Now, answer me truly, and look at those gentlemen (the bench). Was your hus- band ever before this court for riotous and drunken conduct? —Not that I know of. Mr. Ashton (the magistrates' clerk).—That has nothing to do with the point. Defendant: I say that it has; I appeal to the bench. Mr. Ashton: You should have cross- examined the complainant upon that point. Defendant: I declined to do so because I knew that he would not tell the truth. Cross-examination continued—Has your husband ever been before this court for assaulting or ill-treating you? Witness (indignantly) : No.—Well lam very glad to hear that.—Witness went on to say that she called a lady named Mrs. Yates into the house during the disturbance, as she became afraid.—Defendant: You need not have been afraid, for I pledge my word you are not so good looking.— The Magistrates' Clerk (to defendant) : Get on with your cross-examination, if you please, and don't insult the wit- ness. Miss Susan Okell, neice to the complainant, corroborated the statement of Mrs. Yarwood.—ln cross-examination the witness maintained the correctness of the statement. Walter Henry Yarwood, complainant's son, also gave cor- roborative evidence. Defendant, in reply to a question from the Magistrate's Clerk, said he had nothing to ask the witness. Each of the witnesses appeared to have "learned his lesson" very well. Mrs. Yates, of the Rifleman, Church-street, said she was passing Mr. Yarwood's shop at the time the defendant was in the kitchen, and was asked by Mrs. Yarwood to come in, as she was afraid. The witness then related exactly what has been stated by the previous witnesses.—Defendant: What time was this ?—Witness: I should say it was Sunday morning.—Defendant: What were you doing out at that time ?—Witness: I had been to a shop close to, and Mrs. Yarwood asked me to come in, as she was afraid.—Defend- ant: Then you are not afraid ?—Witness: I am not afraid of one man—(laughter)—and if you had said as much to me as you said to Mrs. Yarwood I would not have asked a husband to have put you out. I would have put you out of the house myself. (Loud laughter.)—Defendant: We have got some game here at any rate! (Laughter.) Defendant, in reply to the bench, said he denied all the statements which had been made against him from begin- ning to end. He was then put into the box, and stated that he was taken to complainant's house by Mr. Peck, a cab proprietor in the town. After being told that complainant would not supply him with a cab, he (witness) asked for some milk and bread, and whilst sitting drinking the milk be rapped on the table with his cane and inquired if he was going to keep him there all night. Complainant came down with only his trousers and boots on. He told him he wanted a cab to take him to Weston Point, on which Mr. -Yarwood seized him by the throat, pulled him off his chair, and dragged him through the kitchen into the shop. At the shop doer he managed to get upon his feet, when com- plainant caught him by the shoulder, tripped him up so that he fell backwards, and he "had the mark of the blackguard's on his body then." He could produce a medical man led him in Dublin, and another in Runcorn

div.head: EXAIIINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 14, lBB2.
div.p: THE EXAIIINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 14, lBB2.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Board was held on Wed- nesday. Present—Mr. Joseph Harrison (chairman), Rev. J. Yonge, Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Darbyshire, Black- butst, Kilshall, Houghton, Greenall, Mackie, Woolfall, Cooper, Owen, Cartwright, Appleton, Humphries, Fairhurst, Hunt, and J. C. Sutton (clerk). THE CONSUMPTION OF WINES AND SPIRITS. The Rev. J. YONGE drew attention to an account from Messrs. Rowson and Sons for £2O for wines and spirits from October to the end of the year, and remarked that, if there was a similar account for every quarter for spirits and wines, apart from ale, it appeared to him the account was getting extraordinarily heavy. The CHAIRMAN (to the master) : How do you think it compares with the bill for this time last year? The MASTER: I do not think there will be much differ- ence.

Mr. MACKIE said it would be well to bear in mind that a few months ago the doctor made a special complaint about the quality of the wine supplied for medicinal purposes, and it was agreed that wine of a superior—which, he presumed, meant as well of a more expensive—kind, should be sup- plied. If they were told whether the old stock was got rid of, and this apparently large sum was for a fresh stock, or merely the ordinary consumption, it might turow a little light on the question. The MASTER said it referred to a fresh stock, and the Board were paying more per g?llon now than they had done. They were paying 18s. a gallon for whiskey. The CHAIRMAN: But does it not go further than the other, Mr. Mackey? (Laughter.) The MASTER: I don't know about that, sir. obliged to give what the doctor orders. Mr. MACKIE: Is your stock in hand heavier than usual The MASTER: It is rather heavier than if was la& quarter. Mr. BLACKHURST : I should like to know what the cost is for the whole twelve months, because this must be an exceptional quarter. The CHAIRMAN said the expenditure for wines and spirits during 1881 was as follows: quarter enclitic, March £2O, June £l7 16s. 9d., September £l3, and December £2O is. The Rev. J. YONGE said that during the past week, amongst the females, there was a smaller consumption than there was in the corresponding week of last year in every case, excepting that of wine, which was exactly the same. With regard to the males, it appeared that the consumption was greater during the past week than it was in the corres- ponding week of last year in every case excepting that of wine, of which there was none this year, as against 14 ounces in the corresponding week of last year. He had noticed these accounts week by week for some months, and found they did not vary very much. Major CARTWRIGHT : They are generally larger in the winter months. The CHAIRMAN said the amount charged this quarter did not seem abnormal. Mr. DARBYSIIIIIE said it was a question for the doctor whether the wines and spirits did any gool at all. The doctor appeared to think they did, but he thought many Guardians thought they did not do any good. Mr. WOOLFALL and OTHERS: Not many. Mr. DARBYSHIRE went on to say that in some workhouses, although they had discontinued the supply of intoxicants, it was found the patients did not suffer in consequence, but that they were better, and lived longer. He did not know whether or not it was the object of the Guardians that their inmates should live a long time—(laughter)—but in the unions where the use of alcohol had been discontinued in every shape, the inmates lived longer, according to the returns shown him, than in those workhouses where it was used. The CHAIRMAN said that was an important statement to make, and it would be curious to ascertain it was true beyond all doubt. The Rev. J. YONGE believed that in life assurance returns they would find it unquestionably a fact that abstainers lived longer lives than non-abstainers. The CHAIRMAN did not admit that abstainers lived longer than people who took alcohol in moderation. (Laughter.) Major CARTWRIGHT : I believe as a rule all the people who get inside this house, whether they have drink or not, live for a very long time. (Laughter.) The subject then dropped. THE COST OF LUNATICS' MAINTENANCE. Mr. MACKIE called attention to one or two of the cheques the Board were asked to sign that morning. He said the Finance Committee had been going through the bills, and one of the things which had struck them, and not for the first time either, was the fact that Her Majesty's Govern- ment, who kept an asylum for criminal lunatics, charged the Board in the case of one prisoner 7s. 7d. a week for his keep merely because the jury happened to find he was insane, whereas if they had not done so he would have been kept at the general expense of the country. He admitted this was not a question open far discussion, but they required an explanation why they should charge 14s. a week for a person named Margaret Davenport, whilst they only charged Ts. Td. a week for the maintenance of Samuel Bolton. 14s. a week was a very serious sum to charge for even lunatic prisoners, and he ventured to say that other things being equal, he would guarantee tbeir safety for a very much less percentage than was charged. Perhaps the Clerk would give the Board some explanation cf the matter. He also called attention to a bill from Mr. Beaman, Haydock Asylum. He had no doubt the charges were the customary ones; but lt• was no doubt a matter for inquiry why the Board should pay 15s. a week for no less than five epileptic patients. Fifteen shillings, he understood, was three times the amount for which ordinary patients could be kept at the Workhouse, and he believed other lunatic asylums, not private ones, charged only about Bs. 7d. The fact that they were epilep- tic patients might probably warrant this full charge, but he did know that epileptic patients required special keepers or special provision, except oversight, lest they were overtaken by the disease to which they were subject. If they could get those five patients sent to the ordinary county asylum, he believed they would not cost the Board. much more than half what they now cost. He then referred to some cheques from a number of local tradesmen for very large sums— £2OO and £3OO. The cheques were in payment of accounts extending over at leastthree months, and he suggested that it would be very much to the interests of the Board, sup- posing they had capital enough, to purchase everything on the monthly account system. The CLERK said whether they made monthly or quarterly payments it really made no difference in their experience, because it was all by contract.. Mr. MACKIE: The tenders would be reduced, you know. The CLERK said as a matter of fact the tradespeople quite understood the Board were willing to pay monthly if they preferred it. If a tradesman only sent his bill out at the end of the quarter, it was because it was a convenience to the tradesman as well as to the Board. But to pay monthly would involve this difficulty. The Board made their calls half yearly—they never kept a large sum in hand—and they fixed the days of payment for the respective townships. But he might tell them he had very great difficulty in getting the money on those days, and had frequently to come and say they had no money to pay with. If they changed the system they would press upon the township at a time when it would be very inconvenient for them to pay. It would not benefit them in the least degree, and it would greatly inconvenience the townships. As to the charges at Broadmoor it was certainly very absurd that the Board ehould be charged 14s. for one inmate and 7s. 7d. for another. He dared say they were aware these were two criminal lunatics, and were removed to Broadmoor by order of the Home Secretary. The absurd arrangement they had, and one they could not interfere with, was this: If Davenport was being charged 14s. d week, according to the rate in Lancashire, when trans- ferred to Broadmoor, they would charge that rate, and if Bolton was being charged 7s. 7d. a week at the time of his removal they continued to charge that 7s. 7d. for all time. Regarding the charges for the patients at Haydock, the charges were not more by reason of the patients being epileptic. They went to Haydock for the reason that none of the county asylums had room for epileptic cases. Mr. Bleckly and himself visited Broadmoor a few years ago, and they got two persons, for whom they were paying 14s. a week, transferred to this county. Bolton they did not think it wise to remove, and Davenport having committed murder very recently they thought it best to leave her alone. He thought they pointed out the absurdity of the charge not being fixed and regulated according to a scale to apply to 11l persons in their asylum, but nothing came of it. Mr. DA.RBYSHIP': thought there were about 100 lunatics ingng non in the various asylums, who were . cost of £2,000 a year. He thought 1r at Haydock who cost about 15s:a ich for whom they were charged 7s. 2d., Lo cost Bs. 9d. a week. What was the patients at Prestwich was so much 'he other county asylums? Mr. OWEN : Is there any Oliver Twist attending it? Mr. APPLETON : I think Oliver is there, and that he has to go short. Major CARTWRIGHT: Where have you got your informa- tion from, my friend? Somebody has been "stuffing" you. Mr. COOPER: I got my information from one of the Guardians. Major CARTWRIGHT; They are not very clever, I think. If you want to make a comparison—what does it cost them per head? Mr. COOPER: I cannot say. Major CARTWRIGHT: That is the way to get at it. The CHAIRMAN: Ido not think there are many Unions where it costs less per head than it does in the Warrington Union. I think our expenditure in that respect is a very small expenditure. As to Mr. Cooper's remarks, he said the question of having contracts had been fully discussed and it was thought most desirable to have contracts. Regarding the cost of the inmates at Broadmoor, he said to charge the Board simply because a man was a lunatic when he com- mitted murder seemed to be most inconsistent. He could not see why the authorities should not deal with the case, and his maintainance be paid out of the Imperial exchequer. THE BOARD AND ITS CHARACTER. The CLERK said nearly two years age he became aware, from the person who held money on trust on behalf of the executrix, that two persons in the house were entitled to a sum of money. One, the son, was to come into possession when he was 21, and the mother would be entitled to 3s. per week, an to 2 years pay, about the same date. He had occasional interviews with the person who undertook to give him private notice when the time for payment came. That person did give him notice and he sent for the inmates last Friday week in order that he might see them, and when they came, the young man told him, and persisted in his statement that he was to have £3O. He, however, knew he was to have more, and made an arrangement with the young man that if he was not to have £lOO he would ask the Guardians to let him off altogether paying for his past maintenance. The young man would not sign anything without they went to Mr. R. Davies's office. They therefore went there, and Mr. Sharp concurred that it was a proper thing that he should pay for his maintenance. The result was the payment of the money, £3O Bs. for the son, and .£1.5 Os. for the mother. The CLERK then complained that although the Master knew that these persons were entitled to money, and went out of the house to receive it while the Board and their officers were • sitting on the previous Wednesday, no information had been given to him about it, and a record of the matter only appeared on the minutes of the House Committee that morning. Major CARTWRIGHT said he was surprised the Clerk had made the statement, because before the persons went oat, the House Committee were aware of the arrangement that had been made. The Clerk must not suppose for one moment that the House Committee were net quite as wide awake as himself for any money coming in to anyone. The CLERK said he only made the arrangement on the Friday, and how the House Committee could know of any arrangement made by him by letter with Mr. Sharp, be did not know. His complaint was that on the previous Wed- nesday, December 28th, knowing that within the week the youth would be 21, and knowing, as the Master did, that the money was due to them, no reference was made either to the Board, the officers, or the House Committee, of the youth's right to the money, and no entry made in the book until they had gone to draw the money, and had in fact, actually drawn it. Major CARTWRIGHT could assure the Clerk, the House Committee were quite as anxious to get money as he was. The CLERK, in reply to Mr. Appleton, said it was entirely by accident he got to know of the money being due in the first instance. The MASTER said he was sorry the Clerk was trying to mislead. The case had been reported. Mr. MAextE said for the sake of their ordinary character, which was being criticised very adversely by the other eminent body to which some of them belonged, he must pro- test against an official or guardian using such a word as misleading when applied to any other gentleman in the room. He had no doubt Mr. Mackey did not mean it in its offensive sense, but when it got into print it was an ugly word. He did not want to be held up to odium as they had been for using words which were un- gentlemanly. During the time he had been a member, the business had been conducted admirably. Only once or twice had there been a little feeling—feeling he cared nothing about, but he had a decided objection to any such words as that which had been used, and he asked the chairman to ask the Master to:withdraw it, and substitute something less offensive. The CHAIRMAN said the observation certainly implied a wilful and improper attempt on the part of the chairman to mislead, and he hoped the master would withdraw the observation. The MASTER was sorry the Clerk had attempted to mis- lead— The Rev. J. 3/ONGE rose to order. This was not the first time Mr. Mackey had done this thing, and he considered it almost impertinence. The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Mackey, you will withdraw -the observation you made? Major CARTWRIGHT remarked that the Board considered the obsera ation offensive. • The CHAIRMAN: It is offensive. Major CARTWRIGHT said " misleading " was not so strong a word as Mr. Mackie had stated. He was rather surprised Mr. Mackie should say they were this that and the other. In:regard to the Town Council. be held that the Board's busi- ness was conducted as wellas that of that august body. (Hear, hear.) When Mr. Mackie had been a member of the Board a number of years longer he would consider the conduct of the Board would bear comparison with any other Board in Lancashire. [Mr. MactriE : I quite agree with you.] The Master, perhaps, ought. not to have made use of the word; but it was not so very strong as Mr. Maakie re- presented. This CHAIRMAN: I think Mr. Mackey used the words "try- ing to mislead." Major Canrwramtre said that was quite true. He also said the Master ought to withdraw the expression, and use a milder word. , Mr. OWEN said it was not for the Master to say anything was misleading, but to prove that it was so. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Mackey might 3vith great pro- priety have said the Cletk was mistaken. The MASTER adopted the Chairman's suggestion, and said it was well known to many members of the Board the woman was entitled to the money left by her deceased husband. The matter had been talked over and reported several times years ago. It was known also that the money could not be ob- tained until the son came of age, which he did on the 4th inst.—that day week—and they did not go out to draw the money but to inquire about it. The CLERK, however, maintained that they were allowed to go out of the house to draw the money, and did draw it, and if he had not written a letter to Mr. Davies to take care that advantage should not be taken they would have drawn the whole of the money. If the person who held the money had not privately attended to say the boy would be 21 in a few days and would receive it, the Board must have lost the money. The Rev. J. YONGE moved that the matter be referred for investigation to the House Committee. They had got to blank contradictory words by Mr. Mackey and Mr. Sutton, and it had got to a point which should not be discussed by the Board. Mr. MACKIE seccnded the motion, which was carried. THE BARRACKS' WATER SBPPLY. The minutes of the Schools Committee contained the fol- lowing :—The Clerk attended before the Committee, and reported as follows: "Preliminary to the adoption of pro- ceedings against the Waterworks Company, and with a view to an equitable arrangement, I met Mr. Ross, their secretary, and subsequently Mr. Geddes, their vice-chairman. It was understood between us if we failed to agree that ary offer to be made was without ptejudice, and that any agreement effected was, on the ground of brief duration of contract, exceptional and not to affect the legal position of the Com- pany in case of dispute as to the supply of water to other premises. I view a reduction of the supply of water to the schools to be inexpedient, and that the substitution of other pipes and fittings for those in present use would occasion delay and be attended with considerable ex tense. One half- inch pipe is represented in area as 1963, and six of such pipes as 1•1778, whereas the present 1± inch pipe represents 1.2272 an excess over six half-inch pipes of .0494. The water consumed during the quarter just closed averaged 3,250 gallons per day on an estimated population of 230, or 16 gallons per head. Upon the basis hitherto charged the bill for the quarter would in round figures be £l5. It was stated that the average cost of water to the company is 6d. per 1,000 gallons, atha by way of compromise an offer to supply at that price, or one-half the previous charge, was made and declined. The result of the conference was an arrangement to pay £3 ss. per quarter, that sum to include water rent (hitherto 50s. per annum), the supply of water to continue as hitherto, and the agreement to be retrospec- tive, except for the period in respect of which the water rates had been paid." Mr. ArnEvoN moved the confirmation of the minutes, and said the Board ought to feel very grateful to the Chair- man for the speech he made at the Council meeting in respect to the charges for water. Mr. DARBYSHIRE, in reply to a question by Major Cart- wright, said the decision come to with the Waterworks Co. was that the last quarter's bill should be , subject to the reduction which would take place in future quarters. • Major CARTWRIGHT said that certainly was a little more satisfactory, but he still maintained they were paying more than they ought. He would have felt inclined to fight the matter out. The Rev. J. YoNGE You are pugnacious. (Laughter.) Mr. BLACKHURST said there was no doubt Mr. Sutton had made the best arrangement he could, and the committee were perfectly satisfied with what he had done. The CHAIRMAN said although he thought with Major Cartwright they were paying more than they ought, still he questioned whether it would not have cost the Board very much more to have fought the question out. Therefore he thought the Clerk had chosen the least of two evils when he agreed to pay the company perhaps a little more than they eould fairly claim. The minutes were confirmed.
