div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. –
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. -

SATURDAY.—Before Captain Litton and Alderman Chandley. THEFT OF COLL.—Michael Kay was charged with having on the 18th December last stolen a quantity of coal, value 6d., the property of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons.—P.C. Street was on duty at Bank Quay on the day named, and on passing Messrs. Crosfield's works saw some coal on the wall. Thinking something was wrong he crouched behind the wall, and in a short time he heard footsteps of a man, but as he was getting sip his coat made a rustling noise, and the man made off. He followed and caught the man, who turned out to be the prisoner, and apprehended him. Pri- soner gave the name of John Jones, and as the constable was going with him to ascertain if he had given his right name prisoner made his escape. A summons was issued, but he failed to appear, and was apprehended on warrant.— Prisoner was committed for a month. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and the ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclough). AN "OBSTRUCTIONIST."—Margaret Burns, a young woman, was charged under a warrant, with obstru;:ting the footpath in Horsemarket-street, by standing there an unreasonable time. The offence was committed on the 26th April, 1881, and P.C. Crickett having proved the case, the prisoner was ordered to pay the costs 7s. 6d., and be kept in custody until six o'clock. FUSTIAN CUTTERS AND THE FACTORY ACT. James Welsby, master fustian cutter, was charged with having on the 29th November, employed a child named Jane Mather, without a certificate of attendance at school; and a similar charge was made with respect to Eliza Birch.—Mr. Moore, junior, appeared for the defendant and pleaded guilty.—The factory inspector sasd the defendant habitually neglected to obtain the children's school books, and in consequence these proceedings were taken.—Mr. Moore said the children had made up 15 attendances since the inspector had visited the defendant's works, and defendant was wilting to allow them to make up the whole number at his own expense.—ln reply to a question by the Mayor, the Inspector said the practice for which defendant was summoned was very common among the fustian cutters.—Defendant was fined 20s. and costs in each case. THE EXTRAORDINARY DEMOLITION OF PROPERTY.—Jas. Higgins, Michael Hughes, Patrick Mulkearn, Michael Mannion, junior, William Manion, Daniel McCormick, and Thos. O'Brien, all boys, were charged with having on the 26th and 27th December, unlawfully and wilfully injured the house of Jane Lightfoot, in Bakehouse-yard, Latchford. —The particulars of the case have previously been stated in The Examiner.—William Fov, who was fined 20s. and costs on Wednesday last for his part in the destruction of the house, was called as a witness, and he said he saw O'Brien, the least boy in the deck, breaking the windows and window frames of the house, and carrying away the wood for fire- wood. He had not seen the others commit any damage.— Mr. Hunt said the witness had given the names of the defen- dant's as being concerned in the affair and made a state- ment which he had not repeated that morning.—Mr. Moore, junior, appeared for W. Manion and Michael Mulkearn, and pleaded not guilty.—Defendants Higgins, Hnghes, Michael Mannion, junior, and Daniel McCormick, pleaded:guilty.-Mr. Lomas said he had had his property in the same neighbour- hood demolished.—Higgins, Hughes, Michael Mannion, and McCormick were each fined ss. and costs, the other prisoners being discharged.—The Bench commented upon the manner in which Foy had given evidence. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Monks.

DRINK A.G4lN.—Joseph Battersby, hawker, was charged with having, on the 6th inst., made use of threats to his wife Jane.—Complainant said her husband threatened to "wash his bands in her heart's bluod." He had lately been drinking heavily.—The prisoner said be had been accus- tomed to move in a different sphere of life. It was the drink that had brought him down. He pleaded hard to be let off, and promised his worship "never to drink no more." —Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace, and ordered to pay the costs, 125., in a month. A DESERTER.—WiIIiam Futlong was charged with being a deserter from Her Majesty's 103rd Regiment of Foot, stationed at Salford.—Police-sergeant Spinks apprehended the prisoner, who was in a very dirty condition, in Butter- market-street, and be afterwards admitted having broken out of barracks.—Prisoner was remanded to Regent Road Barracks, Salford, for safe custoffb. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Alderman Davies.

ALLEGED ROBBERY.—John Houghton, striker, Heath- lane, was charged with stealing from the premises of John Barlow, blacksmith, Beamont-street, on the 26th Desember, one pair cart arms and bushes, value £2 lOs , his property; and James Tomlinson was charged with receiving the same. —Prisoners were remanded until Friday. SETTING FIRE TO BEDDING,—Ed ward Dineen, labourer' was charged with being drunk and committing wilful and malicious damage by setting fire to the bedding in the house of John Stephens, 19, Blackhurst-street, on Tuesday night, thereby doing damage to the amount of 15s. or there- abouts.—Fined ss. and costs or 7 days, and ordered to pay the amount of damage. USING, MALICIOUS THREATS.—James Green, cab driver, Heath-lane, was bound over to keep the peace six months for having, on the 9th inst., made use of malicious threats towards his wife. THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Webster, and Captain Litton. ROBBERIES FROM THE " RAG " MARKET.—Mary Daniels, a married woman, residing at 194, Manchester-road, and Catherine Warren, also a married woman, residing at 14, Robson-street, were charged with stealing from the stall of Isaac Ginsberg, draper, in the Market Place, on Wednesday, a cardigan jacket, value 65., his property, and further, with stealing from the same stall, on Wednesday, the 4th inst., a neck shawl, value is. 6d.—Mrs. Warren was also charged with stealing from the stall of Mary Ann England, on Wed- ' nesday, the 21st December, three-quarters of a yard of velvet, value ls.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for Mrs. Daniels, who pleaded guilty; Mrs. Warren pleaded not guilty.—On Wed- nesday morning, about half-past 11 o'clock, the prisoners went to the prosecutor's stall several times, and on one occasion they were seen to handle a cardigan jacket and asked the price of it. The prosecutor told them the price was els. and they went away. In consequence, however, of what a woman told the market inspector, Mr. Place went to the prisoners and asked to be allowed to examine the basket carried by Mrs. Warren. She declined for some time, but on being pressed consented, and Mr. Place found in the basket the jacket produced. The women were given into the cus- tody of P.C. Clynes who brought them to the police station. On entering the police station, Mrs. Warren said Mrs. Daniels picked the jacket up close to the stall, and gave it to her to put into the basket. The prisoners' houses were afterwards searched, and in that occupied by Mrs. Warren the police found a large quantity of property, which Mr. Hunt said looked very suspicious, and the accounts given respecting some of it were very unsatisfactory.—Alderman Webster said it was very painful to see women like the prisoners in the position they were in, but they felt it was a very serious matter. People must be protected in exhibiting their wares. —Mrs. Daniels: It is very tempting to women to go through that market.—Captain Litton: You have not youth on your side to plead temptation.—Alderman Webster: You must each be imprisoned for two months. AssAtrur.—James Reeves, a wiredrawer, was bound over in his own recognisance of £lO to keep the peace for six months, towards Edward Clive, foreman at Messrs. Smith ' and Son's wireworks. 1 WEAK CASE. Francis Warren, husband of the second prisoner in the last case, was charged with stealing from the factory of Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, Cockhedge, some time during the last two months, about 31bs. of cotton rope, value 35., 11b. of cotton waste, value 3d., and a quan- of screws, value 35., their property.—Mr. Hunt stated the property was found by the police when searching the prisoner's house.—Mr. Brown, manager for Messrs. Armi- tage and Rigby, said the prisoner had been in their employ over six years. He could not swear positively to the rope and screws being their property, but was certain about the waste. He gave the prisoner a very good character.—P.C. , Neil said he found in a bag in the back bedroom banging against the wall, the rope, waste, and a bag. The bag the Prisoner said he found thrown over his wall, the rope he found in the Sixpenny Field, and the waste he had taken bit by bit in his pocket, but the screws he bought in Penketh three years ago.—The prisoner was discharged. ASSAULT BY A HAWKER.—A tall powerful-looking fellow named Joseph Bennett, a hawker, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Orford•street, and with violently assaulting Elizabeth Stead, in Crown-street, on the previous afternoon.—From the evidence it seemed the prisoner had given the woman a number of articles to pawn. When she had pawned them they went to a pnblic-house, and prisoner asked the woman if she would go down the street with him. She consented, and he took her into Crown-street, and made an improper suggestion to her. Ske declined to accede to his request, and the prisoner struck her a blow which knocked her to the ground, and gave her two shocking black eyes. Prisoner was also seen to strike the woman three or four times, one blow sending her head against a window, the sound being distinctly heard by a young man a?,ross the street. A policeman was fetched, and the prisoner was taken into custody by P.C. Clynes, who stated that he was very disorderly on the way to the police station.—Prisoner was committed for one month, with hard

labour. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Alderman Burgess. A PENSIONER AND RIS MONEY.—Elinbeth Bassett, a woman of bad character was charged with stealing about £2 from the person of Michael Connelly. an old pensioner. From the Chief Constable's statement, it appeared the prose- cutor went to the police station on Wednesday, stating he was on his way from Liverpool to London, and wished to leave £2 10s. with the police for safety. He was allowed to do so, and had it returned to him on Thursday morning, when he went to a common lodging house, 18 Hill-street. There, he with a number of other persons, were carousing for several hours after noon, prosecutor paying for the liquor. About four o'clock he went to sleep, and when he awoke at about eight o'clock. a man whom he did not know, seized him by the throat, and held him on the ground, whilst the prisoner rifled his pockets, which contained about £2. Information was given to the police and P.C. Neill went to the house, where prosecutor identified the prisoner as the person who robbed him. The inmates of the house were all drunk. The constable took the prisoner into custody, and at the station she stated she had about Is. 6d. in her pocket, whilst there was over £1 in her pocket, and 4s, 6d. secreted in her stocking.—P.C. James, who had had charge of the prosecutor's money, stated positively that a half-sovereign found on the prisoner, was one which he had on Thurshay handed to the prosecutor. It was desaced on the reverse • side.—Prisoner stated she was innocent of the charge, but failed to account for the money she had in her possession, and she was committed-to gaol for three months with hard labour.

FUSTIAN CUTTERS AND THEIR APPRENTICES.— Ann Bibby (13), apprenticed to Mr. Ockenhallt fustian:cutter, was summoned for unlawfully absenting hers,elf from her work, whereby a claim of Z 1 4s. was made. Defendant had not attended work since November 4th, 1881.—In answer to Mr White (magistrates' clerk), Mr. Ockenhall said the de- fendant was a half-timer, having been apprenticed in May. —The father of the girl said she was a "full-timer," and that Mr. Ockenhall said he would screen her from every- thing.—Mr. Ockenhall denied this, and said it was the fault of the father, who had said the girl had never been to school. —Captain Reynolds said there had clearly been an infringe- ment of the law.—Mr. White said Mr. Ockenhall had, made himself liable to a penalty under the Education Act and the Factory Act. Captain Reynolds : We are not informers here ; but still for all that you stand in a dangerous position. We shall dismiss the case. We cannot deal with it because she has no right to be there.—Mr. Ockenhall: It has been the parents fault.—Alderman Burgess; No, you must not.— Captain Reynolds said before engaging a girl in that manner, he should require proof of her age and position at school. --Patrick Carroll wes summoned for a claim of Li 19s. for unlawfully leaving his work.—An order was made for his return to work, and to pay the claim at is. per week. MAINTENANCE OF PARENTS—Peter Griffiths, captain of a flat, was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute towards the maintenance of his mother Margaret, who is chargable to the common fund of the union. Mr. Shearer represented the Guardians, and asked for an order of 2s. per week. The Bench made an order for is., and told Mr. Shearer to obtain is. from defendant's brother.—A similar order was asked from William Riley in regard to his aged mother, who is in the workhouse. The Bench made an order of is. per week, it having trans- spired that there was another son equally able to pay. • ASSAULT ON A WomAN.—John Price, a joiner, working at Liverpool, was charged, under a warrant, with assaulting Elizabeth Massey, living in Clifton-terrace, Knutsford-road. —Mr. Percy Davies defended.—lt transpired in evidence that the prosecutrix had charge of the defendant's child, his wife having died in September. It had been agreed that he should pay for its maintenance, but he had failed to do so. On Saturday night he came to Warrington, and prosecutrix asked him for some money. He protested that ' "he would not pay a cent.," and violently assaulted her. He kicked her "all down the sides and legs shamefully," and ,[ struck her on the faco.—The case was adjourned for the at- tendance of a witness.—Defendant was released on bail.

COMMENCING HIS MARRIED LIFE. John Houghton, alias Garnett, a blacksmith's striker, was charged, on re- mand, with stealing, from the house of John Barlow, black- smith, Beamont-street, on the 26th December, two cart-arms and bushes, of the value of £2 10s. ; and James Tomlinson, a broker, was charged with stealing, or receiving the articles, knowing them to be stolen.—Mr. Percy Davies defended the prisoner Tomlinson. From the statement of Mr. Hunt, it appeared that P.S. Berry and P.C. Taylor, re- ceived information a short time ago that Tomlinson had had a rather suspicious transaction with Houghton. After in- quiries they discovered that the latter had sold two cart arms and bushes to the former for 10s. ; and also that ley had been stolen from the proseeutor, whose name was on the articles. The prisoners were then apprehended.—Proseeutor identified the articles as his property, and stated he had not sold them.—A wheelwright, named Massey, living in Win- wick-stteet, deposed to purchasing the cart-arms and bushes from Tomlinson for £1 6s. On last Saturday, Houghton went and told him he and another man had stolen them, and asked for them to be returned. In consequence, witness saw Tom- linson, who owned that the property had been stolen, and agreed to take it back, telling witness that if ques- tioned concerning the robbery, he must "know nothing about it." He promised, and on the Monday following in- formed the police.—Alfred Blinstone, and P.S. Berry were also examined. When charged in the presence e Tomlin- son, Houghton said 'Yes. I took them to the old brewery. I afterwards told Tomlinson, who helped me to carry them to his house, and he paid me a half a sovereign for them. I was going to get married, and wanted some money. On Mon- day last, I saw Tomlinson' who took me into Kenyon's and gave me a glass of beer. I told him I wanted the arras back. He refused, and wanted to know if there was any bother." Tomlinson stated that he gave Houghton £1 for the arms.— In answer to Captain Reynolds, Houghton said he had since" been married.—Botk prisoners were committed for trial at the quarter sessions.

div.head: MR. 61ADSTONE ON THE COMING SESSION.
div.p: MR. 61ADSTONE ON THE COMING SESSION.

Mr. Gladstone made an interesting speech on Thursday, on the occasion of the recent audit dinner at Hawarden. He addressed himself first to the position of the farming class since the adoption of Free Trade in this country, showing that the change was followed by a quarter of a century of unprecedented prosperity to agriculture, as evidenced by the almost general advance in the prices of produce. He warned them against looking for a remedy for the depres- sion of late years to a return to Protection. He thought, however, that most of the farmers of this country were too sensible to be likely to share in any of the gross delusions which some persons were holding up as remedies for their sufferings, which were due to bad seasons and the bad trade of this country. The right hon. gentle- man reminded his hearers that a period like that through which they had passed produced benefits by leading them to examble into their position. Referring to the question of rents, he thought that was a matter which in this country would be settled by the natural operation of supply and demand. He did not believe that it was desired by the farmers any more than it was by the landlords that any court should determine how much rent should be paid. But changes would have to be made in the land laws of this country. The transfer of land ought to be a great deal more free and easy and cheap and rapid than it is. (Applause.) Then land ought likewise to be relieved from many restraints that affect it. These were steps in which he believed the tenants had a very consider- able interest,lbut still it was an interest less direct than the interest they felt in many matters which now press upon them. The relation of landlord and tenant was not sufficiently provided for by law. (Applause.) An attempt was made—no doubt it was very well meant—some years ago, which resulted in what was called the Agricultural Holdings Act. That Act excited no interest whatever in this part of the country. It was not found available for dealing in any satisfactory manner with the relations of landlord and tenant. He did not think it would be possible for him to enter into the details of that subject, but he ex- pressed confidentially the belief, that they would find no in- disposition whatever on the part of the present Parliament to adopt the best, fullest, and most effective measures for securing the legitimate interests of the cultivators of the land. They knew very well in this country that so far as regarded reasonable permanency of tenure there never had been any want, at least so far as his recollection went back, on these properties in giving leases to the tenants, but there had been no general disposition to take them, and at present he did not suppose, under the existing state of agricultural relations, any one was greatly looking for them; but whether it be by leases or whether it be by security of the unexhausted improvements of the tenant, or whether it be by any other means, he gave a confident opinion that they would have nothing to complain on the part of the existing Parliament as to its willingness to do what was just and reasonable. (Applaese.) There was a subject which must come before Parliament in the session about to com- mence in which they had a great interest, and that was the local government of counties. Provision had been made for local government upon representative principles in the towns and cities of the country, but it had not yet been made in the counties. (Hear, hear.) The desire of the present Administration was to propose a thoroughly efficient measure of local government which should give to the in- habitants of the counties an effective power of controlling the county expenditure with the same principles of freedom and of representative government which belongs to our central Legislature, and those principles should be carried into effect under the local government of rural districts just as much as it was now in the cities of the country. (Ap- plause.) There was another subject upon which they would no doubt wish to hear what be had to say. What was to be done for them with respect to assisting local taxation from Imperial sources? The Government was most desirous that they should have, in the first place, the means of controlling local expenditure and authority over the sources from which local taxes were raised; that they should have the means of con- trolling expenditure, and that the means should be so arranged as to give no temptation to waste, but that they should have every inducement to economise the outlay of money. It was a very important question whether, and in what measure, in what degree, they should receive assis- tance from the Imperial exchequer. They received a great deal of assistance now, but in his opinion in a bad form— the police of the country, the gaols of the country. These expenditures were borne either entirely or in part, and some of the poor-law charges were borne either entirely or in part, by the exchequer of the country, but they were borne in such a way as in general not .to contribute to economy, in such a way as to induce a gi'eat deal, and, as he thought, probably too much, of central interference or what was called centralisation in the local government, and rather to draw them away from the old principle of English institu- tions which lay at the very root of them—namely. the principle that local populations shoald have the mauage- ment and control of local affairs. (Applause.)

div.head: Xetter to the editor.
div.p: Xetter to the editor.
TRE RESTORATION OF ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.

Sir,—l don't wish to grumble, but I would like to call the attention of the parties concerned, to a heap of dirt outside the church gates, which is extremely dangerous to passers by, especially at night. Last Sunday evening, upon reach- ing this spot, I stumbled over this heap and fell full length, and as the ground was wet I was in a pitiable plight. I understand that I am by no means the only one who has come in contact with this obstruction. I should be sorry to see the authorities troubled with claims for dama- gee, therefore, I would advise them to clear the way.—Yours, truly A SUFFERER.
A sliding scale, characterised by mutual con cessions on the part of the employers and the employed, has been agreed upon in connection with the payment of wages in tha Cleve- land iron trade.

Following the recent strike in the Staffordshire Potteries, a scheme has been set on foot for establishing pottery works in the district on the co-operative principle, in which only shareholders will be employed.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday afternoor. Major Cross occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. Carey, Brown, Pankhurst, Heyes, Ga.skell, Handley', Foster, Matthews, Kershaw, Shuttleworth, Sadler, Allen (clerk), Roberts (engineer), Higginson (surveyor)/ and
Dickson (nuisance inspector.) THE DISPUTE WITH THE NEWTON BUILDING SOCIETY. ,

The following letter was read : "Local Government Board, Whitehall, 27th December, i88t1,; —Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board tir e that they have under their consideration the report of tshec inspector, Mr. Harrison, made after his enquiry with referreinn to the appeal of the Newton. Haydock, and Golborne Pe nent Benefit Building Society, against the demand of Widnes Local Board for the payment of certain Privatteionied provement expenses. The amounts originally appor appear to have included certain items for interest and establily_ ment charges. It seems to the Board that the items n'!ce))l interest were improperly included, as the only interest w for the L -cal Board are empowered to charge is that provided the establishment charges, the Board consider thain section 257 of the Public Health Act, 1875, while as regarre t no in°. , than 21 percent. on the cost of the actual worhs for the suPteh'e vision of them during their execution, should be charged to owners. The Board are not aware of any objection to the otheel charges made by the Local Board. Calculated nixnl the rid duced basis above indicated, the amount which should be by the Building Society is apparently £l3B 165. 7c1., belp,ri; £6l 2s. 4d. in respect of Bank-street, and £77 11s. 3d. in res,P„—ne of Oakland-street. The Board will, therefore, proceed an order requiring the society to pay the sum of £l3B 18s. c the Local Board.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, ROTTEN, Assistant Secretary."

A NEW YEA.R OF HAPPINESS. • THE Year Eighteen Hundred and Eighty-One has passed away unto the limbo of departed years, and one more is placed on the shelf—ticked off on the roll of Chronology, with its obstruction—Bradlaugh and bad trade, Parnell and Forster, Transvaal muddle and Mother Shipton's unfulfilled prediction. Eighteen Hundred and Eighty-Two opens with brighter hopes of returning commercial prosperity, peace abroad and remunerative employment for the people at home. The GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY enter on their fifth year of war against big profits; and they are pleased to recognize the substantial support they have received from the working classes—the class which bentfits most by the Grand Clothing Hall Com- pany's system of selling only their own Manufacture of Goods at a fair profit; and what they mean by a fair profit is not the 50 to 150 per cent. charged by Credit Tailors, but a mere fraction over the prime cost of production, to cover working expenses. A large turn over at a small profit is the aim of the Grand Clothing Hall Company; •and they cannot, neither do they desire t). boast of the enormous profit they have made, but that they have sold more Clothing, and given better value, and saved the pockets of the people more than was ever known in Warrington.
